op:Lib.image.analyze.CompareImages.note: Use it as a reference overlay: it slices through two images so you can eyeball how your build matches a target's color distribution side by side.
Load a reference photo and put it side-by-side (or wipe) against your render to rebuild a look methodically — the core technique for learning by reproducing an image.
Wire two variants in for a split-screen A/B so you can see side-by-side how a change (e.g. base-color tweak) alters the bloom result.

op:Lib.io.video.PlayVideo.note: Load a downloaded MP4 as a moving reference clip to scrub and study frame by frame while rebuilding it.

Why the Media-Foundation backend can't prefetch, cache, or change playback speed and always lags keyframe animation by a few frames; the motivation for moving to an FFmpeg/libav decoder that keeps frames on the GPU.
Drop a video into the project's resource folder and it appears instantly in the file picker, ready to scrub — the workflow for using footage as a live source.

op:Lib.point.generate.LinePoints.note: Wire [LinePoints] into [RepeatAtPoints] to clone one line across a set of positions; on its own the copies stack invisibly until you give them spread and orientation.
A line of points, randomized and colored from a gradient, stands in for a row of lights to preview Artnet output before any hardware is connected.
Emitting from a line into a particle system is the minimal starting point for a falling-spray effect; pair it with a draw operator and an orbit camera before adding any forces.
Audio-bars/frequency-modulation effect: sample a rendered texture's brightness into point X offsets, then repeat a single line across a 16×9 grid so each line displaces by the image under it.
Lines are centred by convention, so zero the pivot to make a generated strand actually reach outward from its anchor instead of straddling it.
A quick emitter for shooting particles at a surface: rotate its direction to vertical and flip the initial velocity so points stream onto the collider face you want.

Combining two line sources — one with start/end colors, one slid through a color gradient — then layering a noise offset whose amount you crank via the infinity slider, since leaving point counts unmatched lets the offset bite.
Listed among operators that gained the bias-and-gain control to reshape their output distribution or response.
How fully procedural point setups replace heavy meshes in demos: nesting line chains, alternating 180° rotations, and swaying them through a noise field.

op:Lib.point.generate.RepeatAtPoints.note: Wire [LinePoints] into [RepeatAtPoints] to clone one line across a set of positions; on its own the copies stack invisibly until you give them spread and orientation.
The orientation axis decides which way the copies fan out; switch it (e.g. to Y) and raise the count so stacked duplicates spread into a usable grid of lines.
Audio-bars/frequency-modulation effect: sample a rendered texture's brightness into point X offsets, then repeat a single line across a 16×9 grid so each line displaces by the image under it.
Drive many IK chains at once by repeating one line-point chain over a [RadialPoints] ring; you must set "points per chain" to the chain length and strip the separator points.

Clone one point set onto every point of another to get spiral/sunflower layouts; because the clones live in each target's local space, a [TransformPoints] offset slides them along their host ring rather than in world space.
Replicate a small point cluster at each of a few base points; randomize the cluster after repeating (not before) so the copies differ instead of looking identical.
Add synonyms like "copy", "replicate", "instance" to an operator's description so search finds it under everyday terms, not just its technical name.
How a compute-shader scatter repeats a *prebuilt point cluster* (here a set of digit glyphs) at each target point, so each target becomes a copy of the whole sub-mesh rather than a single dot.

op:Lib.point.transform.TransformPoints.note: Pair a point selection with a transform so a squeeze only affects points inside the selected volume, leaving the rest untouched.
Scale instances by transforming in point space, not object space — scaling in object space squashes the whole cloud toward the origin instead of resizing each instance in place.
Stretching point sprites via a point-space transform (scale/stretch) is far more efficient than scaling the drawn geometry, which wastes transparent pixels.
After snapping points to a surface, move them forward in their own point space (or scale them) to extend reach-lines out from the contact point.
Apply a move/rotate to every point but scale it by the F1 factor so only masked points actually shift — the canonical "modify only the selection" pattern.

Why rotating points around an axis seems to do nothing at the origin: scale→rotate→translate order means object-space rotation has no visible effect until you offset the center; converting to a single quaternion matrix also prevents multi-turn (helix) results.

Adding a universal strength factor by lerping every modified field (position, scale via lerp, rotation via spherical quaternion lerp, F1/F2) against the original by a strength parameter, so any effect can fade in or be exaggerated/negated from a neutral default of 1.
Drive its strength factor from an F-attribute set by a sphere SDF selection so the rotation/translation only applies to points inside the field region.
Select points by a plane SDF and use the selection attribute as a per-point strength factor in a transform, so only points to one side of the plane get squished or rotated.

Clone one point set onto every point of another to get spiral/sunflower layouts; because the clones live in each target's local space, a [TransformPoints] offset slides them along their host ring rather than in world space.
Translating in point space rather than object space, then rotating, multiplies the visual complexity of an overlapping-shape pattern far beyond what an object-space move gives.
Stack one on a warp's corner points to nudge an edge outward for curved or lattice-style surfaces when the flat four-point fit isn't enough.
Use object/point space and push along local Z (the surface normal) to lift scattered labels off the mesh they sit on.
Centre-facing orientation gives each point a slightly different angle; for clean screen-aligned labels you want them parallel to the camera *view axis*, not pointed at the camera position.

op:Lib.point.modify.SelectPoints.note: Pair a point selection with a transform so a squeeze only affects points inside the selected volume, leaving the rest untouched.
Switch the volume shape from sphere to plane and rotate it to get a directional falloff band; the bias softens the selection edge for a smoother transition.
Writes a 0..1 selection state into each point's W attribute based on a region, so a single operator can mask which instances react downstream.
Enable its gizmo to drag the selection region through the cloud live; scale, stretch and rotate the region to reshape what gets selected.
Falloff softens the selection edge and the region shape can switch between sphere, box and a noise field for organic masks.
Drive the noise-shape phase from a time source so the selection field animates on its own.
Chain multiple selections, multiplying or adding their W contributions to compose complex masks.

Write a 0/1 mask into F1/F2 from whether a point sits inside a shape; the SDF variant binds the test to any distance field (a torus, noise-displaced) instead of the legacy fixed sphere, making it far more expressive as a selector.
The bare select-points op is legacy with no description; prefer the SDF-based selector instead.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawLines.note: Disable "use selection for width" so a selection drives the deformation but not the rendered line thickness.

A new fade-out-if-too-long length cutoff gives a near-free Plexus-style effect: scatter PointsOnMesh, raise the count, and hide long connections so only short links between nearby points survive (also culled cheaply via alpha).
Driving line thickness from the per-point F1 factor adds weight variation to a line field.
A fade-out-long-lines parameter cleanly suppresses stretched links, great for plexus-style effects.
Hold Ctrl while picking a color to push values past 1.0 into HDR, so lines read as glowing emitters once a bloom pass is added.

Connecting a small point set draws one continuous polyline through all points; reach for it over [DrawRayLines] when you want the points linked in sequence, and use the fade/length-cutoff to hide the wrap-around segment.

Under the hood it is a Bresenham-style rasterized line done in the vertex shader, almost a geometry shader; the genuinely tricky cost is corner mitering, which has no one-size solution and is deliberately not exposed.
Provides corner point sets (cube/cross/quad) for repeating geometry or drawing wireframe cages; build a grid by combining offset line points and rotating a copy 90°.

Closed-loop line drawing needs awkward extra separator points and breaks one corner; motivates a dedicated closed-line operator that takes points-per-shape as a parameter so repeated shapes (triangles, quads, stars) close cleanly.
Rendering a LineTextPoints buffer as strokes is what makes the text usable for transitions and texture-emit tricks, since you then own the raw line geometry.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawRibbons.note: It needs correctly oriented points: if ribbons come out twisted, rotate the source points' orientation (about 90°) so the flat side faces the camera.
For shaded lines, extruding a curve into a mesh is the expensive route; draw-ribbons is the lighter option but is flagged as currently unreliable, with spin/pin parameters affecting the result.
How fully procedural point setups replace heavy meshes in demos: nesting line chains, alternating 180° rotations, and swaying them through a noise field.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetMaterial.note: Set the base color to a gradient and rotate it 90° to shade ribbons across their width instead of along their length.
The standard lighting trio for an SDF scene: add a point light, set a not-too-glossy material, and swap the default studio environment for black to control reflections.
When two combined fields disagree on material the result is undefined, so push a single material below the combine to cover both; its color input wants a color field, not a raw shape.
Works on both meshes and SDFs; lowering glossiness moves a surface from shiny toward a frosted matte look, and bypassing it shows the bare default shading underneath.
In a stack the last material wins: evaluation is pull-based from the output backwards, so a material lower (later) in the stack overrides earlier ones — set a default then override one object.
Assigning a very bright material early so an object reads as a light-emitter once glow post-processing is added.
Pair a material with an environment so the surface picks up image-based lighting from a surrounding texture instead of looking flat.
A faint dark-blue emissive on a neutral material reads as distant water — a small emissive tint shifts perceived color without lighting the scene.
A collision force can stamp a material color on impact, so coloring the collider white and the base plane another color gives foam-on-contact tinting you can invert to taste.
Roughness controls how much of the environment a PBR surface reflects; with a black environment there's nothing to reflect, so highlights vanish.
A quick ray-march scene: feed it an SDF field and set a hard, glossy material to get a clean reflective sphere to test variable-driven parameters against.
Drive emissive color plus a high luminance (e.g. 10) for a self-lit glowing surface, or lower roughness and raise metalness for a reflective metal look.
A per-surface roughness/anti-artifact factor can't easily live here because the material is carried in a shared PBR buffer that's painful to merge — better placed on the drawing operator.

op:Lib.point.modify.SetPointAttributes.note: Spreads a gradient's colors across all points in a buffer so a color ramp maps onto a line set as a per-point attribute.
The repeat mapping mode tiles the gradient across the points, so a narrow range becomes a repeating banded pattern you can scroll.
Animate the gradient phase by linking it to time with a slow preset, then enable background motion to preview the looping crawl.
Smooth interpolation plus an asymmetric range gives a directional ramp — a sharp edge on one side, soft on the other — instead of a symmetric band.
Write a 0 and a 1 onto the two endpoint sets so a per-point factor (noise amount) interpolates smoothly along a strand instead of stepping.
Carries a rotation/axis field you can use to override per-point orientation instead of computing it from velocity.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.AnimValue.note: Drive a phase value from an oscillator instead of raw time so you can shape (e.g. to a sine) and slow the repeating pattern's movement.
Zero out unwanted axes of the amplitude so an oscillation moves cleanly along one direction, and set the shape to sine for a slow, gradual back-and-forth.
Drop it onto a parameter for keyframe-free motion: it oscillates at a rate (e.g. 120 BPM) and its shape can switch from a pulse to a back-and-forth ramp.
Break a size or transform value out into an animated driver and feed a wave so the parameter pulses without manual keyframes.
Typed as "AV" to wire an animated value onto a parameter, then a wave-shape preset chosen to drive it.
Driving a periodic value into a metaball-style radius demonstrates beat-synced animation once a network clock source is connected.
Override playback time from a sampled ramp so a simulated IO clip loops on its own clock — note simulated event data replays this way but audio clips, living in a separate update loop, will not.

op:Lib.image.use.BlendWithMask.note: Feed a [LinearGradient] as the mask to make blur fall off across the frame; align the gradient angle (here ~131°) and use ping-pong to blur both edges while keeping the center sharp.
A favorite for compositing two images through a mask channel, useful for layering a keyed result over a background.
To layer a logo over the effect, wire the background to the first input and the logo to the second; an already-connected input is what blocks a re-plug.
Pairing a blurred copy with a mask texture is reached for as a quick, reliable way to add a soft glow pass over a rendered scene. (speaker says "blur with mask")
Mask a blur with a low-res [RadialGradient] so only the frame center softens, faking a radial/zoom blur cheaply; bias-and-gain tunes the masked edge. (speaker: "blur with mask")
Use plain [Blend] when you just want A over B; reach for the mask variant only when a separate image should gate where the blend happens.
Crossfade two scenes by masking with a [RadialGradient]; set the gradient interpolation to smooth so the wipe's starting circle stops being a visible hard ring.

op:Lib.image.generate.basic.LinearGradie.note: Feed a [LinearGradient] as the mask to make blur fall off across the frame; align the gradient angle (here ~131°) and use ping-pong to blur both edges while keeping the center sharp.
Sample colours straight off a reference with Alt-click to recreate its background; flip the gradient direction if the picked endpoints come out reversed.
Generate a band with an offset and width you animate, then use it as the wipe mask that reveals a logo over time.
Stack two color fields and combine them as a proper multiply (not an alpha crossfade) to layer gradients for a scrolling color-cycle look.
Drives a mask or tint input by feeding a gradient ramp that you rotate and reposition to sweep the effect across the frame.
Stuff one into a point's texture input to shade the sprite from bright front to soft tail; combine via a blend's alpha channel to carve a rounded-capsule particle shape.
Beyond the default linear ramp, switch its interpolation to smooth for visibly softer transitions between stops.
A spline interpolation mode lets you hand-tune the ramp shape between stops for very fine gradient control.
Size-mode "align to height" vs. "align to width" decides which axis the gradient spans as the canvas aspect changes; align-to-height keeps a circle drawn over it perfectly round at any resolution.

Sample separate color channels of a scrolling ping-pong gradient to drive different point transforms at once (red to Z-offset, green to rotation); switch its interpolation from linear to smooth to kill the stepped, non-moving look.
Use it as an editable displacement curve — pick a preset, switch interpolation to smooth for a clean wave, and animate its offset since it's just a texture.
Use a gradient as a line texture and drive its lookup from a UV/attribute (with wrap mode and an animated offset) to render scrolling dashed lines; make it HDR so bloom makes the dashes glow.

Renaming a gradient input on an operator that exposes a gradient (a reference-typed value) crashes the symbol update; rename it in the code/source instead. Also: apply contrast as gain-then-bias, matching this operator as the canonical reference.

op:Lib.image.analyze.ImageLevels.note: Drop it into a chain to read the average brightness/histogram of the current image, useful for judging how close to HDR your output is.
An "energy levels" analysis overlay that slices the image at a movable line and plots the colour there; a blinking warning marks where brightness clips and that highlight detail is lost for good.

Inspect an image's brightness histogram to tell whether transparent regions sit on black or white; that hidden base color decides how bloom/glow spreads and why two visually identical logos bloom differently.
Drop it on an image to read the live color distribution of a buffer slice; pushing brightness up makes it flag where channels clamp, useful for spotting blown-out grades.
Reads out the actual intensity along a slice as a graph overlay, a quick way to verify whether a gradient really reaches 0 and 1 or is clipped short.
Briefly used to inspect the smooth falloff of a blurred mask before converting it to a normal map.
Slide its slice to read an image's actual brightness distribution and discover a "white" sprite is really ~75–85% gray, or that a gray image carries a slight tint.
Drag the level down to isolate a mid threshold, then widen it to expand a blurred mask — a quick way to turn a soft image into a controllable cutoff.
An over-bright HDR background (values ~6×) defeats the anti-aliasing when you blend lines on top; re-bloom then tone-map back under 1.0 so the composite edges resolve instead of fringing.

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.Glow.note: It barely glows until the source is actually HDR: push a color's brightness above 1 (Ctrl-drag the color past white) and the glow then spreads that over-bright energy across the image.
Beyond intensity, its glow-gradient knob colour-tints the bloom by brightness, letting the bright core read one hue and the soft falloff another.
A restrained post chain — screen-space occlusion plus bloom and glow, no color grade — is enough to finish a procedural scene.
Its default strength is deliberately very intense, so expect to dial it down — this is what makes bright/emissive materials bloom.
Adds the HDR bloom that makes emissive surfaces bleed light; ease the amount back so highlights glow without blowing out.
Glow on a transparent image clamps and smears at the frame edge when artwork runs to the border; fix it upstream by giving the image empty margin (Crop with negative/expand values) before glowing.

op:Lib.render.basic.Layer2d.note: Composite a soft glowing shape over a scene by scaling a [Layer2d] down and feeding it a [RoundedRect]; crank feathering and tune the aspect ratio for the shape you need.
Add a second texture output to a wrapped operator (right-click → add output, set type to texture), then a 2D layer lets you place that rendered image as a plane in 3D space.
It draws a texture as a camera-facing quad whose aspect follows the texture's own resolution, so a screen-in-scene squashes when the canvas changes unless you pin the source to a fixed resolution.
Skip clearing the target each frame to accumulate a cheap trailing-history "motion blur"; reintroduce a near-transparent clear layer to slowly fade old frames instead of letting them stick forever.

op:Lib.image.generate.basic.RoundedRect.note: Composite a soft glowing shape over a scene by scaling a [Layer2d] down and feeding it a [RoundedRect]; crank feathering and tune the aspect ratio for the shape you need.
Used as a quick environment/HDRI stand-in; give it fixed resolution so its aspect ratio doesn't follow the output window and warp the lighting.
Roundness 1 turns the rect into a circle and stroke-only (no fill/background) gives a ring; enabling its mip-map generation is what fixes the shimmer when the shape is later minified by a camera.

op:Lib.numbers.color.SampleGradient.note: Sample a gradient from a moving value to tie an element's brightness to its position — dark at the extremes, bright in the middle — though it expects a scalar, not a vec2.
Named while wiring per-fixture colors so each light samples its hue from a gradient along the point set.
A new interpolation-override lets you force linear vs. spline blending instead of inheriting it from the gradient type, decoupling output interpolation from the source.
Reads a color out of a gradient at a given position, so you define start/end colors once and then drive the read-out position to sweep through them.
Remap particle lifetime through a white→blue gradient to color the spray by age without a separate color operator.
Look up a per-point color from a gradient by an attribute value, so a palette (e.g. a themed ramp) colorizes the whole point set in one step.
A first points lesson wires a 3D noise into a point's position and a gradient sample into its color/size, demonstrating that point attributes are just inputs you connect like any other.
Reading a beat-synced progress value into it produces a color that cycles in time with the music.
Feed a stepping index into a gradient sampler to flash a new color on every beat, e.g. as an animated clear color.

Inside a custom shader, sample the operator's gradient input by a float coordinate so an exposed parameter slides the sampling point along the ramp, and that parameter can be keyframed or driven by an external value.
Map a beat-synced phase value through a gradient into a colour for an on-beat flash; reversing the gradient flips the attack/decay feel.
Feed particle age (fx1) into a gradient whose first stop is a sharp bright spike then quick decay, so each particle flashes at birth and dims over its life.
Inside a custom point shader, sample a gradient by the field's signed distance (`field.w`) and write it to point colour — distance-banded colouring straight from an SDF.

op:Lib.image.color.RemapColor.note: Maps an image's tonal range onto a gradient (black→left, white→right) and clamps at 1, so it fits LDR/after-glow stages but not HDR; Alt-pick colors straight from a reference image to match its palette.
A glue op between an input texture and a gradient: switch to spline interpolation and insert handles to reshape contrast like a Photoshop curves adjustment.
Pair it with a spline gradient to apply Photoshop-style curve corrections to an image, from subtle grades to extreme remaps.
Maps each input colour through a gradient per-channel or in grayscale; a hold-interpolated step makes a threshold, and its own gain/bias positions where that threshold falls.
Recolour a displacement/glitch pass into a single tint (black-to-orange) before blending it back over the original.
Paired color-adjustment operators that benefit from bias-and-gain; the larger one now does color cycling for generated effects.

Maps image brightness onto a gradient (reverse it to invert the picture); the deeper value is the bias/gain, cycle and over-cycle knobs plus parameter presets that turn one operator into many distinct looks.

op:Lib.point.modify.ResampleLinePoints.note: Smooths a line by re-distributing points along it, but it doesn't handle multiple disconnected line segments — they get mangled, so it's unsuitable for a repeated multi-line set.
Line-point bias/gain shapes uneven segment spacing along a chain (longer joint at one end), shaping how an IK limb tapers. (speaker: "bias and gain on the line points")

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.ChromaticAbberat.note: Add it for a subtle lens fringe; the presets are the quick way to find a distortion look before fine-tuning size.
A final color-fringing pass at the edges to lend the rendered image a lens-like finish.

op:Lib.point.generate.RadialPoints.note: Substituted for a grid of points to fan instances around a ring; widening its radius spreads the scattered shapes into new arrangements.
A ring of emit points, color-mapped through a gradient, as the seed for ribbon particles.
Unlike LinePoints or GridPoints it lacked a per-point color; the F1/F2 factor-plus-offset pair (also discussed here) drives a value range along the radius that turned out useful for many setups.
Distribute N points evenly on a ring around a driver point; disable "close the circle" to avoid a duplicate seam point when you need exactly N.
A second, smaller ring of points around a leg tip becomes a grippable claw when meshed with a cylinder and twisted.
A closed ring aligned to the up axis becomes a horizon/constellation circle the camera can orbit through.
Reuse one scaled radial ring as a reusable sub-pattern, re-centering and re-scaling copies to nest smaller circles inside larger ones.
Dropping the ring count to 2 and back up turns a constellation into Arabic-lattice / mashrabiya tiling — a hint that a dedicated circle-pattern operator with presets would be handy.
Source of a ring of points that gets noise-displaced and used to scatter mesh instances.
Listed among operators that gained the bias-and-gain control to reshape their output distribution or response.

Insert extra in-between points along a sparse line (e.g. a three-point ring) so the shape has enough density to deform smoothly afterward; pair it with a close-shape flag when the source loops back on itself.

Its default orientation (Z kept, X pointing radially outward) is one of several valid 90°-rotated choices; the chosen convention is why points twist unexpectedly once a particle system reorients them.
Animating the side count gives shape morphs, but to keep the shape top-aligned you must also animate the start angle — the radius/angle params are coupled for alignment.

op:Lib.point.modify.AddNoise.note: Perturbing a point buffer's positions is what turns a clean generated layout into something organic; insert it mid-chain like a geometry-node step.
Drive noise strength by a per-point attribute (0→1 along a strand) so displacement grows toward the tip, giving a tapered organic wiggle.

Most point modifiers expose a strength plus an F1/F2 picker that defaults to 1 (a neutral factor); pick F1 to gate the displacement per-point by a mask written upstream, or drive the noise amount from it.
Stacking it on a point set after a field selection lets the selection attribute scale the noise amount, so displacement is strong near a centre and fades outward.
Why you subdivide a line first: noise displacement only bites where there are points, so a low-vertex outline must be densified before [AddNoise] can roughen it.
Layer a little animated noise on top of a finished look to break up flatness, driving its phase with a time value.

op:Lib.point.combine.CombineBuffers.note: A short tip showing that each point operator emits its own GPU point buffer, and how keeping the original and modified buffers around lets you wire them together — pairing positions to draw lines, then scattering meshes across the same points.
Merge several point sets into one buffer so an entire constellation draws in a single draw call instead of many.

ui:EvaluationContext.note: A video with a large GOP (group-of-pictures > ~100) seeks slowly; re-encoding it with small GOP in the background fixes scrubbing at the cost of file size.
Why TiXL splits work CPU-side (positions, sizes, names, file loading) from GPU-side (the buffers and textures it generates), and what that division costs you in flexibility.
What the Z-buffer is: a depth buffer parallel to the colour buffer that decides per-pixel whether something is drawn based on its distance from the camera plane.
Refactoring a graph criss-crossed with long connections into per-frame context variables (booleans, ints, vectors) set once up front and read wherever needed downstream.
A camera reference passed by id through the evaluation context lets distant operators read the same camera without a direct wire — the basis for keeping a projector and the main view in sync.

When two consumers both pull the same sub-scene, it can be evaluated twice per frame; operators update in the order their inputs are declared, so declaration order decides whether one path sees last frame's result and lags by a frame.

Why a per-shader time constant buffer breaks multi-pass effects: a node like [RenderWithMotionBlur] renders several sub-frames that each need their own time, so reading time from the shared evaluation context rather than a baked constant is the robust choice.

How requested resolution flows: a node writes the target size into the evaluation context, and any image op asking for 0×0 resolution falls back to that requested value — the hook for overriding output size downstream.

The recurring camera-sync bug: when the projector camera and the view camera update at different times, the shadow map ends up rendered with last frame's camera and misaligns with the texture — the core hazard of cross-referencing cameras.

Effects should cache to a static image when nothing animates; connecting any animated parameter (even from a static gradient that's being dragged) breaks the cache and forces per-frame re-render, so watch for effects that fail to fade-out (the cached indicator).
Disable the depth (Z) test on a draw call to stack a layer purely by render order — useful for fake shadows or screen-space overlays that must ignore scene depth.

The pull model that drives everything: data wires point toward the output, but evaluation starts at the pinned output and walks backwards, each operator reading time, resolution, camera, material and light from a shared context it must restore afterward.
Why a static node renders dimmed/cached and only goes opaque while recomputing: an output that never changes is cached and costs no shader load until a parameter forces re-evaluation.

Parameter-input smoothing (default ~6 frames) softens every knob change, so changing a time-evaluated animation's rate "jumps" to where it should be — smoothing can't fix it because the value isn't accumulated.
A faded-out branch's per-frame CPU cost drops almost to nothing because it's no longer evaluated, but its cached buffers stay resident — the RAM it holds is not freed.

ui:Graph.note: The three operator output colours encode where data lives: a texture lives on the GPU and is regenerated each time you modify it, a buffer is an opaque GPU pointer you can't read back but can draw from, and a green node is a draw/command. Knowing the colour tells you what an output can and can't do.

The magnetic graph: long-press selects a single op, long-press-and-drag plus a shake disconnects it, and dropping a node near a connection snaps it into a vertical stacked batch — clicking a stacked node then drags the whole stack.

A disconnected operator costs nothing — TiXL ignores anything not wired into the graph, so duplicating (Ctrl+D pastes at the mouse) a material as a safety copy has zero performance impact until you drag it into the stack.

A multi-input (the angled socket) accepts any number of connections shown as blinking insertion points; wiring the same object twice into a group renders it twice, e.g. to build up opacity on a transparent object.

Z-fighting (flickering where two coplanar surfaces meet) and its fixes: nudge one slightly up, or disable the depth test — but with the test off the object draws regardless of depth, so you must reorder it in the group's multi-input to control what ends up on top.
In a code operator you can override how inputs update; otherwise inputs evaluate strictly top-to-bottom in declaration order, which is what introduces a one-frame delay between dependent branches.
The magnetic graph lets you grab and reorder aligned nodes without a hotkey — snap connections by lining nodes up, a workflow worth a dedicated tutorial.
A non-obvious copy shortcut in the graph: single-click to grab a node's value/expression, then Ctrl+N to spin it into a new node — handy when refactoring inline code.
Control+Shift+D duplicates with connections, correctly handling multi-inputs, and shaking an operator out now reconnects all compatible inputs rather than just the first.
Horizontal snapping (Alt+A) aligns operators so the connection-line router knows they're related and keeps parallel wires from overlapping — subtle but it cleans up tangled graphs.
Image-comparison unit tests render convoluted scenes and flag a failure when output drifts; run them before each commit to catch rendering regressions across the PBR paths.
A fully static subtree caches and costs nothing; selecting an operator invalidates it (params might change) and breaks the cache, so deselect to let scenes settle.
Node text blurs when zoomed because ImGui draws every glyph as a textured quad from a fixed font atlas (only four font sizes); a future 2D-SDF font shader would make it crisp.
The whole composition is one node graph you freely arrange operators on, then dive into sub-graphs; framed for someone coming from layer-based tools.
Operators no longer auto-disconnect when dragged out of a group (it broke graphs too often); you can still reorder within vertical/horizontal stacks, with connections temporary during the drag.
You can finally drag vertical connection lines, and connections about to be replaced now blink red before you drop.
Thumbnails now show on every connection (even snapped-in ones), toggled by the toolbar preview button; horizontal snapping is on by default.
How a GPU buffer-copy node graph differs from CPU geometry nodes: some ops are far faster on the GPU, but certain operations stay hard there, so the trade-off flips per task.
A maintainer's pull-request review workflow: small diff + operators-only changes (no editor/core) means low blast radius and a quick merge.
Right-click "select connected ops" gathers everything wired to a node, making it easy to duplicate a whole sub-network as a backup before refactoring.

The node-drawing routine is large because one method decides, per node, which connection lines are visible, whether to show a dot or a thumbnail or labels, and whether corners round — all the per-node visual state lives in that single draw method.
Custom node UIs are checked first; only when a node has none does the drawing fall through to the generic thumbnail/preview path.
Node previews are deliberately dropped below a zoom threshold to save draw calls, which is what lets very large graphs stay responsive when fully zoomed out.

With hot code reload you can edit the live node-draw method and, when a node has no current texture, fall back to a stored thumbnail looked up by the symbol's id and package — the returned rect reports whether the thumbnail is ready before you try to draw it.
In a vertical operator stack you can long-press-drag a member out of the chain, or drop a new one between two blinking insert lines to control exactly where in the render order it lands.
Roadmap preview: the magnetic-graph system shown last year is slated for integration to make patching snappier and more live.
Cleanup workflow: "select connected" to isolate a branch, group into a named [Group] or lighter [Execute] (used purely for labeling), or combine into a new symbol while keeping the output connection.
You can't keyframe a node's bypass/enable directly; the simplest workaround is driving an effect's strength to its neutral value (0) rather than toggling the node.
Lay post-processing chains out as vertical stacks for readability, and don't cram operators into tight gaps just because they snap — your future self has to read it.

op:Lib.render.transform.Transform.note: Drop a transform into a sub-graph to reposition and scale an element independently before animating it.
Continuously rotate a scene by feeding [Time] into one rotation axis, avoiding the gimbal-lock you hit when animating the camera directly.
Sits on a point branch so its rotation can be animated externally, turning a static cloud into one that slowly tumbles.
Render one scene twice with offset clocks: duplicate the group, feed each copy a different time so the same deterministic animation appears at two phases at once.

op:Lib.mesh.draw.DrawMeshAtPoints.note: Scatter a mesh (here a cylinder as a sprinkle) across a point set; it's the auto-suggested op when you connect points to a mesh, and it instances the geometry at every position.
Swap raw points for actual geometry by instancing a mesh at every point; the point set supplies position while a separate mesh input supplies the shape stamped at each one.
Instanced meshes inherit the point grid's scale, so an oversized result usually means dialing the per-instance size down rather than touching the points.
Another consumer of the shared color field: scale instances down and drive their surface color from the same field as the rest of the scene.

A short tip contrasting two ways to multiply a mesh across scattered points: baking copies into one large mesh (cloning) versus drawing the same mesh repeatedly per point (instancing), and the trade-offs in memory, performance, and what you can still modify afterward.
The PBR path was aligned across all the main draw ops, and they can now all override color through fields.
Render a cylinder along each solved bone so an IK chain reads as a jointed robot limb instead of bare points; transform the mesh to align its long axis first.

Used to teach point attributes — instancing a cube at each point shows that a point carries far more than position (color, size, rotation), since rotation only becomes visible once you instance an oriented mesh on it.

To fold an imported scene into the mesh-effects pipeline, take the scene's separate mesh and material outputs: feed the mesh to a point-instancing draw and wire a material operator into the material slot.
Scatter a mesh instance across a grid of points; rotating the instance fails on a single-axis float because the rotation input expects a vector.
Reach for mesh-at-points instancing over RepeatMeshAtPoints when you want per-point vertex colors to come through and to stay light on large counts, since the latter bakes one combined mesh.
Drawing small oriented meshes at particles only reads well once they're stretched along their flight direction by a turbulence force, instead of all facing the same way.

Opening tip in a points series: explains the eight-value point structure (position, weight W, quaternion orientation), pushes a point list to a GPU buffer, then instances a mesh onto every point and shows how W and randomization drive the result.
Can't be the first node off a render source because its first input is the mesh, not the command — a wiring order quirk to watch for.
Instancing cube meshes across a point cloud; a pre-existing custom point shader on the points was overriding the up-vector and breaking orientation.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.CubeMesh.note: Scatter cube instances over a single-row grid by drawing the mesh at grid points, adjusting the grid's Y count to one layer and the cube pivot to sit on the ground.
Instancing cube meshes across a point cloud; a pre-existing custom point shader on the points was overriding the up-vector and breaking orientation.

ui:PerformanceMonitor.note: Render targets are kept cached indefinitely by the driver; a "flush resources" action would free targets not requested for a while, which matters when sharing the GPU with Spout/Resolume.

Read the small numbers under the frame rate, not just the FPS: compute-shader count, triangle count, and draw calls reveal which of the three bottlenecks you've hit. Jittery (not steady-slow) frame times on a laptop mean thermal throttling, not your scene.
Used to confirm the recording overhead stays low (single-digit CPU) while iterating on the heavy effect.
Reading per-frame milliseconds to judge the cost of the ray-march shadow pass while dialing shadow resolution up and down.

Reading the top-left graph stack: top line is frame *duration* in ms (16 ms = 60 fps budget), then UI-update time, then per-frame allocations (~80 fine, ~500 risks drops), plus draw-calls and shader-dispatch counts to spot the real bottleneck.

Read the frame-time and allocation histograms by their bucket axis: tiny buckets are scaled up so an occasional jitter looks worse than it is; a healthy allocation count stays in the small immediately-freed range, so a spike out of bounds flags a real leak to hunt.

ui:Timeline.note: String-valued time clips could stand in for the missing string keyframes, giving you named markers along the timeline.
Quick improvised intro graph: text points feed line drawing, then subdivide and noise-displace the lines, with the noise animation driven off the current time.
Two clips that overlap in time are rendered in order and crossfaded, giving a proper blend between adjacent shots.
Time clips structure a linear edit; only clips actually wired to the active output render, and unconnected ones fade out as a warning that they have no effect.
New time clips auto-stack to avoid overlap, and Ctrl+X splits a clip at the playhead while re-wiring the new half into the same group — much faster than hand-editing overlapping clips.
At any point you can drop keyframes to pin a parameter and scrub a deterministic animation, unlike non-deterministic feedback which won't reproduce the same frame.
Time clips auto-avoid overlap, the clip area is resizable, and clips connected to nothing fade out and say so in the tooltip since they're never evaluated.
Set color/brightness keyframes over time to script a short intro animation, then scrub or render it straight to video.
With a soundtrack assigned, the timeline background renders the audio waveform so you can align keyframes to the music.
Scrubbing with the left mouse jumps playback; releasing lets time continue forward from that point, which lets you preview a moment then keep rolling.
Insert a clip on a layer to both label a time range and gate visibility: outside the clip its layer is skipped, inside it renders — a cleaner on/off than animating a switch index.
A short tip on snapping keyframes precisely in the timeline: pinning parameters, switching the ruler from seconds to bars/beats/ticks, and using ALT to scale and insert keyframes onto snap targets.

The rewritten dope-sheet adds a drag handle on the time region, shaded value backgrounds for scanning, and post/pre extrapolation per keyframe selection (cycle, cycle-with-offset to step the value up or down each repeat) for endless loops.

Tangents now default to a fast fixed-length spline (Kochanek/Hermite-style); hold Ctrl or Ctrl+Shift to lengthen a handle and switch that key to a fully expressive cubic spline, and snap a handle flat to flip it to linear.
Keyframes don't auto-snap to the grid, but the background grid is driven by the project's BPM/FPS so you can snap the outer keys to it, select all, and "space evenly" to lock a sequence to the beat.

Drag an mp3 straight onto the timeline to load it as an audio clip with computed spectrum; multiple parallel audio tracks (no longer one fixed soundtrack) move TiXL toward video-editing-style layering.
Tap a beat live by holding Alt and pressing Shift+C to drop keyframes in time with music; polyrhythmic tracks won't land evenly, which is what the redistribute tool then fixes.

ui:AssetLibrary.note: A proposed always-open assets panel where dragging a file in copies it into the project's resource folder and drops the matching loader op, asking which loader when a type maps to several.
The asset library shows per-image thumbnails plus where each image is already used, and lets you swap one asset for another in place.
Why a single central thumbnail pipeline matters: every place that needs a preview image pulls from one renderer instead of each view computing its own.

The new browser lists every asset across all open projects, filters by type and by which operators can consume each, shows usage dots that jump to the referencing operator, and supports drag-out and external-file drop (copied into the project's asset folder).

A requested workflow: dropping a mesh asset directly into a 3D scene (not the graph) to auto-create a placed group — "scene bashing" — distinct from dropping onto the graph, which just instantiates the loader.

op:Lib.image.generate.load.LoadImage.note: Dropping an image asset would auto-wire this with its file-path field already filled, since images have a single obvious loader.
Unpinning its output shows the image directly; it's the typical starting node you then branch off in two directions to add effects.
Some operators expose a custom node UI instead of a plain preview, which is why an image loader can surface its file path on the node face rather than a thumbnail.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.LoadObj.note: When a file type has several loaders, the drop prompts you to choose — e.g. mesh vs. point-cloud import for the same OBJ.
Pulling in a bundled mesh asset (here a beveled cube) as the building block for an instanced scene before any displacement or shading.
Standard scene scaffold: LoadObj into DrawMesh under a Camera as the starting point for a 3D setup.
Restricting a path parameter's file filter (here to .obj) makes the resource picker show only matching files; many operators were missing these filters and returned noise or nothing.
Loading and drawing a mesh as the surface to scatter labelled points across.

op:Lib.point.helper.LoadObjAsPoints.note: When a file type has several loaders, the drop prompts you to choose — e.g. mesh vs. point-cloud import for the same OBJ.

ui:Symbol.note: How an operator's full namespace is User → optional sub-namespace → operator; the optional middle level groups projects (e.g. client/show) and is editable per symbol.
How to turn a finished prototype graph into a reusable operator: select the whole patch, "combine" it into a new symbol, and place it in a sensible namespace (here a render/post-fx folder).
How example/sample scenes attach to an operator: a symbol named "<OpName>Example(s)" in an Examples namespace is matched by name only (namespace ignored) and surfaces as the operator's how-to.

Right-click an operator and "set thumbnail" to freeze its current main-output view as a curated preview; pin a sub-output first to choose exactly which image becomes the thumbnail rather than whatever evaluates by default.
A set thumbnail only shows up once the symbol also has a description, so an operator with no description appears to "lose" the thumbnail you just assigned.

New MSDF font generator (under utilities) turns any .ttf into a usable signed-distance font written straight into the project's resources/fonts; widen the glyph range for accents/umlauts and raise resolution when you add many glyphs.

ui:UserProject.note: Enabling "shareable" on a project turns it into a library other projects can drag operators out of; the primary user namespace can't be removed because operators need a project to compile into.
The alpha build now creates its own versioned settings and project folder so a preview version can't silently corrupt the projects of your stable install.

op:Lib.image.fx.feedback.AdvancedFeedbac.note: Feeding a rendered texture in shows nothing until you pick a non-empty preset; switching presets and dialing the displacement amount/offset down turns frantic motion into a slow reaction-diffusion look.

A deep walkthrough of the AdvancedFeedback effect: how its displace-along-a-slope feedback loop works internally, and a guided tour of nearly every parameter (twist, displacement, sample distance, shade, blur, color shifts, amplified edges, limit brights) and how to drive them for smoke-, water- and reaction-diffusion-like looks.
To get visible trails you must first render the source into a RenderTarget and feed that back through Layer2d, lowering the feedback alpha — a raw connection alone shows almost nothing.
A packaged feedback effect exposing a deep parameter set with presets you can crossfade between (select two with Ctrl, Alt to blend); double-click to open the container and inspect how it's wired.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetRequestedResolu.note: How a fixed output resolution is forced downstream: a zero input forwards the incoming resolution, a non-zero one overrides it — needed when a feedback effect has no resolution input of its own and you want it as a height map.
It writes a resolution factor into the evaluation context so downstream image ops that ask for 0×0 inherit it — an easy way to oversample or render a subtree at lower res.

Overrides the requested resolution carried in the context: positive values force a fixed size for all downstream 0,0 operators, negative values fall back to the output window, letting a post chain ignore an odd incoming image size.

A short tip explaining how an image operator's resolution is resolved: the "magic" 0×0 default pulls resolution from an incoming texture if present, otherwise from the output window, and how -1 or an explicit size overrides that.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.HeightMapSdf.note: Turning a grayscale texture into raised terrain: raise the displacement size for relief, then push the ray-marcher's max-slope parameter to shrink its internal step size so steep valleys stop showing march artifacts.
Turns a single noise channel into terrain as a distance-field operator, pairing cleanly with an SDF-to-color step for a procedural landscape.
A new field op that turns a height map into an SDF for building terrains.

op:Lib.field.render.RaymarchField.note: Turning a grayscale texture into raised terrain: raise the displacement size for relief, then push the ray-marcher's max-slope parameter to shrink its internal step size so steep valleys stop showing march artifacts.
Why raising the normal-sampling distance softens the surface — it blurs the sampled normals so a low-res source height map reads smoother instead of pixel-stepped.

The intuition for the max-slope knob, sketched: it sets how steep a displacement the marcher assumes so it can shorten steps near the surface; set it too permissive and the ray exhausts its max-step count, giving an inception-like warped "trippy" space.
Colorizing a field in the final colorization pass is far cheaper than during ray-marching, because the color is evaluated once per pixel after the march completes rather than at every march step.

Swap an SDF's default shader-graph rendering for this to gain ambient-occlusion shading; its AO-distance knob adds contact shadow the cheaper path lacks. Pick it when you want the SDF surface to read as solid.

A guided tour of TiXL's new SDF/field shader-graph system: the four operator categories (generators, space, adjust, combine), how ray-marching renders fields, performance and aliasing trade-offs, and using fields to drive particle forces and point selection.
A view-direction bug in the PBR specular term made mesh and ray-marched-field surfaces shade differently; unifying the PBR shading into a shared include keeps both paths visually aligned.
Shares the unified light/environment so an SDF torus matches a mesh torus, but it does not support normal mapping yet — keep normal maps off that branch.
Cost scales with empty marching distance — it gets slower as the object shrinks in frame because rays hit the max step count; capping max distance (and min distance) would be the big optimization.
A community SDF-on-the-fly setup loads SDFs as JSON nodes and must be wired into a RaymarchField to show anything; flagged as needing cleanup and documentation.

The expensive part is ray-marching the distance field to find the surface (worst-case full step count per pixel); lowering max steps degrades the far field, and for particle collisions you skip surface rendering entirely so it stays cheap.
The PBR path was aligned across all the main draw ops, and they can now all override color through fields.
Because the scene is one SDF, you can boolean-combine extra primitives (a sphere) into it so IK legs re-snap and grip the new surface live.
A quick ray-march scene: feed it an SDF field and set a hard, glossy material to get a clean reflective sphere to test variable-driven parameters against.

Counting ray-march steps gives a free edge/distance glow: where the march takes many steps it grazed close to the surface, so use that step count as a glow term added before the specular-AA stage in the field template.

Pipe an SDF plus a color field into its material input to shade the surface by sampled distance; pair with [SDFToColor] and a [TransformField] (animated by [PerlinNoise3]) to map a fractal's distance onto a gradient. Unlike image effects, field nodes compose inside one shader path rather than each allocating a buffer.

An anti-firefly "geometric roughness" trick (fade glossiness toward grazing Fresnel angles) belongs as an optional compute-PBR parameter here and on draw-mesh — its cost on a raymarch pass is negligible, and it cleans up glittering edge artifacts on glossy surfaces.

op:Lib.image.generate.misc.Sketch.note: Reached for as a quick on-canvas diagramming tool to reason through how another operator works.
Switching medium to rough on-canvas sketching (with onion-skin) to block out a storyboard before committing to particle work.
Used as a quick freehand scratch surface on the output to illustrate ideas live; cheap to drop in and draw on.
The revamped sketch op stays useful for annotating animations or blocking out storyboards.

op:Lib.render.shading.PointLight.note: The standard lighting trio for an SDF scene: add a point light, set a not-too-glossy material, and swap the default studio environment for black to control reflections.

A default scene already has lighting on so beginners see something; create a point light for full control, but the still-lit far side comes from indirect/environment light, not this op. Order between point lights doesn't matter — last eight win.

Prefer it over SetPointLight: it wraps the same setup but also draws a gizmo sphere you can grab and move in the viewport; the specular term was previously computed from the wrong light position and is now corrected.
Rendering a very dense radial point cloud with PBR shading, a point light, depth-of-field from the depth buffer and SSAO approximates ribbon-like volumetric structures (at heavy point counts).
Attach a light's position to a moving body point and break its intensity out to a [PerlinNoise] for a living, flickering source.
Raise decay (≈6) so falloff stays near the source instead of washing out distant elements, then balance intensity (≈5) and tint the light for mood.
A second light placed off to one side in a contrasting color adds rim/fill separation; brighten it to gauge its effect, then pull intensity back down.
Writes up to eight light positions into the evaluation context, which downstream shadow and material operators read — break the position out into a [Vector3Gizmo] to drag the light interactively.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetEnvironment.note: The standard lighting trio for an SDF scene: add a point light, set a not-too-glossy material, and swap the default studio environment for black to control reflections.

Supplies image-based / indirect lighting (HDRI-style); switch among built-in presets to relight the whole scene, set it to black to kill ambient, and toggle whether the environment itself is rendered as background.

Its order relative to the camera matters: it renders the background first, before the camera is known, so placing it after the camera (and with an opaque, non-transparent source image) is required for a consistent background — the image-based-lighting math fails on a transparent input.
Force a black environment before the projection pass so the projected light reads against an unlit background instead of the scene's ambient lighting.
Pair a material with an environment so the surface picks up image-based lighting from a surrounding texture instead of looking flat.
After assigning an environment texture you must trigger an "update live once" so the lighting actually samples the new cube map.
An advanced "background blur" option blurs the environment backdrop independently of the depth-of-field on the geometry.
Switch to the new "black" environment preset to isolate and inspect a single light's direct contribution with no ambient wash.
Sets shared light and fog parameters consumed by every "draw" downstream; it isn't a shader, so a background not actually drawn (no backdrop mesh) won't pick up the fog.
Now auto-converts to a cube map and updates only when needed (no Live-Update toggle), with presets including a black one that fully disables environment light.
Supplying any environment texture (even a cheap [TileableNoise]) is what gives reflective PBR materials something to mirror; animate its phase for a moving sheen.
Beyond an HDRI, plug a [TileableNoise] or any texture into it to light a scene with a synthetic environment, optionally with no visible background.

op:Lib.field.combine.CombineSDF.note: Use an intersection combine with a box to crop an infinite displaced field down to a finite block — but you must scale the box up first or it clips everything away.
Smooth-combine several SphereSDFs into one blobby shape used as the target surface for point placement.
Subtract a tall, wide cylinder from a plane to carve a channel or basin into the collision field that particles then flow along.
An infinite field is hard to preview, so union it with a finite box and grab the second (box-bounded) output to clamp it into something you can actually see and control.
Combine several sphere SDFs into one field and feed it as a force to pull particles toward the SDF surfaces; zero the drag and disable collision reflection for an orbiting two/three-body attractor.
Build a radial star from a stretched capsule/cylinder SDF by repeating around Z, then intersect with a centered ring SDF to clip the spokes into a banded star shape.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.BoxSDF.note: Use an intersection combine with a box to crop an infinite displaced field down to a finite block — but you must scale the box up first or it clips everything away.
Author a color-in-space field by setting each shape's color, combining them, then slicing it flat with an image op instead of ray-marching — a cheap 2D preview of what a 3D color field looks like.
Drop one in as the missing field input of a volume force to get a clean box-shaped collision region; pair it with a [Translate] to offset the bounds off-center.
Intended to zero-out or mask point radii that fall inside an SDF region; here it misbehaved and was flagged as a likely bug rather than user error.
A distance function over space you can feed a point shader's field slot; shape it first with [RepeatAxis] and rounding before sampling per point.

op:Lib.field.use.SDFToColor.note: Drives surface color from distance-to-a-shape: feed a sphere's distance, set a falloff range and a gradient, then watch an expanding colored ring sweep the surface as the range grows.
Colorizing a field in the final colorization pass is far cheaper than during ray-marching, because the color is evaluated once per pixel after the march completes rather than at every march step.
Read the plain distance from ground level, perturb it with noise, then map that distance onto a color gradient to paint a terrain SDF.
Turns a distance field into a color you can route into DrawMesh, RepeatMeshAtPoints, or DrawMeshAtPoints so every PBR path colorizes from the same field identically.
Feed a plane SDF into a draw operator's color-field override and convert distance-to-ground into a gradient, so color climbs the geometry from the floor up.
Fixed so it works correctly when feeding particle effects.
Converts a field's distance into a color gradient — use this rather than the bare distance value when you want hue, not a grayscale falloff.

Convert a field's signed distance into a color ramp and feed it to a mesh's fragment-field input, turning a moving [PlaneSDF] into a procedural light/gradient that washes across the scene — rotate or repeat the field for projector-like sweeps.

Color a fractal by its *internal iteration count* rather than surface distance: copy the fractal's [CustomSDF], modify it to output an iteration-based gradient, and feed that to the color so different fractal layers read as different colors.
Maps an SDF's sampled distance through a color gradient so a raymarched surface picks up color from a field rather than a flat material.
Converts an SDF's distance into a scalar so a field-driven force can sample it; though for distance-only use the first SDF channel is already read directly without it.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.PlaneSDF.note: Swap the shape feeding a distance-to-color for a plane to get vertical height as the input, so a glow gradient lands only on the upper ranges of the terrain.
The up/down axis was flipped to fix a sign bug — a breaking change, so projects relying on the old orientation need updating.
Build a collision floor by feeding a plane SDF into a field volume force; enabling collisions makes particles bounce off the field surface.

Feed it a field through its amount input to mask where turbulence applies — e.g. a plane SDF so only particles above the floor get disturbed; reverse/scale the field's distance range to shape the falloff.
A single plane field with low repulsion and no damping makes particles oscillate above/below the surface into a sine-wave-like motion.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.SphereSDF.note: Author a color-in-space field by setting each shape's color, combining them, then slicing it flat with an image op instead of ray-marching — a cheap 2D preview of what a 3D color field looks like.
Chain a field-color op after a shape-based point selection so you can mask which points get recolored — useful for scattering colored LEDs in 3D space.
A hard projected-shadow edge looks wrong; the fix is to soften the shadow-map sampling so edges fade rather than cut sharply.
Used as a simple animated field to drive a per-point selection factor; render it alongside via VisualizeFieldDistance to see exactly where the selection falls.

Turn an SDF surface into a directional field and use it as a vector force so particles accelerate along the surface normal; invert the amount and the shape becomes an attractor you can drag through the cloud.
Feed a sphere distance field as the selector so moving the sphere sculpts which instances grow — a MoGraph-style field effector driving scale.

op:Lib.image.fx.distort.FieldToImage.note: Author a color-in-space field by setting each shape's color, combining them, then slicing it flat with an image op instead of ray-marching — a cheap 2D preview of what a 3D color field looks like.
Its distance mode renders the combined field fine, but the direct-color mode is broken here (colors don't survive the combine) — a bug to watch for when previewing color fields.

op:Lib.field.analyze.VisualizeFieldDista.note: The go-to op for seeing an invisible distance field, though it only works on distances — a color field needs a different visualizer.
Renders the shape of a distance field so you can see how it's structured when particles won't follow it the way you expect.
Drop it in to actually see a field's distance bands while tuning a selection range, instead of guessing where the gradient sits.

ui:ShaderGraph.note: End-to-end of authoring a point-modifier shader op: duplicate a similar op as a new type, "edit" its generated shader to open the source, set p.color to a constant first to confirm you're in the right shader, then strip the unneeded mapping/noise branches.

When writing a C# operator's value you assign through the output slot's value (the slot also tracks dirty/update state) rather than returning directly — return a constant first to confirm hot-reload is live.

A guided tour of TiXL's new SDF/field shader-graph system: the four operator categories (generators, space, adjust, combine), how ray-marching renders fields, performance and aliasing trade-offs, and using fields to drive particle forces and point selection.
Mapping shader constant buffers to inputs: separate buffers carry parameters, resolution, and the two camera matrices — knowing which slot is which is what makes the bound values land correctly.

File > New scaffolds an image effect from a template, copying needed resources into your namespace and opening the shader in your editor; VS Code with the HLSL Tools extension is recommended for highlighting, autocomplete, and error squiggles.
Most effects are containers you can dive into; double-click and keep descending until you hit the single shader setup node, then Edit to reach the raw HLSL.

Image effects build on an ImageFX-Static template (cacheable, nothing animated); add a parameter via right-click add-input, convert it to int/float, route it into the params buffer, then edit the fragment shader — clone the repo for read-write access to library operators.

Run TiXL in Debug from the IDE and capture a frame with RenderDoc (Ctrl+Shift+F12) to inspect each draw's bound shader, textures, and constant-buffer values — the fastest way to see what isn't bound or is mis-packed in a custom shader.

op:Lib.point.modify.SelectPointsWithSDF.note: Used as the template to clone from when building a sibling point-field op, since both walk a point buffer and sample a field per point.
Chain a field-color op after a shape-based point selection so you can mask which points get recolored — useful for scattering colored LEDs in 3D space.
Feed a CustomSDF in and write the selection to an FX attribute; that attribute then drives anything per-point — here emit speed from a grid into a ParticleSystem, varying by region of the field.

The range mapping modes (centered / from-start / ping-pong / repeat) plus gain-bias decide how a field's distance maps onto the 0..1 selection; zero distance reads as maximum selection, and the strength factor lets a second selection localize the effect.
The headline point op: select points by their distance to a field to unlock a wide range of masked point effects (covered in depth in a recent meet-up).

Write a 0/1 mask into F1/F2 from whether a point sits inside a shape; the SDF variant binds the test to any distance field (a torus, noise-displaced) instead of the legacy fixed sphere, making it far more expressive as a selector.
Using a plane SDF as a near-linear ramp: distance-to-plane grows with height, so it behaves like a gradient you can feed into F1 for size or displacement without a texture.
Drive its strength factor from an F-attribute set by a sphere SDF selection so the rotation/translation only applies to points inside the field region.
Select points by a plane SDF and use the selection attribute as a per-point strength factor in a transform, so only points to one side of the plane get squished or rotated.
Intended to zero-out or mask point radii that fall inside an SDF region; here it misbehaved and was flagged as a likely bug rather than user error.

Use an SDF field to select/scale points by whether they fall inside a shape: a sphere's interior raises building heights with a range and gain/bias falloff, and a second selection in multiply mode can subtract a street channel through the grid.

op:Lib.point.generate.GridPoints.note: A grid of points drawn straight to screen is the standard scaffold for testing a point-modifier op — wire its strength to point scale so you can see the effect take hold.

Each drawn point becomes two triangles (a quad), so a count in the millions tanks the frame rate; pushing the count up via the infinity slider is the quickest way to feel the poly-count ceiling on your hardware.

Cell mode keeps a fixed spacing between points as you add more; bounds mode instead fills a set volume by redistributing them — reach for cell when the gap matters, bounds when the extent matters. Drop the Y count to 1 for a flat layer.
Randomizing position and scale (and offsetting the random phase) keeps a scattered point field from overlapping a neighbouring element.
Generate a volumetric point cloud (e.g. 10×10×10) as the source for instanced quads; the per-point W value starts uniform and is what you later vary.
Set the initial W attribute and tweak grid depth, count, point size and overall scale to control how the cloud reads before any variation is applied.
Set one axis to a single point and the other two to 100 each to get a flat 100×100 sheet of points; scale the whole grid up to size the surface you'll instance onto.
The default changed to cell mode (fixed spacing between points) rather than bounds mode (a fixed outer extent filled by the count); GridPointsOld preserves the old default for existing projects.
Scatter cube instances over a single-row grid by drawing the mesh at grid points, adjusting the grid's Y count to one layer and the cube pivot to sit on the ground.
Drop the per-axis count (e.g. 3×3) and tighten the scale to get a sparse, compact point set to scatter copies onto.
A flat grid of small sprites drawn with invert blend turns into a self-overlapping tile pattern as the dots grow and overlap.
Visualising a plane-SDF selection as point size shows it selects everything below the plane, not just the intersecting layer.
Lays the instancing grid that a repeated GLTF mesh is scattered across in the VAT demo.
Swapping a scatter source for a single-depth-layer grid of points gives the same Invert-blend trick a more ordered, lattice-like character.

Lay out a flat grid of points and instance a cube at each to block out a city; raise the cube's pivot to its base so the points sit at ground level and scaling grows buildings upward instead of from their centre.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawPoints.note: A grid of points drawn straight to screen is the standard scaffold for testing a point-modifier op — wire its strength to point scale so you can see the effect take hold.

Overdraw demo: with few points but a large point radius, the same pixels get shaded repeatedly and the GPU stalls — shrink the radius and performance snaps back. Watch fill-rate, not just object count.
Temporarily wire it in (and pin the output) just to visualize a generated point set while you tune the generator feeding it.
Render a point set as visible dots and add it into the scene group; reuse the same generator with a wider spread for a separate background layer.

Each point is a billboard stretched to the sprite texture's aspect, so a non-square sprite makes the dots elliptical and canvas-dependent; dive in to find the fallback sprite and set its source a fixed square resolution.

op:Lib.point.modify.PointColorWithField.note: How the new op reads color out of a field per point: call get-field with the "1" selector (0 returns distance, 1 returns color) so the float4 result is the color you write back to the point.
Color points by sampling a field; pair it with [SDFToColor] (not raw distance) so a [SphereSDF] paints a smooth gradient across the cloud.

op:Lib.point.modify.SamplePointColorAttr.note: Named as the existing precedent for sampling color onto points, before deciding a simpler field-driven op was worth building.
Pipeline to colour points by a field's distance: select with an SDF, then map the distance attribute through a gradient ([SDFToColor]) to make an inner glow region.

op:Lib.field.generate.texture.Raster3dFi.note: A procedural 3D texture of grid lines/crosses you can transform, repeat-mirror, and combine with other fields — like the 2D raster pattern but defined throughout space; its line width and feather are adjustable.

Raster3dField places a procedural texture onto SDF geometry; push-pull offsets the computed distance toward the surface like an extrude, and its amount input accepts a noise field to carve cobblestone-style relief.

ui:OperatorSettings.note: Finishing a new op cleanly: mark both inputs required, leave the strength unclamped so negative values still give useful results, and write a one-line description before merging.
Rename any operator by clicking its title field or selecting and pressing Return; a renamed op shows quote marks, and its underlying type is still readable in the top-left corner when selected.
Changing a duplicated operator's type requires assigning a new unique id, or the editor treats it as the original symbol.
A thumbnail/tooltip won't appear for an operator that has no description text — fill in the description or the preview stays hidden.
Per-layout you can hide individual editor tabs and the hidden state is stored implicitly with each saved layout (F1/F2), giving a clean stage layout you toggle into.
Why a maintainer avoids changing an operator's default value (e.g. a polygon's 180° start) — it silently breaks existing projects built on the old default.
Mark an operator's primary input as "required" and move it to the top in the settings page so the graph shows a red warning triangle when it's left unconnected.
Input parameters can now be renamed directly from the editor.

Expose inner parameters as inputs on a combined symbol (Ctrl-break a param, set a default), then save named presets — TiXL auto-generates thumbnails and you can Alt-drag to blend continuously between them.

op:Lib.numbers.color.PickColorFromList.note: Naively seeding a list-index pick with a random value gives ~25% repeats on a four-color list, since nothing stops two consecutive draws landing on the same index.

op:Lib.numbers.float.random.Random.note: Naively seeding a list-index pick with a random value gives ~25% repeats on a four-color list, since nothing stops two consecutive draws landing on the same index.

op:Lib.numbers.int.basic.RandomChoiceInd.note: The "bag-of-seven" idea borrowed from Tetris: shuffle a full pool and draw it down before refilling, guaranteeing even spacing — explained, then found not to solve the deterministic-by-index case.

The hard problem behind a "random index, never the same twice" op: hashing the input index deterministically still collides on small moduli, and a single-neighbor check plus offset just shifts collisions around rather than removing them.
Turn an incoming index into a fresh random index that never repeats the same value twice in a row — ideal for shuffling through images without two identical frames back to back.

op:Lib.numbers.floats.basic.ColorsToList.note: A list op should expose its element count as a secondary output so downstream index math knows the modulus — list lengths are otherwise awkward to fetch.
Builds a reusable color palette as a list you can feed into BuildGradient and rearrange, rather than hand-wiring individual colors.

op:Lib.io.osc.OscInput.note: How to drive live visuals from a phone or tablet over OSC: [OscInput] auto-detects the address of any control you touch (the built-in teach mode), multiple inputs on the same port share one connection for free, and its float output can be split into X/Y/pressure to paint feedback trails whose color and line breaks follow the incoming pressure. A practical walkthrough of wiring a TouchOSC-style device into a generative drawing patch.
Receive a phone's position and quaternion (x/y/z/w) over OSC into a dictionary, then pull individual floats out by key to reconstruct an orientation.

op:Lib.numbers.float.logic.Compare.note: Build a threshold gate: compare an incoming signal against a level, and when it crosses, fire a trigger animation — the manual equivalent of a sample-and-hold/gate from a modular synth.

op:Lib.numbers.float.adjust.Remap.note: Put it between a raw UI value and a target so one slider can feed two places with a meaningful range — e.g. mapping a 0..1 scale into the units the projector actually wants.
Rescale a raw measured value (here a finger-gap distance) into a usable parameter range, then flip/curve the range so "fingers close" maps to the velocity you actually want.
Among the operators that adopted the combined bias-and-gain control for reshaping a value's response curve.
Map a raw MIDI value (0–127) into a usable parameter range and add damping to smooth the jittery controller signal before it drives anything.

op:Lib.image.generate.basic.RenderTarget.note: Feed it a camera and the magic 0,0 resolution to capture a scene into a texture, then crank the texture to 8K to watch pixel count (and effect cost) explode — this is where a heavy post chain actually gets paid for, in millions of pixels per frame.
How the post-effect routes through a render target: the projection pass writes into it and the result feeds the final composite, replacing the prototype's inline render-to-texture wiring.
Pipe a point-quad draw through it to get multisampled anti-aliasing on the result.
Piping into a 32-bit (float) render target instead of 8-bit makes a large visible quality difference for accumulated/feedback-style effects.
Add a second texture output to a wrapped operator (right-click → add output, set type to texture), then a 2D layer lets you place that rendered image as a plane in 3D space.
Used as the entry point of the post stack, here noted for adding multi-sampling anti-aliasing to the rendered scene.
Its 0,0 resolution makes a sub-scene render at whatever size the consumer asks for, so the same graph is sharp at 480p or 8k without edits.
Skip clearing the target each frame to accumulate a cheap trailing-history "motion blur"; reintroduce a near-transparent clear layer to slowly fade old frames instead of letting them stick forever.

A short tip explaining how an image operator's resolution is resolved: the "magic" 0×0 default pulls resolution from an incoming texture if present, otherwise from the output window, and how -1 or an explicit size overrides that.
Collect overlapping draw calls into one buffer so a blend mode can combine them; here it's where Invert blending accumulates the result.
Switching the buffer's blend mode to Invert makes each overlapping shape flip what's beneath it, generating intricate moiré-like interference from a trivial setup.

op:Lib.image.color.ColorGrade.note: Image effects don't overwrite their input; TiXL allocates a fresh same-size buffer for the result so the untouched original is still available downstream (e.g. to recombine with a glow pass).

Push highlights warm and shadows cool for the cinematic "pop" look; the gain/bias control is a contrast curve you drag left/right (steepen into an S for more contrast, flatten for less) and up/down to shift it, like a Photoshop curve in two parameters.
Where most of a scene's final look is set — start from a preset or hand-tune curves to push the overall mood after geometry and lighting are done.
Hold Alt while hovering its thumbnail to flip through built-in presets instead of dialing every knob by hand.
Lift the mid-tones to add contrast and rescue a too-dark composite.

Lift/gamma/gain is the core of pro color grading: lift moves shadows, gamma the midtones, gain the highlights, each neutral at gray; push gain down and midtones up to add contrast, and tint each band toward a hue for a teal-and-orange look. Includes a vignette band with its own radius.
