Tame an over-saturated render by pulling colors down and toning toward a vintage look as a final corrective pass.
Why raising gamma brightens darks toward each other while a low gamma deepens them — the non-obvious reason a graded image can look "inverted" before you adjust brightness.
Push brightness and tune the overall look to set scene mood; can be dialed in by feel rather than by exact values.
Inserted upstream to raise brightness and demonstrate clamping; a quick way to test how far you can push exposure before detail is lost.

A five-minute introduction to color grading in Tooll, centered on the lift/gamma/gain controls of the ColorGrade operator, reading the WaveForm operator's scope, and comparing before/after with CompareImages.

op:Lib.image.fx.blur.Bloom.note: An expensive effect because it runs multiple blur cascades; at 8K those passes are what drops you off 60 fps, so it's a prime candidate to apply at a reduced resolution.
A restrained post chain — screen-space occlusion plus bloom and glow, no color grade — is enough to finish a procedural scene.
Adding it after the projected light dramatically improves the look — the glowing rays read far better with a bloom pass than the raw shader output.
Flagged as a near-mandatory final glow pass, with a caution that what it blooms depends on whether grading clipped highlights first.
Pairs with HDR (>1) line/point colors to turn bright laser/eye geometry into a glow; without HDR input it does nothing visible.
A cheap glow recipe: drive two color tints into the bloom so bright cores bleed a warm/cool halo.
A post bloom over the masked bright tips is what sells the glow/burn looks built earlier — easy to overdo.
Used as the example operator when curating a thumbnail, showing the "set thumbnail" workflow applies to any image-output effect, not just project compositions.
Glows only from areas brighter than 1.0, so pair it with HDR colours (e.g. an HDR step in a material's gradient) to make just the bright bands of a surface bleed light.

Its internal gradient colours the successive blur levels by distance from the source — and accepts transparent steps — so you can tint the outer glow a different hue or cut the core entirely for an underwater halo.
Blooming a rendered texture then converting it to a normal map to drive a downstream particle force.

ui:SearchWindow.note: Long-press the background and type to search; synonyms and fuzzy/substring matching mean "donut" finds the [TorusMesh] and even partial initials like "tm" rank [TorusMesh] and [TransformMesh] first — so small typos still land the op.
Clicking a parameter's input opens a typed search box to drop a driving operator straight onto that input; Alt-clicking instead adds a keyframe.
Typing `?` in the operator search returns a random operator, and cycling seeds yields fresh suggestions — a way to discover unfamiliar ops or set yourself a build challenge.

Pressing Ctrl-F on an empty search shows your recently visited operators as a history, not search results; arrow-down walks it, and Alt-Left/Right steps through your selection history like a code editor.
Typing `?` yields a random operator ranked by relevancy, and multiple `?`s act as a complexity-tunable prompt generator for creative challenges.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.TorusMesh.note: Searching "donut" yields it (a torus is the graphics term); hover its output to confirm it's a mesh buffer, then click the output to get usage-ranked suggestions for what to wire next.
Build a low-segment ring/segment mesh and repeat it along bone points to give an IK limb a mechanical, jointed look.
Thin the ring by dialing its thickness/inner-radius down (here to ~0.03–0.15) so it reads as a slender band rather than a fat donut.

For an endless-tunnel illusion put the camera inside the torus, rotate only on one axis, and scroll the surface texture rather than moving the camera — give it negative/inverted thickness so you're looking at the inside wall.

op:Lib.mesh.draw.DrawMesh.note: The statistically most common follow-up when you click a mesh-buffer output; TiXL ranks connection suggestions by how people actually wire that output type.

Backface culling explained: by default only front faces draw (as little as necessary for real-time), so a flat plane vanishes from behind — switch the cull side or disable culling to make it double-sided.
A view-direction bug in the PBR specular term made mesh and ray-marched-field surfaces shade differently; unifying the PBR shading into a shared include keeps both paths visually aligned.
Build a small cylinder, reduce its segment detail and shrink its radius/height, then draw it stacked on a cube to compose a Lego-style brick from primitives.
DrawMesh now accepts a field: convert an SDF/plane field through SdfToColor and feed it as the color input to paint a procedural color map onto mesh surfaces, consistent with the SDF render path.
The PBR path was aligned across all the main draw ops, and they can now all override color through fields.
Pair a primitive mesh with a draw operator to make geometry visible in the output; shrink the mesh radius before composing it with other shapes.

Why a generic wireframe-thicken op is hard on the GPU: meshes are triangles and per-triangle compute can't see neighbors, so deduplicating shared edges is the blocker — cache one complex shape and repeat it instead.
A new specular-AA option (on by default) removes the sparkly fireflies on rough/raymarched surfaces — toggle it off to see the ugly aliased speculars it fixes.
Loading and drawing a mesh as the surface to scatter labelled points across.

ui:OutputWindow.note: In fill mode the viewer matches its window's vertical extent and pads left/right to the set aspect ratio, so dragging the panel reflows the view without distorting it.
A short tip showing the Save Screenshot button, which writes the current output frame at full resolution to the `.t3/screenshots` folder.

Extended design discussion: replace single-output pinning with a project-level list of outputs (display / Spout / NDI / virtual canvas), routable live (e.g. Ctrl+1/2) and arrangeable on a UV canvas for projection mapping, while keeping the strict output-first evaluation order intact.

op:Lib.render.camera.Camera.note: Without a camera operator the viewer's own orbit isn't stored anywhere; add one and pin its output so dragging the view writes into saveable position parameters instead of a throwaway preview.
Inject a second camera, rename it, and switch the output from auto to that named camera so you can fly an "edit camera" around a pinned background scene without disturbing the final composite camera.

op:Lib.field.adjust.NoiseDisplaceSDF.note: Insert it on an SDF connection to break up mathematically-perfect geometry; dial the noise amount low so the shape keeps structure rather than dissolving.
Offset a flat collision field with noise displacement to roughen it; intersecting a smooth copy with a noisy copy keeps bumps only where they rise above the surface.
Offsetting the color-driving plane field with animated noise warps where the gradient bands fall, and the displacement can be animated over time.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.QuadMesh.note: Used as a floor plane; rotate it -90° on X to lay it flat (it's drawn edge-on otherwise) and scale to taste under the main object.
On a large plane, add subdivisions even though they're invisible up close — sparse geometry can produce shading artifacts that extra triangles smooth out.
A quad faces the camera by default, so it must be rotated (negatively, oddly) to lie flat as a ground plane; subdividing it helps fog and shading interpolate smoothly.
A non-manifold flat mesh still works as a collider, but only its front side repels cleanly; the back side falls away, so prefer a closed manifold shape for predictable collisions.

ui:Gizmo.note: TiXL is a right-handed Y-up coordinate system (X right, Y up, Z toward camera) — unlike Blender's Z-up; rotations go counter-clockwise. The transform gizmo's coloured axes map directly to X/Y/Z.
Set gizmo visibility to "for selected only" so light and transform handles stop cluttering the view until you actually pick the operator.
Enable its gizmo to drag the selection region through the cloud live; scale, stretch and rotate the region to reshape what gets selected.
Mark a Vector3 parameter as a position/translation in the operator's UI layout so it shows a draggable in-viewport gizmo with a meaningful value range.
Disabling z-write/z-test removes back-point cut-off artefacts from alpha-cutout sprites, but you usually still want z-testing.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.TransformMesh.note: Choose it to move the geometry itself versus a downstream [Transform] that moves where the mesh is drawn; the distinction matters when later ops depend on point/object positions.

ui:ParameterWindow.note: Right-click a value to copy and right-click-paste onto another op fills parameters by matching name, handy for transferring a translation between operators.
On a layer/blend op, drag with the left mouse to set opacity and the right mouse to set luminosity directly on the parameter — a fast shortcut for tinting a fake shadow dark.
Expose two artist-facing color knobs — one multiplying the projected image, one tinting the original scene — so the look can be balanced without touching the graph.
Renaming generic a/b/c/d shader params to meaningful names: align each to its buffer slot and delete a parameter to confirm via the warning which downstream use it fed.
Organizing an operator's UI: use "show with group" to bucket parameters into Light / Light appearance / Surface / Shadow sections and order them position-first so the panel reads logically.
Side note: a string input field's max buffer length was raised to 32K to allow longer text in parameters.

How per-parameter snapshots work: instead of flagging a whole operator, right-click individual parameters to expose only those to a snapshot, then capture/recall named states from the empty-input background view.
The selected operator's knobs live in a side panel; the per-parameter keyframes show up alongside them.
Numeric parameters can now be clamped on min, max, or both — ideal for one-sided ranges like particle count or blur radius.
Two reported UI bugs: a parameter popup opens on operators that have no animatable input, and a layout glitch appears when pinning certain operators — both cosmetic and easy to fix.

Per-parameter settings let you group knobs (append "..." to a group name to collapse it by default, while modified params still show), raise display precision, and add a unit suffix that's handy for marking rotations.
Hold Ctrl over an enum/number field (outline turns blue) to scroll through its values with the mouse wheel.

The gain/bias vector2 found on many operators is a remap curve: bias shifts the midpoint toward dark or light, gain bends it toward an S-curve (more contrast) or its inverse, letting you reposition and harden a gradient edge playfully instead of editing keys.
Per-parameter help docs now surface on hover over the help icon; clicking the icon toggles a dedicated help mode.
Enabling the Vec2 control in the parameter settings lets you drag both components of a paired parameter at once and see the resulting distribution/weighting curve live.
Hover-scrub over an enum/preset thumbnail to live-preview each option (Photoshop-style), instead of Ctrl+wheel; the touchpad pinch-zoom integration had regressed the Ctrl+wheel cycling.
A driven (connected) input now shows the driver's name and can't be reset; the param tooltip's question-mark hover surfaces type and what's driving it.

op:Lib.image.generate.basic.Blob.note: A soft procedural shape used as a fake drop-shadow texture under an object; its preview thumbnail inherits the output aspect ratio, which is why you give it a fixed resolution so it stays round.
Add a negative-brightness blob over the image to make a vignette — darkening the corners with one shape, no dedicated effect needed.
A practical sync rig: animate a value, feed it through a wrapping operator, and drive a pulsing radius so you can tap keyframes in on the beat while audio plays.
Reached for as a cheap stand-in scene to feed the projector when no real geometry is connected.
Drop blob billboards at the line points sitting on an SDF surface to add glowing nodes along the crawling-electricity effect.

Stack two image operators and they auto-snap into a chain that composites foreground over background at the target resolution; feathering the edge and dragging brightness down removes the colour fringe between fore- and background.
Driving a periodic value into a metaball-style radius demonstrates beat-synced animation once a network clock source is connected.
Driving its radius/scale from a beat-locked value makes it pulse in sync with detected tempo.

ui:OutputSettings.note: The "magic" 0,0 resolution means "inherit the current output resolution"; set a real fixed resolution instead when a texture's aspect ratio must stay square regardless of the window, e.g. for a uniform shadow sprite.
The final image is rendered at a resolution you set (or override) at the top, much like a game-engine frame, before any operators are stacked on.
The "magic" 0,0 resolution: take the incoming image's size if one is connected, else the output window's; aspect is preserved by cropping left/right, never top/bottom.

op:Lib.image.analyze.WaveForm.note: A per-column brightness scope (the film-industry "waveform") that reveals clipping and colour casts the eye misses — use it to spot where highlights blow out before grading, or to neutralise an existing cast channel by channel.
A live waveform readout helps judge where the image is getting too dark before pulling mid-tones up with color grading.
Shows the per-column color distribution of an image (plus a small vectorscope), so you can read which channels are clipping or where a tint sits before grading.
Its vectorscope mode plots a frame's colors on a hue wheel (with a skin-tone line) so you can read a reference's grade — but it only works on a portrait-shaped input.
Its vectorscope plots the image's colours around a hue wheel, exposing how extreme colours snap onto the RGB primaries — the artefact AGX tone-mapping smooths out.
Its vectorscope mode reveals an image's color distribution at a glance — e.g. that most colors cluster in desaturated orange with a few solid highlights.

op:Lib.image.color.ToneMapping.note: The smartest way to tame over-bright pixels that would otherwise clip: prefer it over simply pulling gain or bloom intensity down, because it compresses highlights rather than crushing them.
Compresses over-bright values toward a center curve; the AGX mode desaturates blown-out colors so a clipping bright yellow rounds off instead of flat-lining the waveform into pure primary.
Pulls clipped super-bright HDR values back into range; the AGX mode blends smoothly toward white instead of letting channels rail to pure R/G/B, avoiding the harsh cut-off look on intense colours.
Place it after [Bloom] so highlights roll off correctly once the glow is added.
An over-bright HDR background (values ~6×) defeats the anti-aliasing when you blend lines on top; re-bloom then tone-map back under 1.0 so the composite edges resolve instead of fringing.

ui:ColorEditor.note: Click the brightness (B) field to toggle modes, and hold Ctrl while dragging to push a colour far past 1.0 into HDR — bright enough to light the scene more than a point light.
A small HDR badge appears once a color's brightness exceeds 1 (Ctrl-drag to push it there); the on-hover mini interpolation curve shows how a gradient blends, exposing OKLab's odd dips through zero.
HDR colors above 1 are now flagged with a triangle (also in gradients), making glow and HDR work much easier to read.
Swatches surface every color used in the project; Ctrl-clicking a swatch selects and centers all operators that use it, so you can audit and unify a palette across a graph.
A pixel keeps its RGB colour even where alpha is 0, so a transparent foreground can still bleed coloured fringes; match fore- and background colour (e.g. both black) to avoid them.
TiXL renders into RGBA16, so colours can exceed 1.0; Ctrl-drag a swatch upward past white to make an HDR value (the up-arrow marker), which is what gives [Bloom] and emissive materials their punch.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetFog.note: Fades the scene toward a colour by camera distance; with too few floor subdivisions the fade reveals banding across large triangles, so subdivide heavy geometry to keep distance-based shading smooth.
Fog is fiddly to tune when its tint animates over the course of a scene.
Stacked after the projection to confirm the post-effect still composites correctly with other scene effects.
A touch of fog adds depth cues and a sense of perspective to an otherwise flat SDF scene.
Stack a second fog node with zero alpha around emissive geometry (laser eyes) so global scene fog doesn't dim things that should glow from the dark.
A quick way to add depth cueing to a 3D scene before rendering it to texture.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.CylinderMesh.note: Prefer the simpler cylinder over a high-res beveled mesh; halving its column count is invisible until very low, so trimming subdivisions is free polygon savings.
Build a small cylinder, reduce its segment detail and shrink its radius/height, then draw it stacked on a cube to compose a Lego-style brick from primitives.
Scatter a mesh instance across a grid of points; rotating the instance fails on a single-axis float because the rotation input expects a vector.
Rotating a capped cylinder leaves the cap normals wrong, so a [SetMaterial] shine reveals the cap shading not updating with the rotation — a known unfixed normal bug.

op:Lib.point.modify.MoveToSDF.note: Snap a scattered point cloud onto a surface by feeding it the points and an SDF field — the way to plant sprinkles on a torus; follow it with point-space transforms to align and randomise the now-surface-bound instances.
Pull a set of points onto a distance-field surface to preview how the field will drive them before committing.
Distributes grid points onto an SDF surface (e.g. a smooth-combined sphere "monkey"); move the source points and they redistribute, then draw a mesh at each to clad the shape.

Its amount factor (drivable per-point from an FX attribute via SelectPointsWithSDF) and surface-offset mode control how far points pull onto the surface; step count and max distance trade quality for speed.
Pushes points along their forward axis onto the nearest SDF surface — the trick that anchors tentacle/leg targets to a ray-marched cave wall.
The output point's Z axis faces away from the surface normal it landed on, which is what lets meshed claws/legs orient correctly against the wall.

Move grid points onto an SDF surface, then subdivide and displace them again with noise to wrap an electric, crawling sheath over any field; keep them in view with [CamPosition] so the grid follows the camera.
Named as the tool to snap particles onto an SDF surface, used heavily in the Ashborn demo.
Snapping a scanning point set to the nearest SDF surface, then drawing original→snapped as lines, gives a way to emit particles from a shape's surface/edges (edge = near-zero distance).
Clamps noisy moving points onto a box SDF surface to make particles wander over a cube; a flat-faced SDF can hit a gradient/gimbal edge case where it fails, fixed by a tiny field rotation.
Because it also aligns point normals to the surface, you can grow oriented geometry off an SDF; on flat faces a gimbal lock collapses orientation, dodged by a near-zero rotation of the field.
Cited as another node carrying a reusable field-normal helper worth copying into the custom point shader.

op:Lib.point.modify.RandomizePoints.note: Stack it as a processing step (vertical, Blender-modifier-stack style): scramble positions before snapping to a surface, then a second instance after to randomise rotation — order in the stack changes the result.
Randomize the W attribute across a cloud so a downstream quad draw renders each instance with its own size/color/rotation.
A line of points, randomized and colored from a gradient, stands in for a row of lights to preview Artnet output before any hardware is connected.
Animate the random phase to keep points churning; pair with a color randomization for saturation/brightness jitter across the set.
A new uniform-randomization mode spreads points evenly (a regression that previously couldn't be done); note its Scale knob now writes to point stretch, while W stays free of scaling by default.
Randomize position and per-axis rotation right after emission to break up uniform spray into a more organic scatter.
Gains a uniform-scale parameter, stops clamping HDR colors, and fixes color randomization.
Insert it behind a points generator and raise the W channel to vary per-instance scale, plus push rotation to ~360 on each axis so stamped copies face random directions.
Spread a cloned point cloud across the whole scene by setting all three position-randomize axes to the same value (e.g. 5) for a uniform scatter.

Scatters points along their orientation (z = surface normal) and its gain/bias controls the distribution of the offset, so most points cluster at the outer shell while a few reach far, giving an animated shimmering surface.
Adds per-point colors and scaling to an instanced point set; its random seed is a float, so sweeping it yields smooth deterministic animation rather than discrete reshuffles.
Randomize a chosen point attribute (e.g. F1 used as scale) and shape the spread with gain/bias and a value curve so only a few buildings tower while most stay short.
Because a particle system outputs ordinary points, you can randomize their size or position downstream just like any point set — particles are point fields, not a closed type.
Used to perturb a point buffer so a RenderDoc capture shows a compute-shader dispatch whose position/rotation buffers can be inspected.

op:Lib.numbers.int.logic.PickInt.note: Drive a procedural choice from a counter through a pick op's multi-input to flip between variants (here swapping sprinkle materials) without rewiring.

ui:Annotations.note: Press Shift+A to wrap selected operators in a named annotation group — useful for parking a finished "divergent" experiment before duplicating it and iterating on a cleaner version.

"Tour points" upgrade free-floating scene comments into an ordered, navigable walkthrough you attach to operators — select a node, add a tour point, reorder by drag — to turn an example project into a guided tutorial.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.SphereMesh.note: Swapped in as an alternate sprinkle shape while iterating; any mesh can instance at the scatter points.
Pair a primitive mesh with a draw operator to make geometry visible in the output; shrink the mesh radius before composing it with other shapes.

op:Lib.image.use.NormalMap.note: Feed noise through it into a material's normal input to fake surface bumps when matching a reference, then tune roughness to place the reflections.
A texture used as a normal map must be authored at a fixed resolution, or its aspect ratio drifts with the render size and distorts the surface detail.
Generating a normal map (rgb-signed mode) from a render to drive forces — but the produced map comes out flipped vertically versus the geometry's own normal buffer, a bug noted live.

Multiply a blurred render of bright screens against a Fresnel/rim pass built from the render target's normal buffer to fake screen-space ambient rim lighting on all geometry edges — no shader rewrite needed.
When generating a normal map to drive forces, it must be a *signed* normal map (negative values for both sides) — switch its mode accordingly or the consumer won't read direction correctly.
Set its output to RGB-signed to produce the negative-valued normal map that a screen-space force needs from an ordinary image.
Blooming a rendered texture then converting it to a normal map to drive a downstream particle force.

op:Lib.field.adjust.PushPullSDF.note: Smooths out and reduces apparent complexity of a busy distance field.

Raster3dField places a procedural texture onto SDF geometry; push-pull offsets the computed distance toward the surface like an extrude, and its amount input accepts a noise field to carve cobblestone-style relief.
Cycling a color band by animating a push-pull offset only sweeps once; repeating the field to loop it must happen before the push-pull, or the repeat has no effect.

op:Lib.field.space.RepeatPolar.note: Build a radial star from a stretched capsule/cylinder SDF by repeating around Z, then intersect with a centered ring SDF to clip the spokes into a banded star shape.

ui:Field.note: Fields can return not just distances and colors but vectors, and vector fields compose under multiply/transform like any other field.
Adding a noise texture into the volumetric sampling to fake smoke/dust inside the light cone.

The core F1/F2 explanation: a TiXL point is a fixed 64-byte GPU struct (position, rotation, color, scale) where the unused 4th lanes of two 3-component vectors leave two spare float attributes; every generator, modifier and consumer can write or read F1/F2, making them a universal channel for masks and side effects.

Why soft point sprites fight the Z-buffer: a filtered edge has partial opacity, so an alpha-cutoff threshold decides which fragments write depth — too low gives noisy edges, too high makes circles hard.

With a point light inside an inverted/back-facing mesh, specular highlights vanish while diffuse still shows — the PBR shader doesn't flip the normal for back-facing triangles; a reproducible rendering bug worth filing.

ui:ProjectSettings.note: A tip walkthrough explaining why all time in Tooll runs in bars rather than seconds, how to add a soundtrack to a project and dial in its BPM rate so procedural animation stays synced.

Redesigned per-project playback/audio: enable playback settings, pick soundtrack vs. live-performance mode, set BPM and a sync offset for tracks that don't start on the downbeat, and choose bars/seconds/frames for the timeline ruler; live mode adds tap-tempo VJ playback and external MIDI-clock sync.

The per-project dependency checkbox now actually controls whether one project sees another's assets, enabling a shared "footage/effects" project that event-specific projects pull from without leaking private resources.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.CustomSDF.note: A heavy raymarched scene driven by an orbit camera with fog, set to a fixed full-HD output, as the test case for viewport-slicing optimization.
Sculpt a cave/environment volume from a signed-distance primitive that downstream ray-marching can both render and snap points onto.

Its generated code wraps the distance function and branches on render path, so the same node can be extended to return a color path as well as distance — the basis for distance-driven fractal coloring.

Feeding a custom field into both the shape and its own [SDFToColor] crashes because the node references its own ID before it's defined; duplicate the node (a separate ID) for the color path to break the self-reference.
Raymarch a custom SDF, add [SetFog] for depth, and drive a deterministic per-step random camera position (via [Steps] into [PerlinNoise]) so scrubbing the timeline reproduces the same scenes.

op:Lib.particle.force.FieldVolumeForce.note: Attract particles to a distance-field surface and transfer the field's color to each particle as it collides with the surface.
Now superset of FieldDistanceForce, with reflect-on-collision and apply-color-on-collision options that sample the SDF's color onto colliding points.
Build a collision floor by feeding a plane SDF into a field volume force; enabling collisions makes particles bounce off the field surface.
Overhauled to support colorization and optional collisions; [ParticleSystem] also gains an FX emit-velocity vector that pairs well with SDF point selection.
Pull particles into an SDF volume and hold them: zero the repulsion so points outside are drawn in but settled points inside aren't bounced back out.

The SDF-based sibling of the mesh collider: same parameters minus normal-sampling distance, and because a box SDF's distance is far more consistent than a mesh's per-face distance it gives smoother, more reliable repulsion.
Combine several sphere SDFs into one field and feed it as a force to pull particles toward the SDF surfaces; zero the drag and disable collision reflection for an orbiting two/three-body attractor.

Emit a single particle (count -1 takes the source buffer size of one) gated by [Once] or a reset trigger, push it with a volume force, and read its evolving position/orientation back via [PointsToCPU] to drive a flying camera.

The powerful SDF-driven force: separate attraction (outside) and repulsion (inside) with adjustable decay, plus surface-bounce reflection with randomizable bounciness; invert the volume to trap particles inside a shape like a container.
A single plane field with low repulsion and no damping makes particles oscillate above/below the surface into a sine-wave-like motion.
To bounce falling particles outward off a floor, bump the plane SDF with an added sphere and set attraction to zero so reflection scatters them sideways.

On a fractal/complex SDF the distance field away from the surface is jagged, so the force pulls particles along non-obvious contour gradients — sample-distance controls how that gradient normal is estimated.

A controllable inside/outside volume push driven by a signed distance field; the speakers weigh it against a mesh-collision force and conclude converting the mesh to an SDF is the practical way to get inside/outside testing.

op:Lib.particle.ParticleSystem.note: An emit-velocity control lets you randomize and scatter points slightly as they spawn, loosening an over-uniform emission.
Emit once per beat by gating emission with a beat trigger; widen the held trigger window to emit a burst of frames rather than a single instant.
The new Emit Velocity Factor scales launch speed; switching emit mode from sequential to lines lets DrawLines render the trails as shaded ribbons.
Emitting from a line into a particle system is the minimal starting point for a falling-spray effect; pair it with a draw operator and an orbit camera before adding any forces.
Spawn from an existing point buffer so emitted particles inherit the source layout, then draw both the originals and the particles together.
Emit from a rotating ring inward, then shape the swarm with forces — emit velocity near zero so particles don't overshoot the attractor.

Emit particles off a mesh's points so they fly along the surface normals; the system writes particle age into F1, which [MapPointAttributes] then maps onto a glow gradient so particles brighten as they age.

Emit-once from input points with a long lifetime; lifetime −1 auto-derives a value from input-count over buffer size, and points carry a default emit velocity so they drift outward even with no force (negative velocity fires them inward through the centre).

A constant emit seed leaves streaks (same points re-emitted each frame) while a changing seed scatters fresh positions; buffer size vs. emit count caps how many simulation steps each particle survives.

Emit from a derived center point and drive emit-velocity from a live input value; add a [TurbulenceForce] for organic drift. Disable Z-buffer writes on the draw if particles flying toward the camera read wrong.

Relative cost budgeting for a particle scene: drawing the points with supersampling dominates (~100 units), the sim itself ~10, a 3D-noise turbulence force ~15, a texture-sampling force ~10, a directional force ~2 — so optimize the draw before the forces.
Recap of the minimal setup: emit event points, add a force, render the buffer as points.

Lifetime reworked: a default of -1 derives the max lifetime from emitted-point count and buffer length, and particle age written to the w attribute is now normalized 0–1 so you can drive color or scale over a particle's life.

Emit a single particle (count -1 takes the source buffer size of one) gated by [Once] or a reset trigger, push it with a volume force, and read its evolving position/orientation back via [PointsToCPU] to drive a flying camera.

To make an emitter deterministic for a demo, drive its reset trigger from a keyframed boolean so jumping home re-seeds it; run-but-hide it early by filtering to a single point, then reveal by raising the count.
Framed as the session's main topic: a real-time GPU particle system positioned as a flexible-but-controllable middle ground rather than a Houdini-class simulator.

It needs input points plus at least one force or it stays empty; internally it builds a particle buffer (carrying velocity) separate from the result point buffer, since particles need acceleration that plain points don't.
Emit count appends into a ring buffer up to max-particle-count, so you can freely vary or animate how many points you emit per frame to grow particle complexity over time.
Disabling its Update freezes the whole simulation for inspection, and is also how you pre-warm particles then hold the result as a static abstract scene.
Never drive max-particle-count from a per-frame-changing value: reallocating a large GPU buffer every frame fragments VRAM and can crash; only change buffer size in coarse steps.

Particles default to flying along +Z, and the right-handed coordinate system forces an awkward choice where local X points left; matters whenever you transform or orient emitted points in particle space.

Emit velocity has a non-zero default (like Unity) so particles visibly move out of the box; zero it for neutral-force setups. The emit-velocity-factor reads an emitter attribute (e.g. F1) so you can shoot some emitters fast and leave others static.

Speed multiplies how much of each particle's velocity is applied per frame, so you can slow, freeze, or briefly reverse motion — but it only affects velocity-based forces, not ones that move position directly.
Drag removes a fixed percentage of velocity each frame (scaled by speed), needed because forces like turbulence keep pumping energy in and would otherwise make the system explode.
Set max-particle-count to -1 to size the buffer to the emit set, then emit only on a beat boolean to spawn a fixed batch and keep it alive indefinitely.
A long-lifetime, zero-emit-velocity emitter seeded once per beat hit: each emission re-seeds, particles live ~40s, and the age attribute drives a gradient so they glow then fade.
Source points and live particles are different buffers, so a value must be written into the particle at emission to survive into the render — you can't just read it from the seed points afterward.

op:Lib.field.space.TransformField.note: A new checkbox rotates the field's stored vectors along with the space when you rotate a vector field, otherwise direction and space disagree.
Scaling a field now adjusts the returned distance too, avoiding ray-march artifacts that a raw scale introduced.
You can't scale a field directly; route it through a field transform to scale and rotate the SDF volume.
Rotating/translating the field that drives a color ramp aims the gradient like a projector, so the "light" can come from any direction.
Rotating/translating a noise field before sampling it (e.g. with a [PerlinNoise3] driving the rotation) animates the pattern that colors a raymarched SDF.

op:Lib.render.basic.Text.note: Read the current playback time, stringify it, and route it into a text operator to build an on-screen time readout.

To benchmark CPU-bound draw-call cost rather than fill-rate, wrap one [Text] in a [Loop] and feed the loop's [GetFloatVar] progress into a position offset — each iteration is a separate draw call, and frame time climbs past ~200 calls regardless of GPU.
Its multi-input lets you stack arbitrary content (e.g. text alongside a 3D strand) into one horizontally sliced view.

op:Lib.string.logic.PickStringPart.note: A short tip-of-the-day walkthrough showing how to split a text into lines/words/characters and step through the fragments to animate text, then pointing to a simpler random-string shortcut.
Split a comma-separated string and pull out the n-th fragment by index, so a counter can step a label through a list of names or words.
Index into a multi-line string with a stepped beat counter to swap displayed words in sync with the music.

op:Lib.numbers.int.process.FloatToInt.note: Convert a smoothly animated value into discrete steps by flooring it (or float-to-int and back), so a linear ramp becomes a staircase that advances exactly once per integer.
Quantising a continuous level into an integer so it can index a structured buffer fed to a shader.
Flooring keeps the integer part (1.999 → 1), giving a step index you can use to pick list items per beat.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.TriggerAni.note: Feed its pulse into a randomized phase so each beat re-rolls point positions; cleaner than wiring AnimValue for the same job.
Turn a MIDI note value into hit triggers (detect increases only) to fire a trigger-animation per note; a sliding-history buffer can plot the activity over time.
Convert a changing value into a one-shot by choosing increased/decreased/changed, then pipe the resulting boolean into an animation trigger to fire an emit or restart on each step.

Build a "trigger keyframe" you don't have natively: step an animated value up with Shift+C per key, floor it to an int, and feed change-detection into a one-shot animation so each step fires an event.
Build a threshold gate: compare an incoming signal against a level, and when it crosses, fire a trigger animation — the manual equivalent of a sample-and-hold/gate from a modular synth.

op:Lib.io.audio.AudioReaction.note: Reacting to raw audio amplitude can be too imprecise and non-reproducible when you need frame-exact, repeatable timing — manual keyframes may beat it for tight sync.

A short tip showing how to feed external audio into the graph and use [AudioReaction] to drive a particle scene — clearing the background and re-seeding randomness on each beat, and steering camera and noise with the level output.
FFT/audio-reaction read the global merged output buffer (the same master buffer written when exporting a video), which is why per-stem reactions aren't possible today without per-channel routing.
Pick an audio input device, set its gain via the level meter, then create this op and connect it to a scene to drive audio-reactive effects; the chosen device/gain is stored per project.
Switch its output from a pulse trigger to a continuous level to drive a parameter smoothly from mic input.
Its accumulated-level output ratchets upward on each detected peak; raise the bias and lower the threshold to make that counter advance faster, useful as a step index.
Switch its source to external-device tapping mode for live VJ use instead of the project soundtrack; the colored input-level meter combines left/right channels correctly.
Tap an audio-reactive value to fire a graph response (e.g. re-randomizing points) on a beat or hit.
Feeding a live external-mic level into a graph; crank the amplitude hard because raw input levels arrive tiny.

op:Lib.numbers.float.basic.Modulo.note: A practical sync rig: animate a value, feed it through a wrapping operator, and drive a pulsing radius so you can tap keyframes in on the beat while audio plays.
Take a rising step counter mod 2 to flip a 0/1 scene-offset, then halve and phase-shift two camera animations so adjacent scenes overlap during a crossfade instead of cutting.
Wrap a rising counter back to a beat-relative phase, e.g. to retrigger a [Bloom] flash once per bar.

ui:DopeSheet.note: Inserting or removing keyframes forces a recompute of the curve values, and the editor surfaces glitches there.

By default it only shows keyframes of selected operators; the new auto-pin mode keeps every animated parameter visible while you jump between ops, and Shift+K clears the pinned set to start a fresh animation group.
A short tip on snapping keyframes precisely in the timeline: pinning parameters, switching the ruler from seconds to bars/beats/ticks, and using ALT to scale and insert keyframes onto snap targets.
Hold Alt to drop warp points inside a selected range, then stretch the interior non-uniformly to retime a block of keyframes without moving its ends.
Right-click a keyframe layer and "set sequential values" (start at 0 or 1) to renumber a row of index keys cleanly instead of leaving them at fractional in-between values.

Copy keyframes and paste them onto any other animated parameter; paste lands the first key at the current time, and for a multi-channel target you must rename/select the matching X/Y curves so the pasted channels map correctly.

ui:CurveEditor.note: Hundreds of keyframes squashed to a parameter's value range become practically invisible; auto-scaling the curve to the visible keyframes makes a dense track readable again.
Curve editing in the dope sheet was re-implemented to be more efficient, so you can work with far more keyframes.
Expand a parameter row to get an embedded curve editor aligned to the dope-sheet, so you can edit values and tangents in place instead of switching to a separate view.
A new "space evenly" command redistributes selected keyframes, but it aligns to the *strength* differences between keys rather than to uniform time — useful for cleaning up hand-tapped beats.

A regression confirmed live: keyframes set to *constant* interpolation stop updating the value when you jump/scrub to them (smooth/linear work fine) — bisected to a November curve-interpolation refactor.
A second, separate bug: switching keys to constant doesn't clear the previously-checked interpolation mode, so the right-click menu shows two modes ticked at once.

op:Lib.flow.TimeClip.note: Beyond switching between demo scenes, time clips double as labelled annotations to carve a soundtrack into named sections you can navigate.
A time clip only gates whether its connected branch is visible during its span on the timeline; vertical order is irrelevant, it must be wired into something, and on its own it does nothing.

Plain dragging a time clip moves only its enable-window, not the keyframes inside; Alt-drag instead and it time-remaps, stretching or compressing the inner animation's local time — powerful but very easy to get lost in.

The remapped time-clip drives a child's local time from 0→1 over its window, and that same local time feeds the child's internal keyframes — the basis for reusable, retimeable chapter/title animations.

A walkthrough of TimeClips: how clips on the timeline gate which parts of a graph get evaluated per scene, and how dragging or stretching a clip remaps the time fed into its sub-graph, with the colour cues (orange/red) that signal time remapping and time-scaling.
Drop a clip onto a layer/branch to enable it only within its span; name clips (press Return) and duplicate them to lay out demo sections without keyframing a selector.

op:Lib.particle.force.TurbulenceForce.note: Record per-note audio volume into a keyframe track and pipe that envelope into a turbulence force so particle motion accelerates on louder notes.
Added to a particle setup to introduce visible swirl and structure into otherwise straight emission.
Now supports value fields as its noise source.
Animate its noise phase (low frequency, into [Time]) to keep a captured particle swarm churning into ever-changing shapes instead of a static blob.

Stack it with a collider so both shape the same swarm; SDF/field forces are cheap here (the field is sampled only twice per particle) so combining several colliders to herd particles costs far less than ray-marching them.
Adds swirling motion that intensifies over a particle's life, eventually dissolving the shape into noise once it dominates.

Emit from a derived center point and drive emit-velocity from a live input value; add a [TurbulenceForce] for organic drift. Disable Z-buffer writes on the draw if particles flying toward the camera read wrong.
Drawing small oriented meshes at particles only reads well once they're stretched along their flight direction by a turbulence force, instead of all facing the same way.
Forces generally edit velocity, not age — so per-age effects aren't yet possible; discussed as the natural place for a future amount-from-attribute/field-graph driver.

Frequency is really noise scale (high frequency = small scale); changing it live injects near-random jumps far from center, and floating-point drift slowly degrades any long-running turbulence into noise. Animate phase from a slowed time for gradual flow.

Feed it a field through its amount input to mask where turbulence applies — e.g. a plane SDF so only particles above the floor get disturbed; reverse/scale the field's distance range to shape the falloff.

op:Lib.render.gizmo.GridPlane.note: A quick background reference plane handy for rough blocking and judging proportions of an effect.

op:Lib.particle.force.RandomJumpForce.note: Makes particle ribbons jump abruptly on note triggers — a striking look, though it can clash with a calmer mood.

op:Lib.image.generate.noise.Grain.note: A built-in animation-speed knob avoids wiring a time source, but a "frozen" time mode is what lets a static result stop invalidating and actually cache instead of recomputing every frame.
Where grain sits in the chain — before or after tone mapping — changes the result dramatically, so its placement is a deliberate choice.
Set a non-zero speed (≈55) so the grain animates instead of sitting static, then keep the amount low so it's barely perceptible.
Adds noise structure to an opaque image but does nothing useful on a transparent one, so apply it before things go transparent.
Adds animated film grain but is costly because it samples a per-pixel random texture; pin its animation speed to zero to cut the expense when you don't need the motion.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.Time.note: A built-in animation-speed knob avoids wiring a time source, but a "frozen" time mode is what lets a static result stop invalidating and actually cache instead of recomputing every frame.

A short tip on overriding the time that drives an animation: wrap a rendered texture in a command-time operator and feed it a custom time signal (a sine, a remapped random, a beat) to scrub, loop, or jump regions of a timeline non-linearly.

Walks the time-source modes: idle/FX time keeps animating while paused, local time follows a [SetTime] remap, playback time ignores remaps, and "last started" time suits damping — pick per situation because each behaves differently when paused or looped.
Prefer time over a frame counter for animation so pausing yields an analyzable still frame and re-renders match exactly — important for testability.
Drive the noise-shape phase from a time source so the selection field animates on its own.
Drive an animation by wiring a running time value into a noise offset so the displacement evolves every frame.
Read the current playback time, stringify it, and route it into a text operator to build an on-screen time readout.
Wire it into a noise operator's time input to give an otherwise static field continuous animation over playback.
Its "always evaluated" output flag forces re-evaluation every frame wherever it's wired, which is how a downstream operator keeps reading the live playhead instead of a cached value.

op:Lib.field.generate.vec3.ToroidalVorte.note: Twists particles into a torus/mushroom-cloud shape — faking such a swirl by hand turned out harder than driving it with this purpose-built field.

op:Lib.image.generate.noise.FractalNoise.note: Drive a height field from one color channel; gain and bias are the knobs to reach for when shaping the silhouette of the mountains.

Feed a noise field into the attribute sampler to push point positions along a single axis, turning a flat grid into a rolling surface; rotate the noise 90° and raise its scaling so the pattern aligns with the grid plane.
Offset and warp-offset values shift where the noise samples, and animating those (rather than the underlying field) is enough to make the displaced surface drift like water.
A 90s-era cloud cheat: render fractal noise unlit to a texture, map transparent-white→white, and stack many offset planes via repeat-at-points to fake volumetric mist.
Noise added to a point cloud and its phase animated to create the moving particles used to demonstrate motion blur.
Push its gain/bias toward high contrast to threshold the noise into leopard-like blotches, then ease off for softer edges.

Drive it from [Time] and crank the output resolution to stress fill-rate: a procedural noise this heavy stays real-time at 256² but falls below 60 fps at 4K, making it a quick way to gauge a GPU's shader throughput.
Listed among operators that gained the bias-and-gain control to reshape their output distribution or response.
Cleaned-up and updated in this release.

op:Lib.image.generate.pattern.SinForm.note: Used to carve a valley through a noise-based mountain range.

op:Lib.field.adjust.SetSDFMaterial.note: Read the plain distance from ground level, perturb it with noise, then map that distance onto a color gradient to paint a terrain SDF.

op:Lib.render.postfx.SSAO.note: A restrained post chain — screen-space occlusion plus bloom and glow, no color grade — is enough to finish a procedural scene.
Adds contact shadows in the crevices between geometry, giving instanced/cluttered scenes much more depth; tame it by lowering opacity or its boost settings if the darkening is too strong.
Rendering a very dense radial point cloud with PBR shading, a point light, depth-of-field from the depth buffer and SSAO approximates ribbon-like volumetric structures (at heavy point counts).

Banding/hard occlusion edges come from poor depth-buffer precision under a narrow field of view; push the camera's near clip plane up to just in front of the object (and match the SSAO range) to restore precision.
Its depth-range parameter ignores geometry beyond a set distance, letting you keep occlusion on a foreground shape while excluding a background plane.
Ambient occlusion does nothing until you wire the scene's depth buffer into it — forgetting the depth connection is why the pass looks like it has no effect.

op:Lib.numbers.float.random.PerlinNoise.note: A small noise source on a camera's rotation parameter gives a subtle handheld camera-shake.
Wire a noise generator into a locator's position to make an object wander smoothly through space rather than follow a fixed path.
Tune the per-axis amplitude to constrain wandering motion to a plane — drop the vertical amplitude so the object circles rather than bobs up and down.
For spin, feed noise into rotation and multiply its ±1 range up to 360°; lower frequency for slower turns and reduce octaves so the rotation holds a steady speed instead of jittering.
Add it on top of a smooth oscillator to layer in organic jitter that still roughly follows the base curve; raise its frequency to make the wobble faster and rougher.
Named as the available 3D volume noise when a Voronoi/Worley pattern was wanted but isn't yet exposed as a field.

Wiring a slow Perlin noise into the depth-of-field focus distance adds constant organic focus drift for free; a bias/gain control biases it to dwell near a center distance and only occasionally swing to the extremes.
Break a target point's value out and add Perlin noise to give a rig autonomous drift so you can watch the motion without dragging the gizmo.
Feed Perlin into a light intensity then shape it with bias-and-gain to get a believable on-mostly-off flicker — a reusable technique for any flickering value.
Reused once more to flicker a bloom/glow intensity, standing in for an audio reaction when the soundtrack can't be used.
Feeding it into a rotation and pushing the gain (gain/bias rename) makes the curve sit at one extreme then snap to the other, producing organic, sudden jerks rather than a smooth wobble.
Listed among operators that gained the bias-and-gain control to reshape their output distribution or response.

op:Lib.render.gizmo.DrawCamGizmos.note: Shows a camera's frustum within the scene, but only once you switch the output window's camera mode from auto to viewer.

op:Lib.render.gizmo.VisibleGizmos.note: Toggles whole sets of helper elements on and off via the gizmo grid icon in the output window — handy for hiding scaffolding during playback.
Inside a force's gizmo subgraph it just repeats arrow points oriented along the force to draw the on-screen indicator.

op:Lib.particle.force.VelocityForce.note: In a stack of guiding forces, a velocity push triggered on each note nudges particles forward for a beat-responsive surge.
Pumps energy in or out along a particle's existing heading without changing direction, with min/max speed clamps so the flow can never exceed or drop below a set velocity.
New force that pushes particles forward along their velocity — handy for syncing bursts to music.

op:Lib.point.generate.PointTrail.note: Pipe a particle system into a trail to record and draw the ribbon each point leaves behind.
A short tip showing how to feed animated, noise-displaced points into a cyclic trail buffer to draw streaking trails, then layer extra noise and fog on the result.
Records past point positions to draw motion trails; reworked to be more consistent and to avoid gaps in the lines, though its interpolation is still not perfectly smooth.
Records each point's recent positions so [DrawLines] can render motion trails behind animated points.
Keeps particles crawling across a mesh surface (emit once with buffer -1); add a point trail to draw twirly lines following the surface, balancing against turbulence that would pull them off.
Trailing snapped-angle particles into lines, with fade-out on over-long segments, produces ship/circuit-like structures.

op:Lib.point.generate.SpherePoints.note: Replicate a small sphere of points on each emitter point, gradient-color them, and jitter their radial distance to build a soft scattered burst.
Better for giving points an outward orientation than for connecting them, when you want shards radiating from a center.
Raise the point count and shrink the radius to wrap a dense shell of points around an object; follow with a randomizer to break the too-perfect spherical surface.

op:Lib.particle.force.ReconstructiveForc.note: Drives particles toward an arbitrary target point set — e.g. replicated grid points randomized into an abstract structure — to reform them into a shape.
Pulls scattered particles back toward an arbitrary target point set within a spherical volume — letting them dissolve into chaos then reform into a logo/shape; ideal candidate for field support.

ui:GradientEditor.note: Procedural gradients and color lists let you randomly sample a constant gradient to tint a generated point set.
Shade instances across a distribution by editing a color gradient and a value curve keyed to W; Alt-click adds keyframes to reshape the mapping.
Gradients can be snapshot-blended only when they share the same number of color stops; mismatched step counts can't be interpolated.
Curve overlays now show on hover and while editing, making the different gradient interpolation types legible at a glance.
Gradient editing now supports undo/redo, and evenly distributing steps before interpolation now includes the final step.

A fully-saturated rainbow gradient in OKLab mode can emit out-of-gamut/negative colours that flicker on an emissive mesh; switch that gradient to Linear interpolation (or clamp the output) to stop it.

op:Lib.point.sim.PointSimulation.note: Stamp/bake the carefully animated motion of a small control-point set so a downstream reconstructive force can guide the main ribbons precisely through the scene.

The pre-ParticleSystem operator; still genuinely useful as a per-point damper, so the proposal is to rename it (e.g. DampPoints) rather than retire it, since ParticleSystem now covers its old particle role.
Acts as a damper for jumpy targets: each frame it eases points a fraction toward their new positions, so nearest-point snapping no longer pops; keep the step below 1 (above 1 explodes).

Useful as a damping/smoothing pass on a noisy point buffer, but it behaves like a particle sim and reassigns point indices — so it breaks any setup that depends on stable per-point identity. (The maintainer wants to rename it "damp points".)

The legacy point-damper: it mutates the incoming buffer in place instead of copying it, so it smoothly interpolates positions toward a switched target and is ideal for de-noising jittery sampled or fed-back point data.

Why the old per-force sim operators were abandoned: hard to control and confusing to wire, which is what motivated the unified particle system; this one survives, to be renamed to a "damp points" role.

op:Lib.image.color.AdjustColors.note: Lowering exposure and saturation on an environment image tones down image-based lighting before it's converted for the scene.
Named as the hue/saturation/brightness tool many reach for, contrasted against lift/gamma/gain as the more powerful grading approach.

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.ScreenCloseUp.note: A five-minute introduction to color grading in Tooll, centered on the lift/gamma/gain controls of the ColorGrade operator, reading the WaveForm operator's scope, and comparing before/after with CompareImages.

ui:LocalTime.note: Using local reference time to dedupe a double evaluation is tricky because motion-blur passes also key off time — a workaround here, not a clean fix.

Why a long-running installation's time eventually loses smoothness: a 32-bit float can't encode enough precision after days/months, so single scalars are headed to double precision (vectors stay float because the GPU wants float).
Time is measured in musical bars, not seconds: four beats per bar, one bar ≈ 2s at 120 BPM, so animation rates expressed in bars stay locked to the beat while still drifting in longer cycles.

op:Lib.flow.LoadSoundtrack.note: Dropping an MP3 onto the timeline makes an audio clip and auto-generates its spectrum image; an auto-playback toggle lets it sound without being wired into the graph.
Add it to a project to override the default 120 BPM so every bar-based animation re-times to the track's tempo.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.SetTime.note: A short tip on overriding the time that drives an animation: wrap a rendered texture in a command-time operator and feed it a custom time signal (a sine, a remapped random, a beat) to scrub, loop, or jump regions of a timeline non-linearly.
How remapping local time upstream changes what an operator reads as "now": feed it a looped/offset value and downstream time-driven nodes follow that remapped clock.
Overwrites the time flowing down the graph (absolute or relative), so a duplicated scene branch can run at a frozen or slowed-down time; note it re-runs the whole particle sim per branch.
Freezes or remaps the playhead for everything drawn after it, so you can drive a sub-scene's animation from any value (e.g. a wave) and play that segment deterministically forward and backward.
Render one scene twice with offset clocks: duplicate the group, feed each copy a different time so the same deterministic animation appears at two phases at once.

Build a manual preloading screen: wrap the whole demo in a branch, animate a sweep 0→100 so every shader/clip is touched and pre-compiled behind a cover layer, then cut to live time. (As of 4.1 the player does this automatically.)
Override playback time from a sampled ramp so a simulated IO clip loops on its own clock — note simulated event data replays this way but audio clips, living in a separate update loop, will not.

op:Lib.image.use.RenderWithMotionBlur.note: It re-renders its subtree across several time offsets to accumulate blur, so anything it drives must source time per-pass rather than from a single frozen value.

Renders a scene over several passes with the time nudged slightly each pass to accumulate true motion blur, which works especially well on fast-moving animated particles; feed it a camera and MSAA-rendered scene.
Accumulates several sub-frame passes at slightly offset times for true long-exposure blur (no post fake); cost scales with pass count, so preview cheap and crank passes only at final render.
Real multi-pass motion blur (not a fake screen effect) that requires a fully deterministic scene; slow but yields true blur over the sub-frame motion.

op:Lib.image.generate.pattern.Raster.note: A short tip walking through the versatile Raster operator: its presets and knobs, then driving it from an input texture and stacking offset copies into a CMYK-style halftone print effect.
Give it an explicit resolution to draw a crisp high-res overlay on top of a deliberately low-res background image, decoupling the effect's detail from the source's pixel count.

op:Lib.numbers.int2.process.ScaleResolut.note: Considered for sizing the shadow pass but skipped — too many edge cases; a plain manual int2 was preferred for predictability.
Stack it in a chain to multiply the incoming requested resolution by a factor (e.g. ×4) rather than typing absolute pixels.

op:Lib.image.use.UseFallbackTexture.note: Supplies a default texture when none is wired; prefer the multi-input "use first valid" variant over this two-input one when you need to chain several optional sources.

Each point is a billboard stretched to the sprite texture's aspect, so a non-square sprite makes the dots elliptical and canvas-dependent; dive in to find the fallback sprite and set its source a fixed square resolution.

ui:Asset.note: Markdown is used throughout the help text, where square-bracket links open assets or operators directly in the library when clicked.

How on-demand previews work: hovering an image generates its thumbnail on the first frame, then it is cached so the next hover is instant; thumbnails are written as small alpha-PNGs to a temp folder so deleting them just forces regeneration.

Previews share one large GPU texture atlas with a fixed slot count (~500); when full it evicts the least-recently-used slot, so the live preview cost stays bounded no matter how many images you browse.
A cached small PNG loads far faster than decoding the full-resolution source, so the preview path checks for an existing thumbnail before ever touching the original image.

Mip-maps store pre-scaled copies so a minified sprite samples a blurred level instead of aliasing; off by default for the small cost, only worth it when a textured thing changes size on screen (particles being the classic case).

Asset paths are now a single fixed `project:asset/folder/file` form with forward slashes and case-sensitivity, always relative to the owning project; absolute paths and startup-relative `./` paths still resolve but won't migrate or drag-drop.

ui:SymbolLibrary.note: Right-click "set thumbnail" on a symbol to capture the current output as its library preview — works for both the operator and its example scene.
How per-project assets, presets and thumbnails are being reorganized into a `.meta` folder (temp/generated ones into git-ignored `.temp`) to stop preset/snapshot confusion.

Why a math/number namespace renamed `Value` to `Float`: a `Float` op is a precise type, not a meta-type, and the trade-off of searchability (you want it to surface when searching "value" *and* "float") drives the naming and synonym choices.
Curated library-operator thumbnails live in a versioned "meta" folder beside the operator (committed with the repo), separate from the throwaway per-project previews in the temp folder.

Pin an operator, right-click and "set thumbnail" to capture a representative frame; after pressing Update the library shows that preview on hover and while dragging — invaluable when scanning many operators for a VJ set.

The pinnable browser groups symbols by namespace; "examples" holds the walk-through how-to operators worth dragging out and double-clicking, and "lib" holds the built-ins sorted by category (field, image, mesh, points…).
Click an operator to jump to its namespace in the library and browse siblings; namespaces like "numbers/logic" group the value-manipulation operators (compare, freeze/hold, LFO) you'd reach for.

op:Lib.image.color.ChannelMixer.note: Its "alpha to grayscale" preset visualises the alpha channel as brightness, revealing that stacked semi-transparent blobs approach but never reach full opacity.
The cheapest way to isolate a color channel: zero out the channels you don't want — a single shader op rather than the multi-buffer cost of converting to and from a buffer.

op:Lib.image.use.Blend.note: A shipped example wires two image inputs with the blend-mode index driven by an integer so it cycles through every mode for comparison.
Two-input compositor with separate colour and alpha blend modes plus per-input colour multipliers; mismatching the two modes (screen colour, normal alpha) is what makes opacity seem ignored.

op:Lib.image.analyze.GetImageBrightness.note: Can drive the alpha-blend term so a layer's own brightness decides its transparency, useful for masking from luminance.

ui:Composition.note: A maintainer's intro to the project's Discord forum structure and the unstructured meet-up format; context, not an operator lesson.
Overlay blend mode leaves mid-grey untouched while pushing shadows darker and highlights lighter, acting like a contrast/structure boost when you composite noise or a second image at low opacity.
TiXL's feedback is built to keep intensity in a meaningful range rather than blowing out to widescreen, but it stays hard to control precisely.

ui:RenderSettings.note: Geometry draw operators expose a hardware blend mode (normal/additive/invert…) that controls how the drawn pixels combine with what's already in the render target — additive on a black background reads as transparent, but a correct multiply isn't available there.
Video export gained audio output, no pre-render format conversion, and an auto-increment version-number checkbox so you can re-hit render with the panel docked to save numbered work steps.

A short tip explaining how an image operator's resolution is resolved: the "magic" 0×0 default pulls resolution from an incoming texture if present, otherwise from the output window, and how -1 or an explicit size overrides that.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawBillboards.note: Points stretch in equirectangular projection because billboards stay camera-parallel; switching draw-billboard orientation to point-rotation (look-at target with translation reset) fixes the distortion at the seams.
Consolidates the many older point-drawing methods into one flexible operator; its color-variations option can map a point's w attribute to per-point color.

Feed it a texture and enable texture-atlas mode to give each point a different sprite cell; build the atlas procedurally by slicing the viewport into a grid and using the loop index to place a character per cell.
Unlike camera-locked point sprites, billboards can be rotated in point space, so feeding rotated squares into an invert blend yields kaleidoscopic tile patterns.
Renders per-point camera-facing sprites; a random-face parameter (among many others) picks which cell of a texture each billboard shows, useful with point colors over a video texture.
Scatter a quad or billboard across a point set to turn flat sprites into a 3D cloud you can then fog and light, rather than drawing each instance by hand.
The existing operator for camera-facing (screen-space-aligned) point quads, the thing to reach for instead of hand-rolling an orient-to-camera setup.

op:Lib.image.generate.basic.RadialGradie.note: A dark-to-transparent radial, flipped so the center is clear, makes a vignette-style mask whose animated offset gently reveals the framed subject.
Gain/bias reshapes the falloff to get a tight bright core that tapers out, e.g. a glowing star centre.

Unlike [LinearGradient] it uses distance from a center point; tuning its width and offset turns the falloff into a clean ring/circle — the kind of "discover the two knobs by playing" lesson it's used for here.

Reworked to share parameter order and direction with [LinearGradient]; the breaking change is that ping-pong mode is now shifted one period, and it gained an optional dither-noise amount that only costs a buffer when non-zero — switch it on to kill visible banding on smooth gradients.
As a transition mask its default stop produces a tell-tale visible edge; switch interpolation to smooth to hide where the wipe begins.

op:Lib.point.generate.PointsOnMesh.note: Scatter shaded point sprites (not spheres) across a loaded mesh's surface; the close-up fade-out seen here was flagged as a bug to fix.

Scatter 100k points over a mesh, then use F1 (a plane-distance SDF mask) to drive a peel-away reveal: displace along normals by the mask, fade via [MapPointAttributes] gradient, add masked noise, and bloom the bright tips into a burning dissolve.
Scatters points across a mesh surface (here a sphere) as the raw material for sparkles or particle emission.
Random surface scatter with a count knob; bring the count and point scale down when the labels get too dense to read.
Why scatter flickers on an animated mesh: as triangle areas change, the cumulative-distribution sampling reshuffles every frame — switch to a per-face scatter for stability.

op:Lib.field.space.ReflectField.note: Reflect a plane SDF to turn a half-space selection into a single thin slice, so an effect driven by that selection affects only points near the plane's centre rather than everything above it.
Mentioned as the not-yet-shipped force that would steer particles along a field's normal vector with a rotation offset.

op:Lib.render.postfx.DepthOfField.note: Needs the depth buffer wired in; set focus distance manually and raise the amount so foreground subjects drift in and out of focus.
Reduce the amount when the blur overwhelms the frame, and lean on the environment's background blur to soften distant areas separately.
Rendering a very dense radial point cloud with PBR shading, a point light, depth-of-field from the depth buffer and SSAO approximates ribbon-like volumetric structures (at heavy point counts).

Wiring a slow Perlin noise into the depth-of-field focus distance adds constant organic focus drift for free; a bias/gain control biases it to dwell near a center distance and only occasionally swing to the extremes.
Pin it and darken/neutralize the blur so bright out-of-focus elements recede, pulling attention to the sharp center of frame.

Applied after a composite/blend it can still blur by depth using the scene's depth buffer, so you composite first and rack focus afterward; pair with a focus distance to fuse a 2D edge-pass into the 3D image.

op:Lib.render.postfx.TemporalAccumulatio.note: Floated as the cure for ray-march sampling noise: blue-noise sampling plus temporal anti-aliasing accumulates jittered samples across frames so the flicker resolves into smooth volumetric light.
Smears frames over time to mimic CCTV/old-camera trailing and to denoise; always apply grain *after* it, or the accumulation averages the grain away.
A built-in feedback blend of the previous frame with the incoming one: a high blend factor smears fast motion into soft trails, useful for taming jittery animation.
Acts as damping for images: raise the amount to smooth a jittery, frame-inconsistent source (e.g. a slow per-frame detector) into a steadier result over time.

op:Lib.image.fx.distort.Displace.note: Drive image displacement from any grayscale source; its modes choose between gradient-based and intensity-based directional push, and feeding a generated pattern yields controllable glitch distortion.

op:Lib.image.generate.pattern.RyojiPatte.note: Drive image displacement from any grayscale source; its modes choose between gradient-based and intensity-based directional push, and feeding a generated pattern yields controllable glitch distortion.

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.DetectEdges.note: Dropped in with mirror-repeat wrapping to dress up a flat output into something more interesting on the fly.
Run on a rendered texture to extract outline/contour structure you can feed back as a mask or as a source for generating new points.
Running edge detection on the scene's normal buffer instead of the color image yields much cleaner, sharper edges — the normals change abruptly at creases even where color doesn't.
Use an edge-detection pass as a mask so a glitch displacement only bites at object outlines.
Feed it a blurred noise pushed through [Steps] to get hard edges first; sample-radius, strength and contrast each shape the result, and a bias/gain knob would make a useful addition.
Pairing an edge detector with a points-on-image scatter as a quick generative starting point when you want points seeded from image features.

op:Lib.image.use.Combine3Images.note: Feed a separately transformed copy of the same image into each of R, G and B to build a manual chromatic-aberration / RGB-split glitch.
Pack three unrelated source images into R/G/B so one texture can feed several independent point-attribute channels.
A two-image custom operator carries presets for blends and color-grading; the same custom-code approach extends to points and geometry, not just images.

op:Lib.image.transform.TransformImage.note: Mentioned while hunting for the texture's aspect ratio so the orthographic projection matches the light image's proportions.
Scale and rotate an image (here the gradient mask) in 2D before it feeds the next stage.
Feed a separately transformed copy of the same image into each of R, G and B to build a manual chromatic-aberration / RGB-split glitch.
A quick horizontal mirror by stretching the texture -1 on X so the on-screen hand matches your real hand; later superseded by the camera input's own flip flag.

op:Lib.render.camera.ReuseCamera.note: How to share one camera definition between two places in a graph: capture the main camera once and reference it downstream so the projector and the view stay locked to the same viewpoint.

Pull a camera reference from a camera operator's extra output and replay it on a second sub-scene so both render from the identical viewpoint, then composite them (one edge-detected, one plain) in post.
When feeding [SortPoints] a camera, note it caches and must be re-evaluated (plugged into the draw path or set to auto/look-at) before the sort sees the correct camera position.

To build a fisheye/distortion rig without breaking projections, copy this node and set the reference as an object transform rather than as the active camera, so the matrix rotates geometry instead of replacing the view.

Extract the active camera out of the render flow with a camera-reuse node so a [CamPosition] read gives you the eye position to orient billboard-style points toward — note it must be evaluated (grouped/executed) before the points that consume it.
A camera read placed after the camera in execution order creates a loop; reuse the camera (or read its position) at a point that evaluates *before* the points you orient, then orient before drawing.

op:Lib.image.use.DepthBufferAsGrayScale.note: Exposes the z-buffer as an image you can feed into a mask blend to do per-depth post selection, the workaround for the missing per-object ID pass.

op:Lib.flow.Loop.note: To benchmark CPU-bound draw-call cost rather than fill-rate, wrap one [Text] in a [Loop] and feed the loop's [GetFloatVar] progress into a position offset — each iteration is a separate draw call, and frame time climbs past ~200 calls regardless of GPU.

op:Lib.io.video.mediapipe.HandLandmarkDe.note: Feed it a [VideoDeviceInput] webcam to get a 21-point-per-hand buffer entirely on the GPU; visualize the points directly and build interactions from them without ever reading back to the CPU.

Why the MediaPipe nodes don't stall the rest of the graph: they run on a separate thread and only push a new buffer when a fresh camera frame arrives (~30 fps), so the particle sim keeps rendering at full rate — the cost is the CPU readback/upload around them, not the per-frame graph.

op:Lib.image.color.ConvertFormat.note: Camera frames arrive as BGRA8 while TiXL works in 16-bit RGB; if a downstream detector misbehaves on a flipped or recolored image, convert the texture to the format the consumer expects rather than fighting the channel order.

op:Lib.point.modify.FilterPoints.note: Pick out the tip point of every chain by filtering with a stride (segment count) and a computed start index, e.g. to place a claw only on each leg's last joint.
Scatter-select a subset of a dense cloud and randomize their scale to sprinkle glitter highlights over a generative scene.
Isolate specific landmarks (e.g. index 4 and 8) by index, then combine two filtered results, to pull just the thumb-and-fingertip pair out of a larger point buffer.
Keep only a random subset of points (say 30 of them) so the tall instances scatter sparsely across the grid instead of every cell getting one.
Why you can't shrink a particle buffer cheaply: deleted points are flagged with NaN size rather than removed, since recomputing buffer length needs a slow GPU readback with frame delay.
Hard-code a count and start-index to split one point buffer into two halves, then pair them into lines — a setup that works regardless of how many points exist upstream.

op:Lib.point.combine.BlendPoints.note: Its blend-with-range mode crossfades whole point paths (great for camera animations), but blending orientations runs slerp, which can suddenly flip an axis at the quaternion hemisphere boundary — and you can't fix it per-point in a compute shader since neighbors aren't accessible.
Blending two single-point buffers yields their midpoint on the GPU — a cheap way to derive a center anchor (here between two fingertips) without any CPU readback.
Used to interpolate an extra control point (a top-edge midpoint) between two corner points so a warp grid gains a draggable handle.
Blends one point buffer toward any other (mismatched counts wrap/twist); its mix-with-sliding-range mode morphs points into the target progressively, driven by buffer position or an attribute.

op:Lib.point.helper.PointsToCPU.note: Read a GPU point buffer back to the CPU and pull an attribute (position) off it directly — you don't always need the intermediate data list.
Reading a whole mesh's points back to the CPU just to follow one index is wasteful; put a [FilterPoints] (length 1, wrapping start index) before it so only the single needed point crosses to the CPU.

Read a GPU point buffer back to the CPU, then pull a specific point's position out of the attribute list by index — note the index input sits below the primary input, so it's easy to miss when wiring.
Pull GPU point data (position plus quaternion orientation) back to the CPU so a single simulated point can feed camera or transform inputs.
Why orientations are stored as a four-component quaternion, not Euler angles: quaternions have no gimbal lock or discontinuities and blend cleanly via spherical interpolation.

op:Lib.numbers.data.utils.GetPointDataFr.note: Read a GPU point buffer back to the CPU and pull an attribute (position) off it directly — you don't always need the intermediate data list.

Read a GPU point buffer back to the CPU, then pull a specific point's position out of the attribute list by index — note the index input sits below the primary input, so it's easy to miss when wiring.
Mentioned as the "drop point information" already carrying per-point data the shader could read to display decimals.
