op:Lib.numbers.vec3.Vec3Distance.note: Feed it the two CPU-read landmark positions to get the live distance between two fingertips as a single float you can drive parameters with.

op:Lib.numbers.float.trigonometry.Atan2.note: Getting an emitter to fire along a line between two points: derive the angle with [Atan2] (radians, remap to degrees), but rotating a single point's axis by that angle fights coordinate conventions — splitting it into two stacked [TransformPoints] (set a known base rotation, then rotate in point space) is what untangles it.

op:Lib.render.transform.RotateAroundAxis.note: Getting an emitter to fire along a line between two points: derive the angle with [Atan2] (radians, remap to degrees), but rotating a single point's axis by that angle fights coordinate conventions — splitting it into two stacked [TransformPoints] (set a known base rotation, then rotate in point space) is what untangles it.

op:Lib.particle.force.DirectionalForce.note: Drop one in as gravity to make emitted particles fall; stacking a second directional force lets you nudge flow direction, but a strong second force quickly dominates and looks fake.
Driving a force's strength from a per-change trigger ramps it up smoothly over the emitted particles instead of restarting an animation from the same frame every time.
Add it as gravity by feeding a directional vector (scale to Y only for clean up/down) so the whole particle field responds to hand height — a trivial-cost force compared to texture-sampling forces.
A constant directional push (gravity by default), combinable additively with other forces; its visible gizmo just orients arrow indicators along the direction.
Its "random amount" really means per-particle variation of the force direction/strength (a naming bug noted on stream).
To bounce falling particles outward off a floor, bump the plane SDF with an added sphere and set attraction to zero so reflection scatters them sideways.

op:Lib.image.fx.blur.FastBlur.note: Swapped in for a cheaper, more striking blur when the plain blur looks flat.

At least 10× faster than [Blur] for large kernels with near-Gaussian quality; it uses a down/up-sampling pyramid, so increasing the level count barely costs more because the highest passes operate on tiny buffers. (Dual-Kawase, by the Playdead/Inside devs.)

A Kawase-style blur that stays smooth where a sample-count blur bands and crawls: roughly 5–20× faster at large radii and clean enough to feed [Steps] for hard posterized gradients without multi-pass tricks.
Reach for it as the cheap go-to softening pass when an intermediate buffer looks too crisp.

op:Lib.particle.force.TextureMapForce.note: Push particles using a texture as a force field; feeding it a rendered normal buffer pushes particles off surfaces, but the force maps to screen space, not world space — a step toward depth-buffer/normal-based collision like game engines do.

Pushes particles using a normal map in *screen space* rather than world space — exactly what you want for camera-driven interaction; needs a signed normal map, and a negative amount pulls particles toward the silhouette center instead of away.

Accelerates particles along a connected normal map (which must use signed-normal mode); a twist parameter rotates the sampled direction — 180° reverses it — and a confine-depth parameter keeps particles within a visible distance from the camera.

Pulls particles toward bright areas of a signed normal map in screen space; twist the pull angle to swirl or (at 180°) repel, great for logo animations and combinable with 2D image effects like reaction-diffusion.

A *screen-space* force: render a layer to a texture, derive a normal map, and push a particle system away from bright areas — easy to art-direct but breaks for 360° output because the push is camera-plane aligned.

op:Lib.io.video.mediapipe.ImageSegmentat.note: The selfie/multi-class segmenter masks the subject from background but runs notably slower than the basic model; pick the lightest model that gives an acceptable mask since it's the heaviest stage in a webcam pipeline.

Why the MediaPipe nodes don't stall the rest of the graph: they run on a separate thread and only push a new buffer when a fresh camera frame arrives (~30 fps), so the particle sim keeps rendering at full rate — the cost is the CPU readback/upload around them, not the per-frame graph.

op:Lib.render.analyze.GpuMeasure.note: An unsupported, rough operator for timing how fast a sub-graph runs; named here as a way to measure part of a pipeline, with the caveat that it needs work and shouldn't be relied on.

op:Lib.io.video.VideoDeviceInput.note: This is the webcam/capture-card operator (anything Windows exposes as a DirectX video device); its device list is the awkward part, currently pulled in via OpenCV.
Video device input now takes webcam input; Artnet/NDI/Spout/MIDI input ops were updated too.

It already exposes a flip-vertical flag, so flipping the camera image needs no separate [TransformImage] node — drop the extra op even at low resolution, on the principle that free optimizations are always worth taking.

ui:SkillQuest.note: How the guided feature-test window turns each new feature into a step-by-step manual test with pass/skip/fail and Markdown links, doubling as a discoverability tour and a release-acceptance checklist.
New visual unit tests render image sequences for major projects and compare them to references, catching breaking changes before release.

A non-linear, map-of-topics learning system where each level shows a hidden target output and you must rebuild it; later levels compare animated value-histories, not just images, so you must reason about the curve rather than just wire nodes.

The new home-panel learning track: a dependency-linked map of levels (basics → images/gradients → points → particles/SDF) you unlock by completing prerequisites, toggleable in settings, with each level a graph you edit to match a reference.

ui:SkillMap.note: An internal authoring tool for laying out tutorial topics as cells, setting unlock rules (complete one prerequisite vs. all of them) and styles for the quest graph.

Authoring tools: the Skill-Map editor wires level-unlock dependencies, and the Tour-Point editor attaches Markdown step text and blinking "call-to-action" highlights to specific operators/parameters; tour points round-trip to clipboard as Markdown for editing and LLM grammar passes.

ui:SkillQuestLevel.note: Building a level: the reference output, the editable "solution" feeding it, and disconnected building blocks the learner wires up; a step that says "connect X to the point's position" via tour points — beware a multiply-blend that lets the wrong wiring still pass.

ui:VariationWindow.note: How per-parameter snapshots work: instead of flagging a whole operator, right-click individual parameters to expose only those to a snapshot, then capture/recall named states from the empty-input background view.
Step or blend between saved states with cursor keys or an index input, so a cycling integer animation walks through presets live.
Grouping snapshot-controlled operators into a new symbol breaks the mapping, because snapshot entries are keyed by the child operator's id, which changes once it moves inside the new symbol.
Idea for laying presets out in a fixed 2D coordinate landscape (via dimensionality reduction) so nearby points differ only slightly and you sample a blend by mouse position.
Why the per-parameter capture stays flat by default: an earlier prototype prompted for a snapshot group every time, but 99% of uses needed only one group, so grouping was dropped for speed.

Snapshot vs. preset: a snapshot is stored on the operator's own symbol and saved into it, while a preset stores the instance parameters into the composition that uses the operator — same blending mechanism, different owner.
Plan to bind number keys to jump to snapshots (and control+number to reset), giving muscle-memory recall similar to bookmarks for graph views and output pins.
As of 4.2 snapshots and variations live in a per-project meta folder (thumbnails plus data) instead of the global roaming settings, so that folder must be kept and backed up.
Select an effect, choose which of its parameters to vary, and generate random variations with adjustable randomization strength; any result you like is saveable as a preset.
Idea for teaching parameter values: store the correct state as a snapshot so the level can warn when a learner changes a parameter that shouldn't move and hint the target value on the slider.

op:Lib.numbers.vec3.PerlinNoise3.note: Feed it into a transform's rotation input to drive smooth pseudo-random orientation; keep the output range small (≈0.2) so motion is subtle.
Lower the octave count (1–2) to trade fine detail for smoother, more continuous large-scale movement.
A first points lesson wires a 3D noise into a point's position and a gradient sample into its color/size, demonstrating that point attributes are just inputs you connect like any other.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.DisplaceMeshVAT.note: Vertex-animation playback driven by translating a mesh's second texture coordinate (TexCoord2); randomizing that F2 coordinate per instance inside [RepeatMeshAtPoints] desyncs otherwise-identical copies so they animate out of phase.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.RepeatMeshAtPoints.note: Repeats a mesh at each point but overdraw gets expensive fast with overlapping tori; reduce density to recover frame rate.

A short tip contrasting two ways to multiply a mesh across scattered points: baking copies into one large mesh (cloning) versus drawing the same mesh repeatedly per point (instancing), and the trade-offs in memory, performance, and what you can still modify afterward.
Scatter cube instances over a single-row grid by drawing the mesh at grid points, adjusting the grid's Y count to one layer and the cube pivot to sit on the ground.
A 90s-era cloud cheat: render fractal noise unlit to a texture, map transparent-white→white, and stack many offset planes via repeat-at-points to fake volumetric mist.
Rebuilding combined geometry every time the driver point moves is the slow path; prefer drawing a cached mesh at points so only the transforms update.
Wire a points set into one input and a mesh into the other to stamp a copy of the mesh at every point; chain it after the points generator that defines the layout.

It bakes instances into a new buffer in local coordinates, so per-instance vertex deformations (like rotating a VAT-animated copy) don't carry through cleanly — you need a custom shader attribute or updated texture to push extra per-copy data.
Stack a [CubeMesh] along [LinePoints] and use its built-in twist (orientation axis Y) plus stretch to spiral the stack — staying one ~1200-face mesh rather than many draw calls.
Scatter a quad or billboard across a point set to turn flat sprites into a 3D cloud you can then fog and light, rather than drawing each instance by hand.

Lay out a flat grid of points and instance a cube at each to block out a city; raise the cube's pivot to its base so the points sit at ground level and scaling grows buildings upward instead of from their centre.

op:Lib.image.use.CustomPixelShader.note: When inline custom-shader code outgrows its usefulness: it lacks helpers like hash functions and external file references don't survive copy-paste, so promote the body to a real `.hlsl` asset for maintainability and syntax highlighting.
Origin/attribution caveat for borrowed shader snippets: a GPU hash function lifted from public shader-hashing lore (IQ-style) carries no clear license, worth crediting in a comment.
Inside hand-written shader code the real hazard is an unrolled for-loop: a huge fixed count can crash the app, so every loop should carry a hard maximum.

Sample the scene normal buffer in a custom pixel shader and dot it against a fixed view vector to build a Fresnel-style rim glow; `1 - dot` gives the edge falloff, a power param tunes intensity, and `discard` on zero-length normals removes the background.
A two-line shader that forces RGB to white while keeping alpha re-bakes a non-premultiplied logo so its glow behaves — a fast way to fix the transparent-edge base color.

After declaring frequency/amplitude params in the buffer at the top of the file, add a sine offset to the UV coordinates to get a live displacement; nothing moves until amplitude is raised above zero.
The custom point shader uses string-replacement to splice your snippet, equivalent to authoring a full compute-shader operator from the menu template but far quicker to experiment with.

A community AI tool generates HLSL for these nodes from a prompt (e.g. "give me a vignette"), with undo history for iterating on the script — the open problem is mapping generated uniforms to operator parameter names.

The fastest way to learn shader work: it hands you an HLSL stub that must return color C (default white, an RGBA vector); read UV from 0,0 bottom-left to 1,1, and sample one of the built-in gradient/image inputs to map position or a parameter to color.

The low-level path: a pixel/vertex-shader-stage helper sets shaders, constant buffers, samplers and resources, runs the draw, then restores the previous GPU state — copy an ImageFX effect's innards here to go fully manual.

op:Lib.point.modify.CustomPointShader.note: The shader alternative to factor remapping: write `pfx1 = 1 - pfx1` to invert a factor, and wrap it in `saturate()` to clamp 0–1 so tiny values don't go negative.
Spherize a point cloud in a few lines: read the original position, normalize it, then lerp original→normalized by a parameter to force every point onto a sphere of equal radius.

Insert it after drawing points to run an on-the-fly compiled GPU snippet per point; each point exposes an f variable running 0→1 across the set, and writing to position gives sine displacement while writing to the w attribute yields a wave-shaped field—fast enough for millions of points.
