Its built-ins for developers: F is the normalized 0–1 point index; sample_gradient(t) recolors by a value; bias() remaps 0–1 with a gain/bias control; FX1/FX2 are two writable attributes downstream ops can read.
Write a height-derived value into FX1/FX2, then drive later modifiers (scale, [AddNoise] strength) by that attribute — e.g. no noise at the base, lots at the crest.

Its field input accepts an SDF chain ([BoxSDF]/[SphereSDF]): call get_distance(p.position) inside the shader to read signed distance per point and deform/colorize by the field; combine with [TransformField] for moving effects.
Recolor points by deriving a value from p.position length into sample_gradient — but a metal material can override the written point color, so the tint may not show.

Address instances individually in a point shader — e.g. test the point index and tint every n-th one — to vary a repeated mesh per-copy, since RepeatMeshAtPoints alone doesn't carry per-point color through.

When you generate points on the fly in shader code you must `return` early in the template, or it writes its own default points over the ones you produced — read the template source before assuming your output survives.

Per-glyph layout maths: copy the right digit's even-length point block, offset by place-value spacing, then multiply by the target point's scale and rotation so [RandomizePoints] on those targets jitters each number independently.
Source the displayed number from the target point itself (e.g. `number = position.x`) instead of a fixed list, turning the glyph layout into a live readout of any point attribute.
Write a vertex/point's own position into an fx attribute (`pfx1 = p.position.x`) so a downstream stage can read coordinates back as data — a general "stash a value per point" trick.

A shader-resource binding bug: undeclared/auto-assigned `register`s let the GPU silently reorder or zero a buffer, scrambling inputs — pin every texture/buffer to an explicit `register(...)` so binding order is deterministic.

Carry a value from emission into a particle by writing it to fx2 (fx1 already holds age) at the emit shader, then reading fx2 in the draw shader — the pattern for "tag each particle at birth and recall it later," since emitter and particle buffers are otherwise separate.

Adding a field input: the field/SDF call and its texture must be registered at the right contiguous register slot (after the int params), and multi-input resources after it shift the count — a binding-order constraint when extending the shader.
`getFieldNormal(position)` plus `RotateToFace`/look-at the normal orients instanced meshes to the field surface; swapping the normal's component order picks which mesh axis aligns to it.
Orient-to-SDF preset: read distance for colour via [SampleGradient], read the field normal to rotate, and drive scale by `1/(abs(distance)+1)` so points balloon near the surface.
A caching glitch: the point-shader output stays stale (frozen yet dirty) until the time input is nudged once, hinting at an evaluation-order issue around the time/mode inputs.

op:Lib.render.scene.LoadGltfScene.note: Context for an Assimp-based multi-format importer demo (FBX/PLY/point clouds) that can also export finalized point/mesh buffers out of TiXL — and the wish to finally get GLTF skeletal animations working.

Loads complete glTF scenes (not just single meshes), auto-combining textures into the correct channel maps for physically-based rendering; expand the scene setup to inspect each node and its material textures.

ui:IdleMotion.note: Even with no timeline running, the scene animates continuously at a steady rate — the always-moving "idle" playback that lets procedural setups breathe without keyframes.

ui:ProjectPanel.note: Install now writes to Program Files like a normal app, so project data lives under Documents (relocatable in settings) and settings/logs/backups under AppData-Roaming.

ui:PlayerExporter.note: The exporter now scans ahead and pre-compiles upcoming shaders (with shader-source caching so concatenated custom HLSL still hits the cache), removing the playback stutter older preloading missed.
Exporting a project as a standalone executable strips the undo/redo system to save resources, so editor-only tricks that rely on undo/redo (like preset blending) won't run in the exported player.

op:Lib.render.scene.DrawScene.note: Renders a loaded glTF scene and exposes overrides for the file's roughness and metallic values to tweak surface appearance.

op:Lib.render.shading.UseMaterial.note: To fold an imported scene into the mesh-effects pipeline, take the scene's separate mesh and material outputs: feed the mesh to a point-instancing draw and wire a material operator into the material slot.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.AbletonLinkSync.note: Syncs to any Ableton Link source on the network (Live, Traktor, Bitwig, TouchDesigner, VVVV, DJ gear); unlike MIDI it shares bar-phase, not just BPM, so bar-based timing locks perfectly.

ui:InfinitySlider.note: Hold right mouse to drag a value field around without changing its value, so you can escape a corner you've locked into.
Drag-anywhere control for pushing a parameter far past its normal range without a fixed maximum.

ui:ParameterPopup.note: The combined bias-and-gain curve acts like a tone curve: an S-shape adds contrast (gain), an inverse S flattens it; bias pushes values brighter or darker — one Vec2 parameter covers both shapes across images, distributions and easing.

op:Lib.image.color.Tint.note: Listed among operators that gained the bias-and-gain control to reshape their output distribution or response.
Paired color-adjustment operators that benefit from bias-and-gain; the larger one now does color cycling for generated effects.

op:Lib.io.video.NdiInput.note: Performance overhaul lets it handle a wide range of source formats and up to 4K footage reliably.

op:Lib.image.fx.feedback.AdvancedFeedbac.note: A deep walkthrough of the AdvancedFeedback effect: how its displace-along-a-slope feedback loop works internally, and a guided tour of nearly every parameter (twist, displacement, sample distance, shade, blur, color shifts, amplified edges, limit brights) and how to drive them for smoke-, water- and reaction-diffusion-like looks.
Successor to [AdvancedFeedback] shipping presets that produce fluid-like feedback looks.

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.Dither.note: Adds a retro dithered look; exposes blend modes plus bias-and-gain, exemplifying few-controls/wide-range effect design.

op:Lib.image.generate.noise.WorleyNoise.note: Two new noise variants added to the noise toolkit.

op:Lib.image.generate.noise.ShardNoise.note: Two new noise variants added to the noise toolkit.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawMeshAtPoints2.note: Offers many options for scaling instanced geometry by a per-point attribute such as normalized particle age.

op:Lib.particle.force.SnapToAnglesForce.note: Nudges particle velocities toward a set of defined angles, producing clean grid-like structures.
Experimental: constrains particle motion to fixed angle steps (e.g. 45°) for circuit/chip-like trails, but currently aligns to the screen plane only, so it can't yet be viewed freely in 3D.

ui:ControlBar.note: Beat-tapping gained shortcuts: Z to tap, X to resync to measure start.

ui:FocusMode.note: With nothing selected, press P (or Ctrl+P in Focus Mode) to pin the current composition.
Switching between foreground and background control by clicking the white edge is now easier.

ui:Settings.note: Audio volume can be pushed above 1.0 (up to 1100%) to make playback louder than the source.
A beat-sync offset adds a fixed lead time so playback runs earlier, compensating for LED controllers or devices with large output latency (e.g. half a second).
Devices can be re-scanned from the settings window without restarting the app.

op:Lib.point.generate.SubdivideLinePoint.note: Add intermediate points along a straight reach-line so it can later bend or carry per-point noise like a flexible limb.

Insert extra in-between points along a sparse line (e.g. a three-point ring) so the shape has enough density to deform smoothly afterward; pair it with a close-shape flag when the source loops back on itself.
Subdivides paired point-to-point lines into many points so you can then displace the whole strand with noise.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawLinesAlt.note: The screen-space line renderer that also closes loops and emits regular lines via separator points; the hard part it solves is mitered corners, which is why miter limits exist in pro vector tools.

op:Lib.numbers.float.basic.Sum.note: Reach for it instead of chaining [Add] when you may later need a third or fourth summand: it takes N inputs and returns the same result, so you avoid stacking binary adds.

op:Lib.numbers.float.process.Damp.note: Drop one in after an audio-driven value to tame jittery reactivity into a smoother motion.
Feed an audio level through it to get instant attack and slow release (jump up immediately, ease down) — the practical way to get separate rise/fall smoothing from a single reaction value.
Smooth a jittery live audio level so the value coasts between peaks and you don't have to keep re-triggering the source.

op:Lib.io.dmx.ArtnetOutput.note: How DMX/Artnet works for stage lights: each fixture is dumb and only knows its start address, so you push channel values to a box's IP over UDP and it converts to the daisy-chained DMX wiring.
A stage-lighting setup points many moving heads at a shared target by driving each head's DMX dimmer channel separately and aiming them all at one locator position.

op:Lib.render.gizmo.Locator.note: A single animated locator acts as one shared position source you can plug into multiple consumers (a mesh and a light) so they always stay co-located.
Drive a light's position from the same locator that moves its host object so the light tracks the object exactly.
Instead of a hand-tuned focus distance, feed a moving locator's camera-space distance into depth-of-field so focus tracks a subject automatically.
A stage-lighting setup points many moving heads at a shared target by driving each head's DMX dimmer channel separately and aiming them all at one locator position.

op:Lib.point.modify.AttributesFromImageC.note: Audio-bars/frequency-modulation effect: sample a rendered texture's brightness into point X offsets, then repeat a single line across a 16×9 grid so each line displaces by the image under it.
Chaining two of these on one texture breaks: the texture-scale of the first one also scales the sample for the second, so they can't independently map different channels.
The current replacement for the obsolete [SamplePointAttributes_v1]: it reads an image's color channels onto point attributes the same way, just the newer operator.

op:Lib.numbers.color.HSBToColor.note: Clear an accumulation buffer with a slowly hue-cycling, low-alpha color so the built-up history tints over time instead of staying gray.

op:Lib.string.list.SplitString.note: Read a text file and split it into a line list to index into with an audio-driven counter.

op:Lib.io.file.ReadFile.note: Read a text file and split it into a line list to index into with an audio-driven counter.

op:Lib.image.fx.distort.PolarCoordinates.note: Unwrap a radial image into its linear "straightened" form (or wrap the other way); changing the radius shows how the circular content maps to a flat strip.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.CylinderSDF.note: Subtract a tall, wide cylinder from a plane to carve a channel or basin into the collision field that particles then flow along.
Build a radial star from a stretched capsule/cylinder SDF by repeating around Z, then intersect with a centered ring SDF to clip the spokes into a banded star shape.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.CapsuleLineSDF.note: Prefer a capsule over a capped-torus SDF for a simple straight spoke; it evaluates much faster for the same look.

op:Lib.point.modify.MapPointAttributes.note: Map a selection attribute (F1) to color so a hand-crafted field paints specific regions of a particle effect — e.g. turn one zone blue.
To invert a particle's F1 factor, set its input/output mode to F1 and draw a 0→1 / 1→0 curve in the built-in curve editor; ping-pong and phase modes let an F value repeat a pattern over time.

A meta-mapper that binds a chosen source (buffer order, F1/F2, random, particle age) to a target (color via gradient, scale, fade) — e.g. colorize points by the F1 mask an upstream SDF wrote, with a multiply color mode that's neutral at 1.

Write a per-point scale ramp from a gradient/curve into attribute F1 so repeated line spokes grow toward the rim, then wrap the strip into a circle with cartesian-to-cylindrical; note the polar transform currently always assumes the Y axis.
Write particle age into F1 (0→1) then drive a gradient lookup from it to colorize particles over their lifetime.

Pairing writes 0 at one endpoint and 1 at the other into an attribute that interpolates along the line; remap it through a curve (peaking mid-strand) to use as a per-point strength mask so ends stay pinned while the middle sways.
Floated as the way to surface a point's own XYZ as a displayable attribute, distinct from a texture-driven displacement.
When an attribute-remap sits between a shader stage and the draw, it can overwrite the value (colour, number) you wrote upstream — watch what each remap touches.
Writing alpha above 1 into a render target via an attribute remap blows out the blend; switch the colour to RGBA (unclamped) deliberately, or keep it normalised to composite correctly.

op:Lib.point.transform.PolarTransformPoi.note: Write a per-point scale ramp from a gradient/curve into attribute F1 so repeated line spokes grow toward the rim, then wrap the strip into a circle with cartesian-to-cylindrical; note the polar transform currently always assumes the Y axis.

op:Lib.flow.Once.note: Emit a single particle (count -1 takes the source buffer size of one) gated by [Once] or a reset trigger, push it with a volume force, and read its evolving position/orientation back via [PointsToCPU] to drive a flying camera.

op:Lib.numbers.bool.logic.Trigger.note: Convert a changing value into a one-shot by choosing increased/decreased/changed, then pipe the resulting boolean into an animation trigger to fire an emit or restart on each step.

Emit a single particle (count -1 takes the source buffer size of one) gated by [Once] or a reset trigger, push it with a volume force, and read its evolving position/orientation back via [PointsToCPU] to drive a flying camera.

op:Lib.numbers.vec3.Vector3Gizmo.note: Plug it into a camera's target or position input to get a draggable in-viewport handle for that vector, instead of typing coordinates.

op:Lib.render.camera.CameraWithRotation.note: Why a free-fly camera needs explicit pitch/yaw/roll and strafe parameters rather than a target vector: a fixed look-at target flips 180° as you cross it, and the editor's WASD fly mode is an editor feature, not part of the camera operator.

op:Lib.numbers.floats.logic.PickFloatFro.note: Receive a phone's position and quaternion (x/y/z/w) over OSC into a dictionary, then pull individual floats out by key to reconstruct an orientation.

op:Lib.point.helper.PointToMatrix.note: A newly added operator that turns a translation plus a quaternion (set rotation mode to quaternion) into a transform matrix you can apply to meshes or points; essential whenever Euler angles hit gimbal lock. (Spoken name was just "transform matrix"; exact operator unconfirmed.)

op:Lib.numbers.vec3.TransformVec3.note: Multiply a local point by a transform matrix to attach geometry to a moving object's own space (e.g. a line "shooting out" of a tracked phone), parenting things through their actual position data.

op:Lib.point.combine.PairPointsForLines.note: Connects two equal-count point sets index-to-index into line segments — the standard way to draw bones, rays or reach-lines between source and target points.
Multiply a local point by a transform matrix to attach geometry to a moving object's own space (e.g. a line "shooting out" of a tracked phone), parenting things through their actual position data.
Snapping a scanning point set to the nearest SDF surface, then drawing original→snapped as lines, gives a way to emit particles from a shape's surface/edges (edge = near-zero distance).

Pairing writes 0 at one endpoint and 1 at the other into an attribute that interpolates along the line; remap it through a curve (peaking mid-strand) to use as a per-point strength mask so ends stay pinned while the middle sways.

op:Lib.flow.context.GetPosition.note: A camera connector that exposes the current viewer's world-space position and forward direction; add a scaled direction to the position to keep an object pinned just in front of the camera.

op:Lib.flow.Switch.note: Drive its index with an int parameter to flip between connected camera/projector definitions; aligning the inputs in declaration order keeps the selected branch predictable.
A switch's index selects which child branch is evaluated; -1 disables all, and unselected branches consume texture memory but no render cost, making it a cheap scene selector.
Page between interactive scenes (an intro text and a rotating-torus scene) by switching its index, the building block for a click-driven multi-scene piece.
Both index between inputs, but [Switch] adds command/layer branching: index -1 disables all, -2 enables all, and positives wrap around — modes [PickTexture] lacks.

Why it's "Switch" not "Pick": as a command (not data) operator it can truly disable its branch — wrapping its index past the inputs cycles them, while magic indices -1 turns everything off and -2 turns everything on, so a faded-out branch stops updating and nearly stops consuming CPU.

op:Lib.io.http.WebServer.note: Serves a live page from inside the patch; the long-term vision is auto-exposing snapshot-flagged parameters so a phone scanning a QR code can drive visuals without a MIDI controller.

op:Lib.field.adjust.SpatialDisplaceSDF.note: Distinguish its sample-position from its offset input: sample-position picks where in 3D space each of the three internal simplex-noise functions (x/y/z) is read, behaving roughly like a seed, while offset and scale feed all three noise functions; avoid leaving the sample position all-zero or large structures look biased.

op:Lib.field.space.RepeatFieldLimit.note: Easier than a full field repeat to inspect a single displaced cell, since it bounds the repetition for a clearer look at one instance.

ui:TimeOverrides.note: A short tip on overriding the time that drives an animation: wrap a rendered texture in a command-time operator and feed it a custom time signal (a sine, a remapped random, a beat) to scrub, loop, or jump regions of a timeline non-linearly.

A walkthrough of TimeClips: how clips on the timeline gate which parts of a graph get evaluated per scene, and how dragging or stretching a clip remaps the time fed into its sub-graph, with the colour cues (orange/red) that signal time remapping and time-scaling.

ui:AnimationArea.note: A slow looping animated value can be wired straight into an effect's strength to make the look breathe over time rather than sitting static.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.GetFrameSpeedFa.note: A short tip on overriding the time that drives an animation: wrap a rendered texture in a command-time operator and feed it a custom time signal (a sine, a remapped random, a beat) to scrub, loop, or jump regions of a timeline non-linearly.
Multiply a frame-duration value into particle speed so movement stays frame-rate-independent regardless of vsync or load.

op:Lib.image.use.PickTexture.note: Used as the multi-input target when fanning several image operators into a single combined input.
Both index between inputs, but [Switch] adds command/layer branching: index -1 disables all, -2 enables all, and positives wrap around — modes [PickTexture] lacks.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.LastFrameDurati.note: Combine with [RunTime] and a value-keeper to read a rough per-frame or precompute time as a debug readout.
Multiply a frame-duration value into particle speed so movement stays frame-rate-independent regardless of vsync or load.

op:Lib.render.camera.OrbitCamera.note: A short tip walking through the parameters of the RandomCamera operator for procedural camera moves, plus how to drive its seed and shake inputs from a beat counter and noise.
Drop it in to drive the projector or view interactively — orbit the captured camera around the scene to preview the effect from changing angles.
Checked as a reference for how a camera op handles being read from two places — it updates the same way, confirming the frame-delay is structural rather than op-specific.
A heavy raymarched scene driven by an orbit camera with fog, set to a fixed full-HD output, as the test case for viewport-slicing optimization.
Frame an instanced scene by orbiting around its center, then lower the camera to find a flattering angle on the surface.
Rotating with the middle mouse used to silently change the distance between camera position and target, breaking saved camera animations; a fix keeps that distance fixed while orbiting.
Its distance and orbit-speed defaults give an automatic circling shot out of the box; just nudge distance for a closer or wider framing.
Connect its override-time input to bypass the internal spin rate and feed an external time/animation source to drive rotation precisely.
Wrap a point cloud in an orbiting camera with a little wobble and distance variation to get an automatic turntable shot.

op:Lib.numbers.float.process.Accumulator.note: Endlessly accumulating a phase eventually loses float precision (visible past ~100k points or when adding large per-frame amounts); the clean fix is to cross-blend between two RandomizePoints toward a zero-phase copy rather than snapping the phase back.
The escape hatch from time-evaluated animation to frame-dependent timing: it integrates an increment each frame, so a live knob (e.g. mouse X) ramps speed smoothly instead of snapping.

op:Lib.point.modify.LinearSamplePointAtt.note: Ignores point world-position and samples a texture/gradient purely by buffer order; right-click the gradient handle to switch interpolation from linear to smooth, and the "blend" stop mode splits the ramp into Photoshop-curve-like zones.

Live code-edit migrating an operator off the legacy point struct and the old W naming: add F1/F2 enum entries (appended, never inserted, to keep old projects working), move flags into an int buffer to avoid float-compare bugs, and apply the sampled value additively or multiplicatively per the mode.
The artist-friendly sine wave: sample a [LinearGradient] by each point's normalized index and map brightness to Y offset; set interpolation to smooth and animate the sample offset for motion.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawPointsShaded.note: Rendering a very dense radial point cloud with PBR shading, a point light, depth-of-field from the depth buffer and SSAO approximates ribbon-like volumetric structures (at heavy point counts).
The PBR path was aligned across all the main draw ops, and they can now all override color through fields.
A shaded-point alternative to drawing lines when you want a tapering strand built from sized points rather than constant-width segments.
Swapping plain point drawing for the shaded variant gives the scattered points lit volume for the burning-reveal look.
Its alpha-cutoff sets the opacity above which a fragment writes depth, and its depth-write toggle trades correct sorting for soft round sprites — with depth off, draw order alone decides overlap.

Inside multi-camera renders like [Equirectangle] its billboards shade wrong because the PBR view direction is taken as a fixed camera-facing vector instead of being recomputed per camera — a real shading bug, not a renderer fault.

op:Lib.point.modify.SortPoints.note: Sorts a point buffer back-to-front for correct alpha without depth-write, but measures distance to the camera origin (radial), so large camera-facing billboards can still sort wrong; reported bug when the count is a power of two.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.DisplaceMeshNoise.note: Raise (don't lower) its frequency to break a regular repeated mesh into organic distortion; keep the amount modest so structure stays readable.
Animating a mesh with noise displacement under a point scatter.

op:Lib.render.camera.OrthographicCamera.note: Effects like [SSAO] can misbehave with it; faking ortho via a perspective camera pulled far back with a tiny field of view restores the depth effect.

op:Lib.image.generate.noise.TileableNois.note: A cheap seamless noise makes a usable environment/reflection map; bias-and-gain turns the blurry field into readable light-and-dark patches.
Faster and better-looking than fading a non-tileable noise; for displacement, read it from a 32-bit single-channel (R) render format — higher precision and faster than 16-bit RGBA.

op:Lib.render.postfx.ProjectLight.note: Building out its inputs: position and target define the light cone, roll rotates it (in degrees), a projector-type enum switches orthographic vs. perspective, and step count controls ray-march sample quality.

Naming and ordering its shader knobs: surface intensity, ray intensity, shadow bias, shadow scale/falloff and ray decay each map to a slot in the packed buffer — keep the parameter order matching the buffer layout.
A dedicated shadow-resolution input lets the shadow render pass run at lower resolution than the main image, trading shadow sharpness for speed on the expensive ray-march.

A projector that casts a texture (orthographic or spotlight); disable its volumetric iterations and additively stack several copies to fake multiple colored screen-lights, each driven by its own texture.
For volumetric/directional shadows: feed it a point light and a separate camera reference (disconnecting the point light's own camera helps the shadows), then choose a projected image.

op:Lib.numbers.int.logic.CountInt.note: Why not to drive an animated shader from a frame counter: counting frames makes renders non-reproducible, so multi-pass video exports and unit-test comparisons break — use [Time] so frames are deterministic.
Pair a counter with a picker (texture, color, string) so each tick advances to the next item in a list — the staple loop for beat-synced cycling.

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.Steps.note: A short scripted tip showing how the [Steps] image effect posterizes a gradient into bands, then animating it by wiring counters and an LFO into its offset, gradient rotation, and highlight color.
Its stride/start-index controls let you sample every Nth point of a packed multi-chain buffer; feed it integer counts via [IntToFloat].
Posterizes a smooth gradient into hard bands, handy to manufacture crisp edges before edge detection.
Quantizes a rising time value into discrete, deterministic indices — one per bar — so you can address a different random seed per beat and still scrub back and forth reliably.

op:Lib.point.generate.PointTrailFast.note: A short tip showing how to feed animated, noise-displaced points into a cyclic trail buffer to draw streaking trails, then layer extra noise and fog on the result.
Uses a cyclic buffer so it's fast, but DrawLines can't tell where the buffer wraps, leaving one persistent gap in the trail line.

op:Lib.point.sim.SimNoiseOffset.note: A short tip showing how to feed animated, noise-displaced points into a cyclic trail buffer to draw streaking trails, then layer extra noise and fog on the result.

op:Lib.render.utils.RequestedResolution.note: How to read the resolution the context is asking for, to size a derived render target instead of hard-coding a number.

A short tip explaining how an image operator's resolution is resolved: the "magic" 0×0 default pulls resolution from an incoming texture if present, otherwise from the output window, and how -1 or an explicit size overrides that.

op:Lib.render.analyze.GetScreenPos.note: A tip-of-the-day walkthrough of the new [GetScreenPos] operator (TiXL 4.0.2), which converts a world-space locator into a 2D screen-space coordinate so a label or billboard can be pinned over a point in a post-processed 3D scene.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.OscillateV.note: Animate per-chain target points so the repeated limbs sway, turning a static rig into a crawling-spider motion.

op:Lib.image.use.FirstValidTexture.note: Wire it ahead of a fallback so an optional texture input degrades gracefully — it forwards the first connected/valid texture and lets a later operator substitute a default when nothing is plugged in.

op:Lib.data.object.PickObject.note: How a generic object-switch is built by duplicating a pick template as a new type: it casts the connected object to an expected interface and the consumer complains if the cast fails — flexible but unchecked, so mind the type you feed it.

op:Lib.numbers.vec2.Vector2Components.note: Split a texture-size vector and divide width by height to derive an aspect ratio, then feed that into the projection so a non-square light image isn't stretched.

op:Lib.numbers.floats.basic.FloatsToList.note: Collect four scalar parameters into a list to hand them to a shader constant buffer in one connection instead of four separate floats.

ui:ShaderNode.note: Passing a loop count as a compile-time constant lets the shader compiler unroll the loop: faster execution but longer compile, and clamp the value so a runaway sample count can't freeze the GPU.
Constant-buffer packing detail: vector4 fields must align to 16-byte boundaries, so insert float padding to keep colors from straddling register lines.

The generated effect ships as a detect-edges template with configurable settings (e.g. texture mode set to Wrap); its context menu adds typed input parameters such as a Vector2 split into floats wired to the shader's parameter buffer.

op:Lib.numbers.int.process.IntsToBuffer.note: When you need an exact integer in a shader (not inferred from a float), pack it through an int buffer so the value arrives precisely.

op:Lib.numbers.float.adjust.Clamp.note: Clamp a user-exposed sample/step count to a safe ceiling so an accidental huge value doesn't hang the graphics card.

op:Lib.numbers.int2.process.Int2Componen.note: Build an int2 render-target size from a base resolution times an aspect ratio: float→multiply→int back, then compose x and y for a separate (lower-res) shadow pass.

op:Lib.image.fx.glitch.SubdivisionStretc.note: Used to build the documentation/sample scene's text-on-render-target promo graphic.
Quick lazy way to render text to a file and stretch it for an intro card.

op:Lib.image.fx.blur.Blur.note: At large radii it artifacts unless you crank the sample count, which gets slow — reach for a Kawase-style blur instead when you need smooth falloff.

op:Lib.image.generate.pattern.ValueRaste.note: A short tip walking through the versatile Raster operator: its presets and knobs, then driving it from an input texture and stacking offset copies into a CMYK-style halftone print effect.
Draws a recursively subdividing grid raster whose line density follows image resolution and the chosen value range — the background grid the math quizzes use to plot curves precisely.

op:Lib.point.io.LineTextPoints.note: Quick improvised intro graph: text points feed line drawing, then subdivide and noise-displace the lines, with the noise animation driven off the current time.
Emits one CPU point per glyph carrying position, color and scale, so downstream point operators can transform, scatter or feed the text into a particle system.
Convert a number string to text points, orient them and place them on scattered cubes to scatter tiny readable labels across a scene as fashion-style detail.
Turn a date or title string into points you can then route through a list buffer and DrawLines, so a background caption is built from the same point pipeline as everything else.

It emits a *buffer of line points* (digit glyphs as strokes), which you push to the GPU and render with [DrawLines]; an internal optimisation that drops empty glyphs is exactly what breaks fixed-width spacing for leading-digit padding.
Drive a per-character reveal by feeding an fx attribute and sliding a value through the glyphs, e.g. animating a "characters" amount for a typewriter-style transition.
Set glyph spacing to a *negative* kerning so every digit stacks on the same spot, the prerequisite for a custom shader to then lay them out as place-value columns.

op:Lib.image.fx.distort.ChromaticDistort.note: Used as one selectable post effect keyed off a snapshot index — picking the index decides whether the distortion pass is applied to a shared texture.
Defaults run far too strong; cut the size way down (≈0.025) and reduce the colorize amount to avoid a greenish tint on edges.
Does a chromatic split but bundles it with a radial blur, so it's the wrong pick when you only want a clean per-channel RGB shift.
Cranked far past its normal range it produces a convincing crash-zoom streak; near zero it leaves the image untouched, so remap a transition curve into it for a punchy speed-ramp effect.

op:Lib.io.video.VideoClip.note: Why playback moved off Media Foundation to FFmpeg's demuxer: frame-accurate seeking and instant play without the start-of-playback frame delay that made scrubbing and tracking work unreliable.

Fast-seeking decodes on the CPU into a ~1 GB frame cache so scrubbing forward and back is smooth, while playback-performance mode uses GPU decode plus a compute-shader conversion to play many heavy 4K streams at once.

Why slow seeking is usually the encoding, not the tool: a large group-of-pictures size (default ~250 frames) forces decoding from the previous keyframe, so re-encoding with a smaller GOP makes seeking effectively free.
After the Media-Foundation removal, [PlayVideo] also runs on FFmpeg and exposes an override-time-in-seconds input so you can seek the playhead from the graph.

op:Lib.io.midi.MidiInput.note: Live MIDI/OSC input can be recorded into clips and later replayed to emulate the same named device, so a teach-enabled input downstream re-learns from the recorded events exactly as if the controller were live.

Its range output is a float list across all keys; switching the input from a single event type to a controller range (e.g. all 108 keys) lets one node expose the whole keyboard as a list you can texture and visualize.
Video device input now takes webcam input; Artnet/NDI/Spout/MIDI input ops were updated too.

Teach mode captures device name, event type, channel and control id only while the op is being evaluated (connected to an output) and a real MIDI signal arrives; the built-in damping smooths MIDI's coarse 127-step resolution, so disable it when you need a clean per-change trigger.

op:Lib.point.io.DataPointImportExport.note: Recorded input streams are plain data channels you can export as CSV, prune noisy sub-threshold samples, and quantize — cutting roughly 90% of OSC/tracking data with no visible quality loss.

op:Lib.render.utils.ConvertEquirectangle.note: Drives a 360° projection-dome setup: render an equirectangular feed, send it over Spout/NDI, and the dome's playback system maps it to the curved surface.
Disabling (not disconnecting) an unused face camera and feeding a black texture in its place, plus passing a lower resolution into the projection op, avoids an extra copy and shrinks the output feed.

op:Lib.render.transform.SliceViewPort.note: How to skip computing unused regions of the output (e.g. a letterbox or an unused dome ceiling) so the renderer never shades those pixels, instead of drawing black bars at full cost.

op:Lib.render.shading.Equirectangle.note: The cube-map path renders the scene six times then reprojects, which is why for pure raymarching it is far cheaper to change the projection matrix directly and march only the visible band.

Renders a scene to a 360° environment map by looping several cameras into viewport regions of one large texture; just plug a group in, no camera needed — inserting your own camera between transform and it scrambles the projections.

op:Lib.image.use.UseTextureReference.note: Briefly explains a shader-resource view as telling the driver to treat a block of GPU memory as a read-only texture (versus a writable UAV).
Stash a render target under a named reference so a distant part of the graph can pull the same texture without a long wire across the canvas.

op:Lib.point.transform.OrientPoints.note: Inserting a point-orientation step before drawing makes sprites face a target so they survive a non-planar projection instead of relying on the draw operator's default billboard mode.
Aiming moving-head lights is the hard part: two tilt angles with order-dependent rotation, so orient each point's gimbal at a target rather than setting angles by hand.
Constrain orientation to a single axis when debugging which axis a generator points down, otherwise three coupled axes make the result unreadable.
Orient scattered points to look toward a center, then scale to flatten them into oval/disc shards facing inward.
A wished-for "orient to camera" mode would billboard points to always face the viewer, an alternative to [DrawBillboards].
Orients points toward a center, gated by an F1 mask so only points inside a torus get reoriented; pair it with a [Vector3Gizmo] to see and move the target.
Give it a target point in space to aim every point's axis at that location, optionally interpolating the alignment gradually.
Drives real moving-head lights so they all aim at one point; combined with measured fixture positions it made seven DMX heads converge accurately in a real installation.
Aim copies at the camera (or at the cluster centre); when the result faces inward, the flip toggle reverses the orientation.
Centre-facing orientation gives each point a slightly different angle; for clean screen-aligned labels you want them parallel to the camera *view axis*, not pointed at the camera position.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawRayLines.note: Reach for it over [DrawLines] when a line can cross the camera plane (front to back): screen-space line drawing fails at that edge, so this skips corner mitering and stays seamless.
Prefer this over [DrawLines] for lines that run to infinity or past the camera: regular lines use screen space to size themselves and look wrong at extreme depths, whereas ray-lines stay consistent.

op:Lib.render.transform.Group.note: Control+Shift+D duplicates with connections, correctly handling multi-inputs, and shaking an operator out now reconnects all compatible inputs rather than just the first.
Combining several meshes under one group yields a single combined mesh you can instance as a unit; reuse the same point set twice (one per sub-mesh) to scatter the composite.
Both expose an "is enabled" toggle, giving a second way to switch a scene branch on or off independent of any switch index.
Combine several geometry branches into one node so you can judge how the shapes relate in scale and overlap.
Forces are additive, so their order in a group usually doesn't change the result (collisions/damping are the exceptions).

Both bundle a sub-network; pick [Group] when you need transform plus fade-in/out, pick [Execute] when you only want enable/disable or to merge inputs — it's lighter because it carries no transform parameters.

op:Lib.io.dmx.PointsToDmxLights.note: Treats each point as one fixture, mapping its position/orientation/color onto channel slots per the fixture's spec; set the fixture's channel count so a color lands on the right three channels.

op:Lib.numbers.float.basic.Multiply.note: For spin, feed noise into rotation and multiply its ±1 range up to 360°; lower frequency for slower turns and reduce octaves so the rotation holds a steady speed instead of jittering.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetPointLight.note: Raising decay shrinks the lit area and intensity brightens it; recolor the light for mood — useful for an emissive object that should cast its own colored glow.
Drive a light's position from the same locator that moves its host object so the light tracks the object exactly.
Push intensity up and decay down together to make a colored light reach further across the scene.
The lower-level light operator PointLight builds on; usable directly but lacks the gizmo, and its position feeds the now-fixed specular computation.

op:Lib.render.shading.TextureToCubeMap.note: Always convert an environment image into a cube map before feeding it as the lighting environment — skipping this step can crash the app.

ui:AudioInput.note: Tap a beat then let auto beat-locking continuously nudge BPM and phase toward detected snares/kicks, so a VJ no longer has to keep tapping; press the resync key on a measure to relock if it drifts.

Why multi-stem audio is hard: audio runs on its own thread at the sound card's sample rate, fully decoupled from the frame loop, with re-seek jitter that must stay inside a ~40ms window or it stutters — far less forgiving than dropped video frames.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.AnimBoolea.note: A tidier on-beat trigger than wiring AnimValue by hand; drive it from the kick and feed its pulse into downstream animation. Internally identical to AnimValue but readable in the graph.
A flashing boolean wired into a particle system's emit makes particles fire on a beat or event.
Set max-particle-count to -1 to size the buffer to the emit set, then emit only on a beat boolean to spawn a fixed batch and keep it alive indefinitely.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.AnimInt.note: Same internals as AnimBoolean's counter but without the on-beat UI; the request raised here is to give it a modulo wrap and a speed factor so it counts within a range and loops.
A stepped integer animation with a deliberately odd weight/offset used to ride a polyrhythmic groove and gate when a counter advances.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.vj.SetSpeedFactors.note: Pin it at the start of a chain to override the global time factors A and B; map a MIDI knob to a factor and everything time-driven downstream speeds up or slows together for live tempo ramps and breakdowns.

op:Lib.io.input.KeyboardInputAsInt.note: Mapping number-row keys to an integer and feeding that into the time factors lets you punch a speed multiplier live with the keyboard during a set.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.vj.ForwardBeatTaps.note: Forwards externally-tapped beats (e.g. an OSC tap from an iPad, or an Ableton click track sending one pulse per beat) into the beat system so someone else can tap for you.

Tap-to-beat sync that, once locked, keeps surfing the BPM by ±0.5 to follow a DJ slowing down — giving one continuous never-jumping bar-progress value you can route into any animation; enable beat detection to also place kick/snare/hi-hat onsets.

op:Lib.numbers.floats.io.PlaybackFFT.note: Feed the playback FFT into a texture history to scroll the spectrogram over time; the basis for sliding-window beat detection that compares each beat's pattern to the previous.
FFT/audio-reaction read the global merged output buffer (the same master buffer written when exporting a video), which is why per-stem reactions aren't possible today without per-channel routing.

op:Lib.render.transform.SpreadLayout.note: Spreads connected inputs evenly in space, auto-spacing more steps as you add more connections — handy for laying out parallel test setups side by side.

op:Lib.numbers.bool.process.DelayTrigger.note: Holds a one-frame trigger open for a set duration so a particle emitter fires across several frames instead of one; also debounces rapid double-triggers down to a single emission.

op:Lib.numbers.bool.process.DelayBoolean.note: Distinct from DelayTriggerChange: it delays a boolean by a number of frames rather than holding a trigger open, useful for staggering events.

op:Lib.flow.context.SetFloatVar.note: Place it first inside an Execute, name the variable, and share one value across many effects; hovering shows highlighted lines to every reader of that variable.

Name a variable once, then read it back anywhere with the matching getter so one source (a noise, a MIDI value, a master volume) drives many places; the setter only exists where its subgraph runs, so wire it under an [Execute] pinned first to guarantee it evaluates before its readers.

op:Lib.flow.context.GetFloatVar.note: Reads a named float set elsewhere with auto-completion from context, letting you reuse one driving value (e.g. an intensity) anywhere in a large project.

Name a variable once, then read it back anywhere with the matching getter so one source (a noise, a MIDI value, a master volume) drives many places; the setter only exists where its subgraph runs, so wire it under an [Execute] pinned first to guarantee it evaluates before its readers.

op:Lib.field.combine.CombineFieldColor.note: Reached for to mix a field with a FractalNoise field; the maintainer notes this slot expects a color/factor, not arbitrary fields, so use it deliberately.
Stack two color fields and combine them as a proper multiply (not an alpha crossfade) to layer gradients for a scrolling color-cycle look.

op:Lib.point.generate.PointsOnImage.note: Seed point positions from an image (or a PlayVideo frame), turning any texture or moving effect into a point field for downstream selection and drawing.
Turns an image (e.g. an edge-detected texture) into a fresh point cloud, closing a CPU→GPU→texture→points loop for layered generative passes.
Reuse the scene camera to render just the moving elements to a separate target, then scatter points where those bright pixels are to pin HUD tracker sprites that follow objects across the screen.
Pairing an edge detector with a points-on-image scatter as a quick generative starting point when you want points seeded from image features.

The wish-list pattern it should grow into: take a depth buffer plus a camera reference and place each scattered point at its reconstructed world position, instead of rebuilding that by hand in a [CustomPointShader] every time.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawConnectionLines.note: Vertically-stacked operators fall back to a spline connection that can't be hovered or disconnected; this top-down wiring case is unfinished, which is why some wires won't detach.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.MeshFacesPoints.note: Re-implemented onto the new colored-point format with FX scale/stretch; a new option scales each point sprite by its polygon face area (computed trivially from the face's three vertices), great for spikes or cylinders that grow with face size.
Cleaned up with new examples; [RadialPoints] also gains a color parameter.
One point per face stays put under deformation, unlike area-weighted surface scatter that redistributes when the geometry moves.

op:Lib.point.io.LoadSvg.note: Loads SVG paths but doesn't close loops or fill, and the underlying standard is huge — treat it as line data, animate its UV/transition-progress, and expect to export SVGs cleanly rather than relying on full coverage.

op:Lib.flow.Execute.note: Use it over a Group when you only need to update/draw side-effects (set variables, run OSC output) with no data output — slightly faster since it skips the Group's transform/color overhead.
Both expose an "is enabled" toggle, giving a second way to switch a scene branch on or off independent of any switch index.

Both bundle a sub-network; pick [Group] when you need transform plus fade-in/out, pick [Execute] when you only want enable/disable or to merge inputs — it's lighter because it carries no transform parameters.

op:Lib.image.use.SwapTextures.note: An execute-then-pass-through texture operator (an "update before output" workaround) that runs side effects first and then outputs an already-rendered buffer without re-rendering it.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.TransformMeshUVs.note: Its pivot is now centered so scaling grows from the middle; this is a breaking change from the old corner pivot, so older projects may shift.

op:Lib.field.use.SdfToVector.note: Returns a position in space near an SDF surface (computed from the field normal) so you can turn a distance field into a directional/vector field for forces.

op:Lib.particle.force.VectorFieldForce.note: Drives particles along a field's computed normals; pair with TransformField to reorient the field's vectors, not just its space.

Turn an SDF surface into a directional field and use it as a vector force so particles accelerate along the surface normal; invert the amount and the shape becomes an attractor you can drag through the cloud.
The shader graph now carries vector fields, and this force steers particles along one (SDF-to-Vector samples the distance-field gradient to generate it).

op:Lib.numbers.color.BuildGradient.note: Builds a gradient procedurally from a color list plus an overridable position list — feed a PlaybackFFT (or any float list) into the positions to make an audio-reactive gradient for displacement and color.
Turns a new color-list type into a gradient, with an optional float list to place the steps.
Feeds on a recorded color list to assemble a live gradient from sampled colors.

op:Lib.io.video.SpoutOutput.note: Needs B8G8R8A8 format, so a ConvertFormat sits in front today; the request is to have it auto-convert internally via a compute shader like PlayVideo does.

op:Lib.io.video.SpoutInput.note: Round-trips frames out to a host like NestDrop and back, letting you borrow that host's effect library and recompose the result in TiXL.

op:Lib.image.fx.stylize.FakeLight.note: Cheap fake relighting of a 2D image stands in for full PBR; the host's wishlist (normal map + environment texture + bloom) marks the line between this quick effect and a real HDR relight.

op:Lib.image.color.KeyColor.note: Pick a target color (e.g. a skin tone) to key it out; turn up the amount and switch its output to return just the mask rather than the keyed image.
Re-keying and nudging exposure up cleans the mask before blending it onward.

op:Lib.image.fx.blur.DirectionalBlur.note: Smears the image along an angle like Photoshop's motion blur, but its angle/strength can be driven per-pixel by a second texture, so feeding the image back into itself warps the smear into swirling distortion.
A refinement-pass count smooths the result, and the blur angle is the knob you animate to morph between the warped look and the untouched original.
Layered over a title so the un-blurred original stays readable underneath, it reads almost like motion blur; driving its amount with a very slow animated value gives a gentle drifting smear.
Streaks an image along a chosen direction by a set sample count; useful as a building block when faking per-channel RGB smear effects.

op:Lib.field.space.RotateAxis.note: Rotating an SDF with a dedicated axis-rotate is cheaper than wrapping it in a full transform, which is slower for SDF stacks.

op:Lib.string.convert.FloatToString.note: Read the current playback time, stringify it, and route it into a text operator to build an on-screen time readout.

op:Lib.mesh.draw.DrawMeshUnlit.note: A 90s-era cloud cheat: render fractal noise unlit to a texture, map transparent-white→white, and stack many offset planes via repeat-at-points to fake volumetric mist.

op:Lib.numbers.color.DefineGradient.note: Break a gradient out of an operator to reuse its exact definition elsewhere; blending two gradients exists but crossfades alpha, which looks poor for hard color cycling.

op:Lib.numbers.color.BlendGradients.note: Break a gradient out of an operator to reuse its exact definition elsewhere; blending two gradients exists but crossfades alpha, which looks poor for hard color cycling.

op:Lib.field.space.RepeatField3.note: Cycling a color band by animating a push-pull offset only sweeps once; repeating the field to loop it must happen before the push-pull, or the repeat has no effect.

op:Lib.image.color.ColorGradeDepth.note: Feeds the depth buffer alongside the image so a gradient grades by distance — e.g. tinting the background cooler — for subtle, very effective atmospheric depth cueing.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.ExtrudeCurves.note: For shaded lines, extruding a curve into a mesh is the expensive route; draw-ribbons is the lighter option but is flagged as currently unreliable, with spin/pin parameters affecting the result.

When you add an input parameter (here a scale factor that varies line thickness) you must triple-check it's actually wired to its [IntToFloat]/conversion node — an easy-to-miss disconnect after a version update.
Its generated UVs don't close perfectly around a swept loop, leaving a visible seam; check with [VisualizeUvMap], it's a near one-off in the number of curves going around.

op:Lib.io.midi.MidiClip.note: A MIDI clip auto-detects its own length from the file; pull a named note (e.g. an A5 channel) out of it with select-float-from-dict to get that note's value over time.

op:Lib.numbers.data.utils.SelectFloatFro.note: A MIDI clip auto-detects its own length from the file; pull a named note (e.g. an A5 channel) out of it with select-float-from-dict to get that note's value over time.

op:Lib.numbers.float.logic.HasValueChang.note: Turn a MIDI note value into hit triggers (detect increases only) to fire a trigger-animation per note; a sliding-history buffer can plot the activity over time.

op:Lib.image.generate.misc.SlidingHistor.note: Turn a MIDI note value into hit triggers (detect increases only) to fire a trigger-animation per note; a sliding-history buffer can plot the activity over time.
Build a scrolling spectrogram waterfall from audio, then crop/amplify/stretch it to drive an audio-reactive displacement of the image.
Stacking FFT frames into a scrolling history texture is how onset/snare hits become visible as vertical streaks over time.

op:Lib.io.video.PlayAudioClip.note: Drives playback from a Time input, but you must set its time unit to seconds or it sounds wrong; multiple clips with offsets can fake a delay/echo layering.

op:Lib.field.adjust.InvertSDF.note: Inverts a field's inside/outside, the quick way to turn a solid into a cavity.

op:Lib.mesh.generate.IcosahedronMesh.note: A new icosahedron primitive with many parameters and examples.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.utils.SetKeyframes.note: New operators that generate keyframe tracks procedurally, for consistent timeline-driven animation.

op:Lib.image.analyze.RemoveStaticBackgro.note: Trains a per-pixel statistical model of the empty scene, then outputs only what differs — its debug range visualizes the difference, and a darker-only suppression mode lets you key people in front of a projector without feedback. Disable the camera's auto-exposure first or the model drifts.

op:Lib.point.modify.SamplePointsByCamera.note: Sorts a point buffer back-to-front by distance to the active camera so transparent sprites composite correctly; needs a bitonic-style multi-pass (≈70 passes for 200k points) but unlocks correct alpha for huge particle counts.
Drive per-instance point size by distance to the camera so sprites shrink and fade into the background as you orbit, giving cheap depth cueing.

op:Lib.numbers.float.process.EaseKeys.note: Eases between keyframes placed directly on this operator (Shift+C to add) — it ignores interpolated values arriving through a connection, so keyframe it in place rather than feeding an animated input.

Pick the curve via the interpolation dropdown (quadratic, exponential, elastic…); the transition duration comes purely from the spacing between keyframes, not a separate speed knob, and a Constant key is the one type left un-eased.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.Warp2dMesh.note: A four-corner bilinear warp, not a true perspective homography, so a flat image projected onto a surface won't line up from corners alone; add interior control points (e.g. via [BlendPoints] for edge centers) to bend it into place.

op:Lib.numbers.color.KeepColors.note: Continuously appends the incoming color into a fixed-length list each frame; drive its input from an [HSLToColor] over time to record a moving hue into a list you can then turn into a gradient or sample randomly.

op:Lib.image.use.KeepInTextureArray.note: Records each frame's texture into a growing array (size must be pre-initialized since textures can't resize in place) and exposes both a single read-indexed slice and the whole array buffer — scrub the read index for a manual history, or feed the array out for time-based effects. GPU-heavy at large counts.

op:Lib.image.fx.distort.TimeDisplace.note: Looks up a frame from a recorded history array by a per-pixel displacement map, smearing motion across time like a slit-scan; note it already contains its own [KeepInTextureArray] internally, so feed it raw video, not a pre-recorded array, and keep the displacement amount large since it counts in frames.

op:Lib.image.transform.ImageFFT.note: Use this rather than the small built-in spectrum when you need a higher-resolution FFT: allocate a bigger buffer and you can analyze finer frequency detail.

op:Lib.image.transform.MakeTileableImage.note: A new tileable noise source used as the input texture being recorded into a history array.
Run a noise through it (plus a [NormalMap]) to get a seamless wrap for an endless tunnel — but a one-off gap appears if the UVs don't span a full loop, often from the curve/extrude not closing.

op:Lib.image.color.HSE.note: A color-space remap that needs the points to already carry color before it has anything to act on; give them color first.

op:Lib.point.transform.IkChain.note: A GPU FABRIK solver (after Aristidou): feed it a bone chain plus target points and you must raise the per-target Influence above zero, or nothing bends.
A hard cap on total chain points lives in the solver for the whole buffer, not per chain, to keep an unrolled shader loop from crashing; the angle constraint controls how far each joint may bend.
Repeat a multi-point line chain to spawn many legs at once; the chain reuses the point scale on one axis as segment length, so legs visibly stretch when you scale.

ui:SymbolBrowser.note: Live thumbnails now render for every operator and its siblings in the browser, so you can eyeball what an op produces before placing it.
Many operators ship without example projects; a good op deserves a browsable example so users can open and inspect a working wiring rather than guessing.

Tab over a single selected operator inserts the new op inline into the connection; suggestions are now ranked by statistical usage, so common follow-ups (e.g. what people typically place between two ops) float to the top.
Dragging out from a parameter offers ops that drive that value; pressing Space after picking an animation op lets you search its presets (e.g. a wave shape to modulate a value).

Select several operators, drag out one connection group, and the browser lists every op with a matching multi-input so you can fan many sources into one; press G afterward to auto-layout the new group.

Long-press the canvas to open the operator browser and search by synonym — typing "LFO" finds the oscillator value op even though that's not its name; report missing synonyms so the description can be extended.

op:Lib.point.draw.VisualizePoints.note: Drop it in to see point index order and orientation axes when a layout behaves unexpectedly (e.g. points running counter-clockwise).
Renders each point's index and local axes, letting you read emission order and per-particle orientation to debug why a particle setup looks twisted.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.SplitMeshVertices.note: Separate shared vertices so a low-poly mesh renders with hard flat shading instead of smooth normals.

op:Lib.numbers.int.logic.HasIntChanged.note: Returns true only when a value differs from the previous frame, so it reads always-false on a paused/non-animating graph — re-enable playback to test it.

Build a "trigger keyframe" you don't have natively: step an animated value up with Shift+C per key, floor it to an int, and feed change-detection into a one-shot animation so each step fires an event.

op:Lib.image.transform.Crop.note: Pad a wide image with empty side margins to coerce it into the portrait aspect a vectorscope needs.
Beyond trimming, negative values pad an image with empty pixels — the trick for adding a transparent border so an edge-to-edge logo has room for a clean glow.

op:Lib.point.transform.SoftTransformPoin.note: Applies a transform only inside a falloff volume, so points caught in the middle get squeezed toward center while outer ones stay — great for zoomed-into-the-core streak looks.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.AnimVec3.note: Animate only the Y component with a slow sine to bob an emitter/center point up and down without touching the other axes.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.CustomVertexShader.note: Custom point/vertex/SDF shaders are "only as good as their presets"; shipping gradient-driven presets is what made the [CustomSDF] ecosystem take off.

op:Lib.render.gizmo.PlotValueCurve.note: Drop it on top of a group to graph a scalar over time inside the rendered scene — invaluable for debugging exported executables where you can't just open an extra output window.

op:Lib.numbers.floats.process.ValuesToTe.note: A redo of the bake-list-into-texture op with a clear input-range / clamp / gain-bias / output-range pipeline; use the input range to stretch a tiny value spread (e.g. 0.0–0.003) into a visible, usable texture.

op:Lib.numbers.floats.process.KeepFloatV.note: Accumulates successive scalar samples into a growing list you can then bake to a texture and visualize as a history.

op:Lib.numbers.floats.process.AnalyzeFlo.note: Feeds the quiz curve plotter: it derives the min/max range of a float list, padded a little, so the same range scales both the raster and the drawn curve consistently.

op:Lib.point.draw.DrawMovingPoints.note: Draws emitted particles with motion so the flying points read as streaks rather than static dots.

Stretches each point along its motion into a pill, giving a cheap motion-blur look; the stretch responds to camera rotation too, so even static [GridPoints] streak when you orbit. Only marginally slower than plain point drawing.

Because it reads last-frame position from a double buffer (not particle age), a freshly emitted point can inherit a stale slot and shoot a wrong streak; clamp this with the velocity-jump threshold so jumps beyond ~1 unit/frame aren't stretched.

Stretching a point's UVs compresses texels toward the edges, which trips the sampler into a blurry mipmap and leaves grey-pixel artifacts; it works around this by sampling a fixed mip level (slower) and shipping a low-res fallback texture instead of mipmaps.

Stretches point billboards in screen space along velocity using camera motion; an option to ignore camera delta is needed for effects (e.g. swimming fish) since billboards must stay screen-facing to avoid zero-width edges.
Stretches points by their frame-to-frame motion (a screen-space effect), even pronounced on stationary points; the maintainers debate renaming it "motion stretch points" since nothing actually moves.

op:Lib.point.generate.MeshVerticesToPoin.note: A mesh is an index buffer plus a vertex buffer; converting its vertices to points (and visualizing them) reveals that hard corners duplicate vertices because they can't share a normal across edges.
Swap a generated point set for a loaded mesh's vertices to drive a per-point shader over real geometry.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.SelectVertices.note: Exists for meshes but its selection semantics differ from the point F1/F2 model, which is why an F1/F2-style mesh selector that points could inherit is still wished-for.

op:Lib.numbers.float.process.SmoothStep.note: Smooth cubic interpolation can overshoot below or above the neighbouring key values; reach for a clamped mode instead when a value like opacity must never dip past its keyframes.

op:Lib.numbers.float.adjust.Floor.note: Convert a smoothly animated value into discrete steps by flooring it (or float-to-int and back), so a linear ramp becomes a staircase that advances exactly once per integer.

ui:IoView.note: IO recording captures live MIDI/OSC line-input as a data clip of timed events; the point is replaying a recorded live set in the studio to craft visuals against real performance data, not audio production.

op:Lib.io.midi.MidiRecording.note: A recorded data clip stores per-channel trigger and interval events (MIDI notes, OSC) that can be replayed as simulated device input, so the graph reacts as if the controller were live.

op:Lib.point.combine.PickPointList.note: Use a picker as a manual bypass: feed both the original and the processed point set in and select between them by index, so index 0 is the untouched version and 1 is the effected one.

op:Lib.render.camera.BlendCameras.note: Switch between several cameras (animated, static A, static B) by index to cut or fade a scene's viewpoint; an unselected camera stops being updated.

Camera interpolation feels wonky because position and target are blended separately; converting rotation to a quaternion and blending that (then inferring the target) would interpolate far more smoothly.

op:Lib.point.sim.SimDirectionalOffset.note: Why the old per-force sim operators were abandoned: hard to control and confusing to wire, which is what motivated the unified particle system; this one survives, to be renamed to a "damp points" role.

op:Lib.point.sim.experimental.SimFollowM.note: Why the old per-force sim operators were abandoned: hard to control and confusing to wire, which is what motivated the unified particle system; this one survives, to be renamed to a "damp points" role.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.animators.SequenceAn.note: A text-digit pattern sequencer (each line a pattern, digits subdivide the bar) usable like a MIDI step sequencer; its index can itself be driven by another instance for nested musical patterns.
Its "hits" recording mode plus a [BoolToFloat] lets you tap a beat live from a MIDI button to record rhythmic values into the pattern.
Never drive max-particle-count from a per-frame-changing value: reallocating a large GPU buffer every frame fragments VRAM and can crash; only change buffer size in coarse steps.
Its "set sequential values" fills selected keys with a counting series; start-at and a jump-to-value entry let you begin the run at an arbitrary number like 16.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.time.HasTimeChanged.note: Its rewind-detect output wired to a reset clears a simulation every time you scrub time back, so tweaking an effect always restarts from a clean state.

op:Lib.numbers.bool.combine.Any.note: Combine several boolean reset triggers (rewind, fade event, button) so a simulation resets if any of them fire.

op:Lib.particle.force.CollisionForce.note: Uses nearest-neighbor search to repel (and optionally attract) particles from each other; pairs well with damping and a field volume force, and gets expensive when many particles clump.

op:Lib.field.space.RepeatFieldAtPoints.note: Building a field by repeating an SDF at particle positions works but is costly, so it's capped (~50 repetitions).

op:Lib.field.use.RaymarchPoints.note: Shoots a ray along each point's Z into an SDF and returns the hit (a per-point laser/raycast), but is still research-grade: its max-reflection-count parameter has an index bug that corrupts results with multiple points.

op:Lib.particle.force.FollowMeshSurfaceF.note: Keeps particles crawling across a mesh surface (emit once with buffer -1); add a point trail to draw twirly lines following the surface, balancing against turbulence that would pull them off.
The closest existing force to "guide particles along a mesh," but it lacks the amount/attraction/decay inside-vs-outside controls a field-volume force gives.

op:Lib.particle.force.SwitchParticleForc.note: Switch between alternate forces over an animation; note its -1 "disable all" magic index is why it's a switch, not a pick — flagged to be renamed to a pick-style operator.

op:Lib.particle.force.VolumeForce.note: The pre-fields predecessor of [FieldVolumeForce] with only a few hardcoded inflexible SDF shapes; kept mainly as a comparison of how much fields improved things.

op:Lib.point.usse.KeepPreviousPointBuffe.note: The double-buffer operator behind frame-to-frame velocity: it ping-pongs two buffers so each point's previous position is looked up by ID, which is what any per-point motion effect needs.

Returns last frame's point buffer (done in C# to avoid fiddly toggle-buffer patching); pair current and previous points into lines to visualize per-point motion, with a keep toggle to snapshot on demand.
Hold last frame's point buffer so you can difference positions to get per-point velocity — the basis for velocity-driven scaling and fake motion stretch.

op:Lib.point.generate.CommonPointSets.note: Provides corner point sets (cube/cross/quad) for repeating geometry or drawing wireframe cages; build a grid by combining offset line points and rotating a copy 90°.

op:Lib.render.utils.DrawAsSplitView.note: Wraps a reusable strand sub-operator twice in a split view to compare instances; same op type, different instance, each deterministic so isolated strands match across views when randomization happens after combining.

op:Lib.particle.force.MeshVolumeForce.note: Pipe any point set into a [ParticleSystem], add this as a force and give it a mesh to collide against; mark its mesh input as required so a missing-input warning shows. Draw the particles before the solid mesh (set draw order so particles write depth first) or they vanish inside it.

Attraction pulls outside particles toward the nearest forward-facing face; repulsion only acts once a particle is detected inside the volume; zero attraction leaves particles untouched. Reflection bounces them off the surface before they enter.

Bounciness below 1 drains energy each bounce, above 1 injects it (things go wild); randomized bounciness and orientation-angle fake a rough surface; moving the collider mesh shoves particles inside and pumps energy into the system.
Inverting the volume flips repulsion so particles are driven to stay *inside* the shape, filling and bouncing within it — handy for trapping a swarm in a box.

Cost scales with face count, not particle count, because it brute-forces the nearest triangle with no acceleration structure — a few hundred faces is the practical ceiling; use invisible low-poly proxy meshes for heavy geometry.
When a force-heavy swarm keeps gaining speed, raise the drag (or drop bounciness) to bleed off the energy that additive forces keep injecting — the go-to fix for an uncontrollable particle system.
A brute-force-over-triangles approach is very slow on complex meshes and doesn't cleanly answer inside-vs-outside, which is why an SDF or depth-buffer approach is preferred.

op:Lib.field.space.Translate.note: Insert it above a field's source to shift the collision volume; copy its values and paste straight onto a matching-name input, which transfers the whole transform at once.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.DeformMesh.note: Animate a twist on the collider mesh (it even exposes a twist pivot and gizmo) so particles crawling its surface get shaken around — a way to drive motion from collider deformation rather than real mesh velocity.

op:Lib.io.file.FilesInFolder.note: Procedurally driving a texture path (e.g. picking a string from its list) disposes and reloads the texture every change, spiking GPU memory; enable "cache resources" so repeatedly visited textures stay resident — the right call for VJ-style scrubbing, overkill otherwise.

op:Lib.render.shading.SetShadow.note: The only thing approaching a directional/spotlight in TiXL, but it gives no brightness or color control; for fake screen-lighting you're better off placing plain point lights, since the PBR lights lack a true directional option.

A two-pass shadow setup: pass one builds a depth map by rendering the scene from the light's position as a camera, pass two puts that shadow texture into the context so the geometry, drawn again, can test against it.

op:Lib.field.generate.sdf.Image2dSDF.note: Builds a signed-distance field from a texture's grayscale, the entry point when you want an image (e.g. a screen's content) to define a shape or mask in field space.

op:Lib.numbers.color.PickColorFromImage.note: Sample an average screen color by enabling mipmaps and reading the smallest level — a cheap way to drive a fake light's tint from whatever a texture is showing.

op:Lib.field.use.SdfReflectionLinePoints.note: Ray-marches lines through an SDF and reflects them off the surface; raise max-reflections for repeated bounces, and beware it's literal ray-marching — a low step count degenerates, and normal-sampling distance must be tuned to avoid jitter on rough fields.

op:Lib.point.transform.ReorientLinePoint.note: Reorients points to face the next one along a chain, the building block for turning a line of points into an oriented camera/spline path before blending.

op:Lib.numbers.vec3.DampVec3.note: Bind several [LinePoints] camera paths to number-pad keys and damp the switch, so hitting a key smoothly eases the camera between dynamic procedural paths during a live set.
Smooths the jumps between per-step random camera positions so the scene-to-scene transition eases instead of snapping.

op:Lib.render.sprite.TextSprites.note: Characters of a string rendered into viewport cells to assemble a procedural atlas texture for billboard sprites.

op:Lib.image.fx.distort.BubbleZoom.note: A flip/inversion parameter is redundant once the magnification factor can go negative; reach for one or the other, not both, to invert the lens.
The edge/feather width controls how soft the lens rim is (0 = hard cut), while radius sets the inner magnified disc — pair a feather with its gradient so the two read as related.
Feed it a gradient that runs transparent→white→transparent and the magnifier becomes a free soft-edged bubble; tint the first gradient stop opaque to fill the lens with color.
Its magnification shifts the UVs relative to the center, so zoom is not anchored to the lens center — a shader-side fix to keep it centered.

op:Lib.image.fx.feedback.FluidFeedback.note: Always pin it to a fixed resolution: as a pixel-space effect its look changes wildly between 2K and 4K, so feedback amount and displacement that were tuned at one size break at another.

op:Lib.mesh.draw.DrawMeshWithShadow.note: Drop any mesh into the shadowed group and it casts and receives consistently because it checks whether the current pass is the shadow pass: on the shadow pass it just writes depth, otherwise it samples the shadow map from the context.

Operators that merely draw depth get shadows "for free" without shadow-pass-specific code, but they still run their full fragment shader on the depth pass — wasteful, since the depth map needs no shading or normals.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.FlipNormals.note: It flips the shading normals but does NOT reverse the triangle winding, so back-face culling still drops the same faces — unlike Blender's flip, so it won't single-handedly make an inside-out mesh render solid.

op:Lib.mesh.modify.CombineMeshes.note: A poor-man's solidify: combine a mesh with a normal-flipped copy of itself so both sides render — though here it exposes that [FlipNormals] doesn't flip winding, so the trick stalls.

op:Lib.numbers.float.process.RemapValues.note: Reshape an animation ramp into a steep ease by lowering its bias/gain, then map its 0–1 range onto a camera field-of-view to zoom in then blow out wide.

op:Lib.io.dmx.DmxOutput.note: Controlled seven moving heads over DMX/ArtNet in a live installation; per-fixture calibration to the centimeter was needed for the aiming to line up.

op:Lib.render.camera.CamPosition.note: Extract the active camera out of the render flow with a camera-reuse node so a [CamPosition] read gives you the eye position to orient billboard-style points toward — note it must be evaluated (grouped/executed) before the points that consume it.
A camera read placed after the camera in execution order creates a loop; reuse the camera (or read its position) at a point that evaluates *before* the points you orient, then orient before drawing.

op:Lib.numbers.anim.vj.GetBpm.note: How beat-locking works: enable "log profile beat syncing" in settings, tap with the V key, and it estimates the best BPM from detected bass transients — robust enough to track a DJ drifting the tempo over time.

Resync locks onto a bar's transient and *holds* the lock so it won't drift; but raw FFT bands are too noisy to reliably tell a snare from a hi-hat, so it solves *timing* rather than classifying drum hits.

op:Lib.flow.context.SetIntVar.note: Publish a computed value (here a count-down index) as a named variable read elsewhere, avoiding a tangle of long connection wires across a complex graph.

op:Lib.flow.context.GetIntVar.note: Publish a computed value (here a count-down index) as a named variable read elsewhere, avoiding a tangle of long connection wires across a complex graph.

op:Lib.string.convert.IntToString.note: Convert the published counter to text to drop a debug readout into the scene.

op:Lib.particle.force.FieldDistanceForce.note: A good source to copy its normal-from-field helper: it samples distance at small offsets to reconstruct the gradient/normal, reusable in a custom point shader.

op:Lib.image.generate.pattern.Rings.note: A short tip tour of the [Rings] operator, walking every parameter that shapes its concentric-ring pattern and pointing out which ones reward animation.
